#3458. 10 Best Western Movie Gunfights Of All Time, Ranked

While Westerns boast breathtakingly rustic vistas and memorably rugged main characters, chances are, we're there to see some sharpshooting gunplay. Many Western movies that everyone should watch at least once are anchored by a riveting action set piece between frontier gunfighters. These sequences range from drawn-out battles throughout harsh landscapes and dusty towns to quick-draw showdowns over in a single burst of gunfire. We're looking back at personal favorite gunfights in the history of Western movies, each earning a spot in cinematic history.

Silver screen legends like John Wayne and Clint Eastwood immortalized themselves through the gunfight scenes in Westerns they starred in. In many cases, the single most iconic scene in a given Western is its gunslinging action sequence. After all, the Wild West archetype is one revolving around its laconic gunfighters, not its bucolic communities on the fringes of civilization.

With those qualities in mind, these are the best Western movie gunfights of all time ranked, epitomizing the genre's gunslinging appeal.

So much of the classic 1953 Western "Shane" is the build-up to its titular protagonist finally showing everyone what he's got. Played by Alan Ladd, the character is a drifter with a mysterious past who comes to work on a farm on the frontier. When these homesteads are targeted by an unscrupulous land baron, Shane's lethal skills quickly come in handy. This comes to a quick-draw climax as Shane kills the murderous crook along with his sadistic hired gun Jack Wilson (Jack Palance), though Shane himself is wounded.

Ladd's Shane is the ultimate gunslinger archetype, though he really only gets one gunfight in the entire movie. Fortunately, "Shane" makes this sequence count, with this violent inevitability expertly staged and crafted. To heighten the mood, much of this climax is filmed in a shadowy saloon as Shane overcomes the obvious trap that he knowingly walks into. Fans still debate over 70 years later if Shane survived this gunfight, which is a testament to how memorable the sequence and its ambiguous aftermath are.

Even though it became a Western that flopped at the box office, the 2007 remake of "3:10 to Yuma" does its 1957 predecessor proud. That said, the difference between the two movies are most acutely felt in how they each end. The 2007 remake features farmer Dan Evans (Christian Bale) escorting outlaw Ben Wade (Russell Crowe) to a train station, with Ben begrudgingly going along for the last run. What follows is a running gunfight against those trying to stop Dan, who still finds the time to convince Ben to cooperate.

The last few minutes of the "3:10 to Yuma" remake are its most exciting, while filmmaker James Mangold still delivers on its main character arcs. Any sense of triumph is quickly undercut by the movie's tragic conclusion, differentiating it from both its short story source material and the 1957 film. The movie handles that fake-out marvelously while not mitigating the excitement that came before during this desperate run. Easily one of the greatest Western movies of the 2000s, "3:10 to Yuma" saves its best for last.

For as breezy as the overall movie is, the most well-known scenes in "Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid" are its most relentlessly intense. Though the duo being pursued by a posse across the Wild West for their train robberies stands out, the movie's ending is arguably its most famous sequence. Having relocated to Bolivia to resume their criminal activities, Butch (Paul Newman) and the Sundance Kid (Robert Redford) are ambushed by the authorities and take shelter in a nearby building. Charging outside, Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid go out in a blaze of glory, with the movie ending on a freeze-frame as the pair are gunned down.

The alternate ending of "Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid" thankfully wasn't used, which would've actually shown its likable duo gruesomely killed. Instead, the scene leaves the carnage to the audience's imagination, rather than treading the same territory as the ending of "Bonnie & Clyde." That freeze-frame approach works well for the overall movie, giving the story its inevitable ending but without dwelling on the violence, staying in line with its general tone. The only gunfight on this list which doesn't show its decisive salvo on-screen, "Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid" focuses on its title characters' legend rather than its tragedy.

John Wayne led a lot of different Western movie gunfights, from classic quick-draws in "The War Wagon" to shadowy shootings in "The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance." But the Wayne-starring gunfight that stands out from the rest of his work is his climactic confrontation in "True Grit." Wayne plays U.S. Marshal Rooster Cogburn in the 1969 movie, finally catching up with a crew of outlaws he had been pursuing for the entire film. After being insulted by the gang's leader Ned Pepper (Robert Duvall), an incensed Cogburn charges them alone with a gun in each hand and his horse's reins in his teeth.

John Wayne considered "True Grit" to be his first decent role in 20 years, and his one-man charge cements his character's place in his legacy. The action sequence isn't just the movie at its most rousing, and it shows a more ornery side to Wayne's usual frontier archetype. Expertly twirling his rifle in one hand to chamber a new round, just as he did in "Stagecoach" three decades prior, Wayne hasn't lost a step. Putting a furiously gun-toting Wayne back in the saddle, "True Grit" proved this old dog still had some new tricks.

Over a decade later, "Django Unchained" is still Quentin Tarantino's biggest movie, at least from a commercial standpoint. The final act of the 2012 movie takes place in Candyland, a notoriously brutal plantation run by the cruel slave owner Calvin Candie (Leonardo DiCaprio). Subjected by Calvin's nightmarish hospitality in an effort to rescue Brunhilda (Kerry Washington), the enslaved wife of Django (Jamie Foxx), King Schultz (Christoph Waltz) kills Calvin. This kickstarts a particularly blood-soaked gunfight, as Schultz is killed and Django battles gunmen around the plantation, until he is eventually forced to surrender.

The sanguine shootout may not be the final showdown in "Django Unchained," but it's a scene that we wish would never end. After the smug cruelty that Django and Schultz endure in Candyland, the action sequence feels like a cathartic release as Django exacts comeuppance on his hosts. To heighten the effusive enjoyment of the scene, Tarantino uses "Unchained (The Payback/Untouchable)" by James Brown and Tupac, while making every bullet hit like an artillery shell. The best gunfight that Tarantino has filmed to date, "Django Unchained" has its titular hero bring bloody retribution to its main villain's antebellum lair.

For much of "Unforgiven," the violent backstory of outlaw Will Munny (Clint Eastwood) was only hinted at, with Munny himself focused on being a farmer and single father. After learning that his old friend Ned Logan (Morgan Freeman) was murdered by the sadistic sheriff Little Bill Daggett (Gene Hackman), with his body mockingly displayed, Munny's lethal demeanor resurfaces. Storming into Little Bill's saloon, Munny shoots him and several of his associates, maintaining a clear-eyed, if furious, focus. After finishing off Little Bill, Munny threatens everyone to properly bury Logan or experience his wrath again before departing from the rainy frontier town for good.

The "Unforgiven" ending reveals that some legends are better left to fade away, and Munny is every inch the killer that he was reputed to be. Moreover, Munny inadvertently demonstrates Little Bill's own insight against him, staying calm and collected during the chaos of the gunfight, allowing him to take down all his enemies. Keeping in tone with the rest of the revisionist Western nature of the movie, this burst of violence isn't particularly flashy or stylized. But that makes the carnage all the more grounded and with understated menace as Eastwood delivers his definitive word on the genre that made him a star.

The most famous shootout in real Wild West history was the gunfight at the O.K. Corral in 1881 between the Cowboy outlaw gang and lawmen led by Wyatt Earp. Though this fateful showdown has been dramatized plenty of times in Western movies, the most entertaining depiction is in "Tombstone." Roughly serving as the centerpiece of the movie, the scene only lasts less than a minute, like the historical event. Several of the outlaws are killed in the exchange, while both of Wyatt's brothers are wounded before inciting the wrath of the other gang members.

"Tombstone" presents its historical figures in a stylized and colorful light, helping make it one of the best Western movies of the 1990s. Comparatively, the gunfight at the O.K. Corral is played relatively straight, which helps it stand out from the rest of the movie. The action is quick, brutal, and consequential, setting in motion the back half of the movie's stakes. Certainly one of the best gunfights in a relatively modern Western movie, "Tombstone" knows a lot is riding on its marquee confrontation and delivers accordingly.

The single most recognizable shot in Sergio Leone's "Once Upon a Time in the West" is the sight of three gunmen confronting Harmonica (Charles Bronson) at a train station. The scene opens the film, playing out largely with diegetic noise as the three gunfighters await the incoming train with their target. This sets the stage for Harmonica's arrival, earning his nickname from his first appearance with a screeching melody played from his mouth organ. Unfazed that he's outnumbered three-to-one, Harmonica takes his position against his three enemies and guns them all down singlehandedly though wounded in the skirmish.

"Once Upon a Time in the West" is bookended with genre-defining gunfights, but the opening sequence is the superior of the two. Leone's masterful positioning his actors in frame and suspense building until the inevitable draw finally punctuates that crescendo with a single exchange of gunfire. With Leone, it was all about finding ways to fuel that tension before letting it finally go off like a pressure cooker, a lesson that has visibly influenced Quentin Tarantino. "Once Upon a Time in the West" is among Charles Bronson's best movies and seeing him anchor the movie's opening gunfight sets the mood for Leone's requiem to the genre.

If "Once Upon a Time in the West" is best known for its opening, the following year's "The Wild Bunch" is best known for its ending. The movie follows a group of aging American outlaws in the early 20th century, led by Pike Bishop (William Holden), who flee to Mexico after a botched bank heist. The ensemble get caught up in the revolution south of the border, culminating in the quartet making their last stand against the full might of the Mexican army. Gathering around a machine gun emplacement, the group are eventually overwhelmed and killed but not before massacring scores of soldiers.

The gruesome to "The Wild Bunch" was reportedly as brutal to film as it was to watch, heightening the verisimilitude of the sequence. In a matter of seconds, this situation escalates out of control, full of fire and fury as Pike and his associates stand in the face of oblivion. There's no mistaking that these four men are marching quietly to their deaths, but as the scene reveals, they're going out on their own terms and they're not going alone. More than just the tale of four old outlaws, "The Wild Bunch" signals that the Wild West era didn't die out peacefully but with a violent fire in its guts.

Of course a Clint Eastwood Western was going to top this list, and of course it was going to be "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly." Virtually every Sergio Leone Western, like "Once Upon a Time in the West," has a standout shootout sequence, but the greatest is in his 1966 epic. The movie reaches its crescendo when it brings its titular trio together in a sprawling cemetery as they search for a hidden stash of loot. With the three gunslingers at odds, the characters have a tense staredown before Blondie (Eastwood) guns down Angel Eyes (Lee Van Cleef).

Powered by a stirring score by Ennio Morricone, the climax is one of the most effectively staged sequences Leone has ever directed. The intercutting of close-ups between the three main characters before being punctuated by a single burst of gunfire with mounting suspense all the while is masterfully done. The moment also provides Blondie with another opportunity to pull a fast one on Tuco (Eli Wallach), secretly unloading his pistol for the duel. The quick-draw gunfight that epitomizes Leone's meticulous style, "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly" ends on a truly iconic note.

#3457. Ebenezer Ending: Sam Claflin On What It Meant To Have Johnny Depp’s Ebenezer Say ‘Merry Christmas’

Johnny Depp’s transformation into Ebenezer is chilling (it even terrified Sam Claflin, who plays Ebenezer’s nephew, Fred), and him throwing out his signature “bah humbug” is intimidating. At the start of Ti West’s take on A Christmas Carol, it’s hard to imagine the grouchy character being capable of saying “Merry Christmas.” So, when he actually does say it at the end of the movie, it makes a big impact. With that in mind, I asked Claflin, who was on the receiving end of the jolly statement, what it meant to hear those words said by Ebenezer Scrooge.

At the end of Ebenezer, after the titular character has been visited by the ghosts and realized his wrongs, he works to redeem himself. He gives Bob Cratchit a much-deserved promotion, he gives a beggar his pocket watch, and he finally goes to see his nephew Fred to apologize and say Merry Christmas. When Claflin was speaking with director Ti West about playing Fred in this book-to-screen adaptation, he didn’t fully get the importance of his character; however, he told me that he quickly realized not only the significance of Fred, but the significance of this moment. He explained:

Well, in all honesty, when I was first talking to Ti about the script, and he sort of said ‘I was thinking of you to play the part Fred,’ I was like, ‘Who's Fred?’ For some reason, that role, that character, had never really resonated with me, or I'd never really taken notice of it. But especially the way that Ti wanted to kind of really focus on that within this version of the story, he really kind of felt like it added so much depth and gave the film even more heart.

Throughout Ebenezer, all Fred wants is for Ebenezer to be happy and to maintain one relationship that ties them both back to Fred’s mom and Ebenezer’s sister. He wants his uncle to be part of the family, and he keeps going back to him over and over again to invite him into his home for the holidays.

Claflin said he “really understood Fred’s objective” and why he was so adamant about keeping Depp’s character in his life. He also explained the lessons we can learn from this relationship, and the way it ends with Ebenezer saying “Merry Christmas.” Telling me why his character’s journey and mission to keep the titular character in his life is so important, the Catching Fire actor explained:

I think it's important to kind of not give up hope on the people that feel like they've lost. You know, it'd be so easy to give up and to move on. But I think the fact that he is just so determined and so true and almost desperate with his love – but it pays to be kind, and it pays to be generous, and it pays to be thoughtful and understanding and loving, and you know, Fred is a great example of how the world should be, really.

I totally agree. Fred’s motivations are so pure and rooted in deep familial love. His way of looking at the world is something worth striving for, and his inability to give up on his family is admirable. Clearly, it works in a way, too, because Ebenezer does come back to him. He does accept the love Fred so desperately wants to give, and they’re able to be a family. That all makes the “Merry Christmas” mean more, as Claflin told me:

Yeah, it was an honor to hear those words uttered from Ebenezer's mouth.

While Ebenezer has gotten mixed reviews, I enjoyed it. And I particularly loved the ending, and seeing Ebenezer realize why life’s worth living. Seeing him bring love back into his life, and feeling that lovely holiday spirit, brought me joy, and clearly it brought Fred and Sam Claflin joy too.

Now, if you’d like to see Ebenezer, you can catch this new take on A Christmas Carol in theaters now.

The 75-inch Hisense U6SF Pro has dropped to $747.97 from $1,399.99 ahead of Amazon’s Black Friday sale—bringing it to its lowest price to date. The rest of the U6 Pro lineup is discounted as well, so you can pick up the same TV in sizes from 55 inches to a massive 100 inches, for anyone with the room for something closer to a home-theater-sized screen. Whichever size you choose, you’ll get free delivery to the room of choice—a service that normally costs $19.99. As for the TV itself, it’s a 2026 model that sits below the U7SG (also on sale for $1,297.99, from $1,999.99) in Hisense's lineup as the brand's entry point into Mini LED, pairing a 4K panel and local dimming with a matte, anti-reflective coating meant to cut down on glare, notes this PCMag review.

For a budget set, the U6 Pro gets a lot right when it comes to picture quality—its high peak brightness helps it hold up during a sunny afternoon in a living room with big windows, so a daytime football game or cooking show won’t look washed out, while its excellent contrast and effective local dimming keep dark scenes looking deep when you settle in for a movie at night. It also does a good job cleaning up lower-quality content, which is useful for older cable broadcasts or compressed YouTube videos—and its Fire TV interface makes it easy to jump between those kinds of content and the major streaming services without needing a separate streaming device.

The U6 Pro also brings plenty to the table for gaming, with HDMI 2.1, VRR, ALLM, and a 144Hz refresh rate that PC gamers can push to 240Hz at a lower 1080p resolution. That said, the panel’s slow response time and poor motion performance can reportedly make fast-moving scenes look noticeably blurry. Viewing angles are limited too, with the picture losing quality fairly quickly when you move off-center—and its built-in speakers aren’t particularly impressive either, so a soundbar could be worth budgeting for.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: Think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

#3455. The Office's Downfall Can Be Traced Back To One Moment

In 2005, two TV shows premiered as mid-season replacements, which isn't usually a great sign for said series' potential longevity. One was "Grey's Anatomy" on ABC, which became one of the longest-running TV shows in history. The other? "The Office," an adaptation of Ricky Gervais' British series of the same name that became one of the biggest hits in the entire history of NBC.

With Steve Carell leading the way as the well-meaning but unbelievably buffoonish Michael Scott (the regional manager of the Scranton branch of paper company Dunder-Mifflin), the American version of "The Office" made it past a somewhat rocky first season and became a small-screen staple, launching the careers of Carell and co-stars like John Krasinski, B.J. Novak, and Mindy Kaling. (It also, arguably, led to an uptick in small-screen mockumentaries like its successors "Modern Family," "Parks and Recreation," and "Abbott Elementary.") After running for nine massively successful seasons, "The Office" wrapped up its run in 2013 with a finale that actually stuck the landing ... but the road to the finish was rough.

You can argue all you want about how to pinpoint the downfall of "The Office," but I won't entertain any debate. The answer is that "The Office" hit a major point of no return in Season 7 when Carell left the show, which led to Michael Scott moving away from Scranton and decamping to Colorado. Despite its best efforts to continue relatively uninterrupted, the series just didn't functionally work without Michael Scott.

It's perfectly understandable that Steve Carell wanted to leave "The Office" behind after spending so long playing one character. (He's a pretty talented guy, after all.) Still, the show should have just ... ended. Even the lead-up to Michael's exit was, all things considered, sort of bleak. This is conjecture on my part, but it really felt like, in Season 6 episodes like "Scott's Tots" and "Koi Pond," the show was leaning into Michael's worst impulses and making him straight-up unlikable instead of silly but well-meaning.

The reason for Michael's departure, however, is undeniably sweet. After human resources representative Holly Flax (Amy Ryan) makes her debut appearance in the Season 4 finale "Goodbye Toby," she and Michael ultimately fall in love before she gets moved back to her original Dunder-Mifflin branch in Nashua due to higher-ups fretting about the pair's relationship. Then, in Season 7, she returns to Scranton, and while Holly and Michael have been broken up for some time when she finds herself back in northeastern Pennsylvania, they get back together ... but their happy ending is threatened when family troubles mean that Holly needs to move back to Colorado.

Thankfully, by this point in the series, Michael is back to being essentially likable again, so he does the right thing: He proposes to Holly and tells his colleagues he's moving with her. His final episode, "Goodbye Michael," is incredibly moving, especially the moment where Pam Beesly-Halpert (Jenna Fischer) says goodbye to Michael in the airport. Yet, the show loses its footing forever as he departs, and it never recovers. Why? Well, the string of potential replacements for Michael is lackluster at best and egregiously unfunny at worst.

One of the many crimes committed in the final two seasons of "The Office" is that the show managed to make English treasure and comedy legend Catherine Tate actively exhausting, but I'm getting ahead of myself. First, "The Office" pulls out the stops by bringing in Steve Carell's "Anchorman" cohort Will Ferrell (the proverbial comedic big gun) as Deangelo Vickers, a deeply confusing and unfunny new manager who's written off after getting a brain injury during a pickup basketball game. From there, Creed Bratton's erratic "Creed Bratton" briefly becomes the manager (and it goes just as well as any "Office" fan would expect), and while James Spader's unfathomably bizarre Robert California has his moments as one of Creed's successors, he doesn't work, either.

Ultimately, Tate's Nellie Bertram and Ed Helms' Andy Bernard are the people who run the Scranton branch most consistently in Michael's absence, and not only are they both terrible at the job, neither of them recreates the magic that only Carell could bring to the series. Instead, Tate's Nellie is, at varying times, exceedingly ridiculous or shrewd (it depends on the episode you're watching), whereas Andy is so expendable that "The Office" briefly writes him off. (This was done to free up Helms to go film "The Hangover Part III" at the time.) Moreover, everyone eventually gets simplified to the point of parody (i.e. Flanderized, to use a popular "Simpsons"-inspired term), so much so that Andy, himself an Ivy League graduate, becomes borderline illiterate. Put simply, it's a mess.

Yes, "The Office" has a great series finale, but the journey to getting there was rough without Michael Scott. Decide for yourself: The show is currently streaming on Peacock.

#3454. Kate Middleton Announces First Major Trip Since Her Cancer Diagnosis

In unexpected news, Kensington Palace has just announced that Kate Middleton will accompany Prince William on his upcoming three-day official visit to Mumbai, India. The trip, which commences on Monday, will mark their first joint tour outside the United Kingdom in the past four years and represents a new milestone in Kate Middleton’s gradual return to public duties since she was diagnosed with cancer in early 2024 and began scaling back her official engagements.

Last May, the princess made a brief solo trip to Italy to learn about early childhood development, but this trip to India (a nine-hour flight from London) represents her first long-distance journey and her highest-profile diplomatic engagement since the Caribbean tour she undertook in 2022 and the Earthshot Awards gala she attended in Boston that same year.

"So proud, I'm very, very proud. She's been amazing. She's been through so much in the last couple of years, particularly," William shared on UK radio show Heart Breakfast in May, pleased to see that Kate was “gradually resuming” her travels. Still, the heir to the throne wanted to be cautious and warned that these visits are very taxing. "Away trips like that take a lot out of you," he explained. "So we have to balance that, make sure she's, she's OK and rested, but she's in good form."

The royal couple at the 2022 Earthshot Prize ceremony in Boston, their most recent joint trip abroad to date

The reason for the visit is the sixth edition of the Earthshot Prize, an initiative spearheaded by the heir to the British throne that each year awards one million pounds (about $1,323,249) to five innovative environmental projects and which, after making stops in other cities abroad such as Singapore, Cape Town, and Rio de Janeiro, is now taking place in the country that has produced the most finalists and winners in the competition’s history.

Standout finalists this year include Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, for its fleet of electric motorcycle taxis designed to reduce urban pollution, and Mahila Housing Trust, which installs reflective roofs capable of lowering the temperature inside homes by up to five degrees during extreme heat. The awards ceremony will be held this Tuesday evening at the Jio World Centre in Mumbai and will feature a performance by the band Take That and be attended by celebrities such as actor Rami Malek.

William and Kate during their 2016 visit to the Taj Mahal

Hours before the main event, the Prince and Princess of Wales will also preside over the first edition of the Earthshot Children’s Awards, a competition in which 15,000 schools from 24 Indian states have participated with environmental proposals designed by young people aged 9 to 17. The itinerary also includes a solo appearance by Kate Middleton, meetings with the Bollywood film industry, cricket-related celebrations, and a possible meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

In addition to being a positive sign regarding the princess’s health, this return to India holds strong symbolic significance for the couple, who last visited the country in April 2016. On that occasion, the then-Duke and Duchess of Cambridge visited the Taj Mahal and posed on the same white marble bench where Princess Diana was photographed alone in 1992—an image that has gone down in history as a reflection of the breakdown of her marriage to the now-King Charles III.

#3453. Halo Defined a Generation of LAN Parties — Then It Killed Them

Four Xboxes, 16 teenagers, and one ill-advised bottle of Sprite

Four Xboxes, 16 teenagers, and one ill-advised bottle of Sprite

Few things make me feel like Matt Damon aging in that endlessly memed shot from Saving Private Ryan quite like seeing a formative part of my childhood turn 25. My hair is thinner. My bad vision is somehow even worse. My eyes look tired. I am old.

So old, in fact, that the upcoming 25th anniversary of the Xbox and Halo: Combat Evolved immediately made me think about the LAN parties my brother and I used to host in middle and high school. There were a dozen or so teenage boys, four TVs, and enough Ethernet cable to turn my parents’ house into a tripping hazard that could also burst into flames at any moment. I’ve played countless multiplayer games since, but none have come close to the majesty of those experiences.

At some point during my obsession with Halo, I discovered that you could connect four Xbox consoles through a router and play across four TVs. You didn’t even need an internet connection. For some mysterious reason, my parents already owned several Ethernet cables that were dozens of feet long. Maybe they’d wanted a wired connection in every room. Maybe there was a sale. Whatever the explanation, we had the infrastructure.

Thus began an exciting era during which my parents kindly allowed us to host massive, very loud sleepovers dedicated exclusively to playing Halo. The living room served as the Nexus. Yes, I called it that, because I’m a huge nerd. It had the biggest screen, the best seating, and the spare router we used to connect everything.

One or two Ethernet cables snaked up the stairs to the bedroom my brother and I shared, where I had a little gaming nook with a modest TV, several consoles, and a beanbag chair. We usually set up another TV in the dining room, pushing the table into a corner. When my parents eventually finished the basement and built my brother his own room down there, we expanded to a third floor.

The first time we did this, I think we had about 10 people, most of them my older brother’s buddies. Some were quite good at Halo. Some were newbies just looking for a fun time. Most were somewhere in between. Probably my favorite thing about these parties was that, for the most part, I destroyed them all with ease.

My best friend, whom I’ll call Connor, was also in attendance. He’s a brilliant guy who’s great at games and introduced me to Magic: The Gathering. His parents were strict about sugar, though, and never let him drink soda. We thought it would be funny to let Connor solo an entire 2-liter bottle of Sprite.

It was the first time I’d ever seen a human being turn absolutely feral. As the night wore on and some players began falling asleep with controllers still in their hands, Connor was scream-cackling as he killed their defenseless Spartans. Sprite turned the nicest guy I know into the Joker.

As word spread, the parties grew in size and extravagance. Before long, four decent-sized TVs became a firm requirement, so we could approach the 16-player limit. Ethernet cables stretched out of the Nexus in every direction. We’d coordinate ahead of time who would bring extra consoles and who could supply controllers for people who didn’t have their own.

We’d play everything from free-for-all Slayer to team matches and Capture the Flag. If we had an odd number of players, I always had to suffer the handicap of being on the smaller team. Sometimes we’d randomly select captains and pick teams like it was gym class.

We kept this up beyond the launch of Halo 2 in November 2004. If anything, the new mechanics and polished graphics only upped our enthusiasm. But as we reached our later years of high school and got busier, gathering everyone became harder. Meanwhile, Halo itself was helping make all that effort less necessary.

There’s something bittersweet about the fact that the sequel we were so excited to play also helped destroy our parties. Halo 2 let us play together without leaving our houses, which made meeting in person less necessary.

Halo 2 wasn’t the first shooter to offer online multiplayer, but its approach helped establish expectations for how console multiplayer games should work. Its party system let friends assemble a group and stay together between matches, while automated playlist matchmaking handled finding opponents. Combined with Xbox Live’s friends list and voice chat, it made organizing a game remarkably easy.

You could get home, turn on your Xbox, and join your friends. Nobody needed to borrow a TV or run a cable up the stairs. For a group of teenagers whose schedules were getting more complicated, that convenience was irresistible.

I understand why we stopped. Once everyone had jobs and other commitments, finding a few hours to play online was a lot easier than organizing an overnight that also required rearranging my parents’ furniture. Nobody had to bring a TV. Nobody had to figure out whose controller was missing. We weren’t risking Connor’s health and sanity. We could just play.

But 25 years later, so much of what I remember about Halo has nothing to do with beating the campaign on Legendary, or that one time I got a Double Kill with a single sniper bullet in Halo 3 that went through two heads. It’s the Ethernet cables running up the stairs, the absurdly large pizza, and the angry accusations of “screen-looking” from people who were absolutely doing it themselves. It’s hearing someone scream from another floor when they got killed, or the playful cussing between matches during our potty breaks. And, of course, it’s Connor discovering what two liters of Sprite could do to a person.

Getting everyone into the same house was a ridiculous amount of work, and I love my parents for not just letting it happen but supporting it. I’m also incredibly grateful to have come up during an era when that kind of thing was possible.

Studios like Obsidian, Playground, and Turn 10 will all see major internal changes

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

I remember more LAN parties from this era involving Counter-strike, UT, and StarCraft, but that’s just my anecdotal experience. If I was a little older I’d probably be saying Doom and Quake.

The Damon/Kimmel faux feud has been going on for decades at this point, and it just never gets old. Matt Damon and Jimmy Kimmel have been pretending to hate each other for years, doing bits about it at the Oscars and on Kimmel’s talk show. And despite actually being great friends, they love to keep this bit going. On that note, the talk show host was recently asked to give a toast to Matt Damon at a huge Hollywood event, and there's a hilarious video that I just can't get enough of!

Damon has had quite a year, having released The Rip, which co-stars his best friend, Ben Affleck. The Rip was also a huge hit for Netflix and allowed for him to continue to work with Affleck amid other projects at their production company. Damon was also most notably the star of The Odyssey, which grossed well over a billion dollars worldwide and is an awards season favorite. As a result, GQ named Damon one of their Men of the Year in their annual issue. At the party to celebrate the magazine. Jimmy Kimmel gave quite the speech, which you can see below:

Kimmel, of course, couldn’t resist mentioning some controversial people named in GQ magazine over the years to compare Damon, too. On top of that, the talk show was quick to say that Tom Holland was more deserving of this honor. Kimmel said:

Matt had a big year and he's in great company. I've made a list of some of the other honorees. Mel Gibson, 1996, 2007, Kanye West. The list goes on and on and you you deserve it. You really do. Not as much as others might deserve it. You know, Tom Holland was in the Odyssey and Spider-Man this year. He was in number one and number two. You're just number two. You're a big number two. You deserve this.

Kimmel then toasted to his faux foe and fittingly called him “Mrs. Ben Affleck.” Of course, Damon had his own hilarious quips as a response. He was quick to point out one key detail about that night, saying:

I would just like to repeat that I did not invite Jimmy Kimmel to this place.

Of course, this is all in good fun, and the riffing is expected any time these two guys are in the same room together. It started back in the early 2000s when Jimmy Kimmel started saying “Apologies to Matt Damon, we ran out of time” at the end of every show. It was a self-deprecating joke, as a way to make fun of how terrible his guests were when his show first started, as opposed to having a movie star like Damon. It became a running joke that continued even as Kimmel’s show became more successful.

Periodically, Damon tries to sneak onto Kimmel’s show, and the host jokingly refuses to have the actor on as a guest. They also make fun of each other relentlessly in public, and hilariously compete for the affection of Ben Affleck. It’s a great bit, and if this GQ speech is any indication, this duo isn’t planning on retiring the quips anytime soon. I hope they continue to dig at each other for years to come, because it is just too much fun to watch.

Fans can check out Matt Damon in The Odyssey, which is still playing in select theaters nationwide. It’s the tail end of The Odyssey’s historic box office run, so make sure to see it on the big screen while you still can. You can also watch Jimmy Kimmel Live!, which airs at 11:35 p.m. ET on ABC and is available to stream with a Disney+ subscription.

#3451. Robert Downey Jr.'s 90s Supernatural Fantasy Flop Is Worth Revisiting

It's no exaggeration to say that Ron Underwood's 1993 fantasy comedy film "Heart and Souls" boasts one of Robert Downey Jr.'s best performances. He wasn't nominated for an Oscar (although he surely deserved to be), but at least he won a Saturn Award for Best Actor for his work on it. Yet, because it flopped at the box office, it's rarely ranked among Downey's best movies of all time.

Downey stars in "Heart and Souls" as Thomas Reilly, an arrogant yuppie who is possessed by a pack of friendly ghosts that have been following him since birth. Thus, over the course of the movie, Downey takes on the speech patterns and affectations of his ghostly co-stars (Kyra Sedgwick, Tom Sizemore, Alfre Woodard, and Charles Grodin), and he does so with utter aplomb. The result is a film that's funny, profound, and sentimental in equal measure. It has the mood and structure of a high-concept Hollywood comedy, but with a toe rooted in the warmth of something like "It's a Wonderful Life." Plus, its view of the afterlife is pretty light and fun and makes sense in a secular way.

The world of ghosts plays by its own rules in "Heart and Souls," but it's not oblique or difficult. Here, the living and the dead are cosmically bound, like sometimes-invisible family members contracted to make wrongs right and assuage regrets. It's a positive and touching movie with its messages tucked in between hilarious bouts of Downey zaniness. Ultimately, Thomas learns to be less selfish and far more understanding to his girlfriend, Anne, played by Elisabeth Shue. See what I mean about the amazing cast?

"Heart and Souls" opens in 1959 and introduces us to our ghost characters while they're still alive, each of them boarding the same ill-fated bus. Julia (Kyra Sedgwick) is hoping to find her boyfriend, whose marriage proposal she regrets rejecting. Penny (Alfre Woodard) has to work a late shift away from her sons. Milo (Tom Sizemore) is a small-time crook who conned some valuable stamps from a local kid and regrets it. And Harrison (Charles Grodin) is a singer who just fled an audition due to overwhelming stage fright.

Sadly, their bus driver, Hal (David Paymer), gets distracted and crashes the vehicle, killing everyone on board in front of a car carrying a woman in labor. The four passengers, now ghosts, then witness a young Thomas being born. Over time, the ghosts realize they're physically bound to Thomas (meaning, they get dragged along if he walks away) and grow up with him. However, because they're invisible to everyone but him, Thomas' parents assume he's mentally unwell. So, the ghosts eventually decide to become invisible to Thomas to protect his mental health.

Fast-forward to the present, and the ghosts are unexpectedly visited by the now-deceased Hal. He tells them that Thomas is their "earthly vessel" and they should've been spending their time using him to right the wrongs in their lives so they can finally enter the afterlife. Now, they have to solve their biggest regrets in the next few days or risk oblivion.

Thomas, meanwhile, has become a heartless foreclosure banker who believes he had schizophrenia as a child, causing him to see his childhood "friends." But after the ghosts reappear to him, he eventually accepts that, yes, they are real, and he agrees to help them solve their earthly problems and ascend.

I maintain that "Heart and Souls" is one of the best films of its year. And, to reiterate, Robert Downey Jr. gives an Oscar-worthy performance in it. However, he wouldn't win his Oscar until "Oppenheimer" decades later, having only just been nominated for an Academy Award for the first time right before "Heart and Souls" came out for his turn as Charlie Chaplin in Richard Attenborough's biopic "Chaplin."

Overall, critics were mixed on "Heart and Souls." Most reviews tended to praise the performances from the movie's gaggle of stars, as seen in Michael Wilmington's review for the Los Angeles Times. He noted that "Heart and Souls" was about the spiritual crisis of modern humanity, "buried under several tons of Hollywood slick." But, he added, you should trust the film's actors. To quote him directly:

"There's one great opportunity for virtuoso fun here: the chance handed Downey to impersonate the mannerisms of his co-stars whenever one takes over his body. With [...] delicate, precise mimicry [...] he slips delightfully into [Alfre] Woodard's feline assurance, [Tom] Sizemore's swagger, [Kyra] Sedgwick's sexiness or [Charles] Grodin's repressions. The character he's playing — the same kind of languid, self-obsessed, inwardly anxious hedonist he played throughout the '80s — isn't deep, but Downey digs something comic out of his superficiality."

If that sounds fun or intriguing, it can serve as your "in" to "Heart and Souls." You may discover a new gem.

#3450. ChatGPT's New GIF Generator Is Fun, but Won't Replace Us Humans (Yet)

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

When it comes to generating AI images, both Gemini and ChatGPT do a passable job. In most cases, the results will look AI-generated, but they likely won’t have glaring spelling issues or missing limbs. Now, OpenAI is trying something new, introducing GIF support for ChatGPT. It's the company's first "moving images" feature since OpenAI shut down Sora, and while you can generate hyper-realistic videos in Gemini, this new ChatGPT feature is trying to fill in the gap, in a small way.

OpenAI is pitching the new feature as an animation tool, not exactly as a way to create looping videos—though that’s how I ended up using it. You give ChatGPT a prompt, as detailed as you can make it, and the chatbot produces a GIF in just a few seconds. You can start with your own drawings or images, too. ChatGPT uses sketches as the base for animations, though it can turn any still image into animated GIFs. Like other AI editing tools, you can edit it if ChatGPT didn't quite get it right: You can ask ChatGPT to make the GIF longer or shorter, remove certain objects, change the style, slow down transitions, among other edits.

AI art can be quite sterile, but I was surprised by how adding motion and animation to the mix makes generating images a lot more fun. Unlike traditional GIFs, which usually pull from existing video clips, you can turn anything you want into a GIF, which is especially cool if you're using your own art. In my testing, I found this to be the most rewarding part. It’s not always possible to one-shot a GIF with a single prompt. But after a few rounds of edits, I ended up creating some GIFs that I actually wanted to share in my WhatsApp groups.

That being said, I think human-made GIFs are still the gold standard here. For example, I asked ChatGPT to generate a video of someone brewing a pour-over, with a gooseneck kettle, showing the coffee blooming process. It did okay, but it’s nothing like actually making a pour-over. The kettle doesn’t move in circles, the water doesn’t rise evenly, there are no bubbles, and the steam is all over the place.

Compare that to the GIF below, which comes from a royalty-free video. Even though it’s a compressed, low-quality, and noisy GIF, it still shows the movement of the pour, the water rising, and even the bubbles. The details captured by a real video just aren’t there in ChatGPT GIFs. If that’s what you’re expecting, you will be disappointed. But I don't think that's the point of this feature anyway.

I found that ChatGPT excels when you’re making something fun, and you don’t look into the details too much. It pulled off a loop of a cat playing with a ball, and it was great at making a festive GIF for Diwali. It even made a GIF based on a photo. I asked it to create a fun promotional GIF for my JBL Bluetooth speakers, and it did the job quite well. At first, the transitions were too jarring, and the movement just made no sense. After some editing, though, I got it to a decent place.

Still, the main issue with ChatGPT GIFs is that complex movement and transitions aren’t nailed down. A hand shifts position weirdly between frames, and colors and objects appear out of nowhere. But if you can get over these issues, you can make some fun, lighthearted GIFs and memes to share with your friends on Instagram or WhatsApp.

Plenty of films left impressions on the 2026 movie schedule, but few managed to really hit the zeitgeist like Project Hail Mary did. Phil Lord and Chris Miller’s science-fiction epic – based on Andy Weir’s 2021 book of the same name – managed to capture audiences’ imaginations (and make some solid money at the box office in the process). Anyone who needs further proof of the film’s popularity should know that a mixed-reality game is in the works and, to quote Rocky, the description of his role sounds “amaze.”

This new game – Project Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars – hails from game studio Maze Theory and takes place during a formerly untapped period of time within the main story. It specifically takes place after Dr. Ryland Grace saves his alien companion, Rocky, and before they return to the latter’s homeworld, Enid. Players take on the role of Dr. Ryland Grace (played by the impeccable and expressive Ryan Gosling in the film) and, as SFX Magazine on CinemaBlend learned from the developers, the game gets quite immersive.

Players can interact with objects, steer the titular ship (Hail Mary), repair it and even complete tasks like opening cupboards. One also only needs a headset to further immerse themselves in the game’s story, which was also talked out with Weir. Of course, all the while, fans can also interact with Rocky (who is not a pet) throughout their travels, and he’ll be actively watching your moves and providing feedback. Gameplay lead Sandy Lockie told SFX this about bringing Rocky and Grace’s relationship to the game:

We wanted to do justice to Rocky and Grace and their relationship. Sometimes they’ll be crabby with each other, sometimes they’ll get a little bit down and need the other one to pick them up.

It just wouldn’t have made sense to craft a game like this without including Rocky in some form or fashion. Since the film’s release he’s become something of a sensation, and he went viral after Amazon posted a video of the character watching himself. Even Neil DeGrasse Tyson praised the character’s design and noted that Weir and the filmmakers avoid the Hollywood trope of making him a humanoid. Judging by Lockie’s comments, even the Maze Theory team was taken with Rocky while they were testing the game:

Even when we’re testing, although you know he’s a character and isn’t really there, I’ll talk to him: ‘Well, what do I do here?’ He has good suggestions and sometimes bad suggestions. It’s one of those things that your brain just kind of lunges into, like, ‘Yep, Rocky’s there. He’s a character now!’ He’ll do jazz hands or prompt you to play rock-paper-scissors and all sorts of stuff . It’s fun to step into that and feel like he’s your friend and companion, your little explorer buddy.

All in all, this game should provide fans with a bit of a taste of being in Ryland’s shoes and present the opportunity to catch up with Rocky in some sense. Project Hail Mary’s ending may have closed the book on Grace and Rocky’s bromance for now, but I still like the idea of people being able to create their own moments reminiscent of the film’s best scenes. So, on that note, why not jump into this sweet-sounding extension of the PHM story?

Project Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars is now available Pico, Meta and Android XR. Also, fans can grab a Prime Video subscription and stream the movie on which the game is based right now.

#3448. Why Walter Koenig Held His Tongue To Keep His Star Trek II: The Wrath Of Khan Role

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

"Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan" gives Pavel Chekov (the late Walter Koenig) one of his meatier arcs in any of the "Star Trek" films. In his new assignment as first officer of the USS Reliant, Chekov and his captain, Terrell (Paul Winfield), scout planets as a testing site for the Genesis device. But what they think is planet Ceti Alpha VI is actually the barren Ceti Alpha V, where the Enterprise left Khan Noonien Singh (Ricardo Montalbán), the 20th century's most infamous genetically engineered warlord, and his followers at the end of the episode "Space Seed."

Chekov and Terrell are captured and brainwashed via Ceti eels implanted in their ears. Khan and his people thus seize the Reliant, and boom, we have our movie. The sequence on Ceti Alpha V is predicated on Khan and Chekov recognizing each other. When Chekov and Terrell come across Khan and co.'s makeshift home, Chekov recognizes the name "Botany Bay" (the name of the sleeper ship where the Enterprise found Khan in "Space Seed"). Once the pair are captured, Khan recognizes Chekov and proclaims "I never forget a face."

Chekov also speaks to and of Khan as if he witnessed the events of "Space Seed." Except, technically, he didn't. "Space Seed" was made in "Star Trek" Season 1, and Koenig/Chekov only joined the cast in Season 2. Ergo, he obviously never appeared in "Space Seed" and shared no screentime with Khan. Oops!

Over 40 years later, Trekkies still note the inconsistency and rationalize it. Koenig, for his part, has said he recognized the error when he read the script, but chose to stay silent to preserve Chekov's role. Considering how often "Star Trek" overlooked Chekov, it's hard to blame him.

"Wrath of Khan" writer Harve Bennett wasn't a "Star Trek" fan when he took the job. That worked for the best. "Wrath of Khan" is widely credited for revitalizing "Star Trek" and part of that is because Bennett and director Nicholas Meyer brought fresh eyes. To that end, they couldn't expect everyone who would go see "Wrath of Khan" had previously seen "Space Seed." So, the movie doesn't rely on the episode outside of its big picture story details, which are easily explained via some dialogue in Khan's first scene. (I saw "Wrath of Khan" before "Space Seed" as a kid, and I followed the former just fine.)

But Chekov knowing Khan is the kind of detail that evidently slipped by Bennett. Koenig, who was asked to read the script and give it a "Trekkie read," had a vested interest in not pointing out the mistake. As Koenig put it when interviewed in "The Fifty-Year Mission: The First 25 Years" by Edward Gross and Mark A. Altman: "I was faced with the ethical dilemma of mentioning it to Bennett or letting it go. I chose survival as opposed to ethics."

Chekov is the only member of the "Star Trek" main cast who shares physical screentime with Khan in the movie. (Khan and Kirk only ever talk via viewscreens and communicators.) It's also Khan's first appearance in the movie, as well as the scene from "Wrath of Khan" that I rewatch the most in isolation. Montalbán's performance, savoring every line, is just spectacular. I can see why Koenig would, as an actor, want the chance to be in a scene as strong as that one, and he holds his own balancing Chekov's courage and fear.

For Koenig's part, his cheeky theory to explain away this inconsistency was that Chekov once made Khan wait an uncomfortable amount of time to use the Enterprise's restroom. "Chekov was on the Enterprise, just offscreen" has become the go-to fanon answer. The novel "To Reign in Hell: The Exile of Khan Noonien Singh" by Greg Cox legitimizes that; Chekov is said to have led a failed effort to retake the Enterprise from Khan, and is part of the detachment that helps Khan and his people get settled on Ceti Alpha V.

Despite the continuity gap with "Space Seed," Chekov was the best pick among the main characters as the one captured by Khan. Amusingly, this is precisely because he's the most ancillary one. The Enterprise can function without him in a way it wouldn't without Spock (Leonard Nimoy) or Dr. McCoy (DeForest Kelley).

While Koenig evidently feared that they would swap Chekov's part out in the script, the only other main character who could work would be Uhura (Nichelle Nichols), which would add some icky subtext to Khan violating her body with the Ceti eels, or Sulu (George Takei). With Sulu, you run into the same problem because he wasn't in "Space Seed" either! While Sulu/Takei was part of the show in Season 1, he was absent for that particular episode. If it had been Sulu who landed on Ceti Alpha V with Terrell and met Khan, you might be getting forum posts highlighting that inconsistency today.

Walter Koenig may have created a small problem in "Wrath of Khan" by staying silent here, but he helped fix a much bigger one, too, by suggesting moving Spock's death to the end of the film.

#3447. Sam Altman Is “Still Unknowable” to Andrew Garfield, Even After Playing the OpenAI Co-Founder in Artificial

In Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial, the director follows the rise of OpenAI and a few of its pioneers: Sam Altman, Elon Musk, Ilya Sutskever and Mira Murati. The result is one of the most talked-about and timely films of the season.

“The topic is not the artificial intelligence for me, but it's the people who imagined it, who created it, who exploited it and who are still in the mix of doing all these things,” Guadagnino said during a discussion led by VF's Global Editorial Director Mark Guiducci, at Vanity Fair’s Screening Room at LACMA on Saturday. “I was very much into trying to decipher, understand this world of this new generation, let’s say tech bros, that were somehow behaving in a way that was not exactly as you could see the previous generation doing … So it was too attractive not to try to meet these people in the eyes and too attractive not to do so with this incredible group of performers who were going to go and jump the cliff of this.”

Luca Guadagnino and Andrew Garfield at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

Guadagnino was joined by cast members Andrew Garfield (who plays Altman), Yura Borisov (who plays Sutskever) and Monica Barbaro (who plays Murati) for a post-screening conversation. The actors were challenged with preparing to play real people who they were not able to interact with ahead of time, instead relying on interviews, video recordings, and other research in order to get into their characters.

Andrew Garfield at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

“[Sam Altman] still is unknowable to me and I'm fascinated by him continuously and exponentially, for here until eternity," Garfield said about OpenAI's co-founder and CEO. “And it's important to try to understand because as Luca said, these are the kids that have the reins of the future and we've somehow allowed them to just hold onto them. And we've kind of given our autonomy over or it's been taken from behind our backs.”

He added: “It's a remarkable thing to have the resilience to go and sleep every night, knowing that you're really doing a lot of damage.”

Barbaro said the fact that Murati is very private helped her understand the former OpenAI CTO. “That is indicative of a kind of behavior and personality type and it pointed me in a certain direction as far as her values were concerned,” she said. “And we also had a lot of wonderful consultants, people who worked with them at OpenAI, but who were no longer with the company, kind of telling us what jokes and things that they would make.”

Yura Borisov at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

For Borisov, he hopes his portrayal does Sutskever justice and that people will want to know or understand him more. “I started to watch videos about him and looked at his social media, trying just to understand what he's talking about in his interviews,” the actor explained. "And step by step, as much as I discovered him, it was more and more scary for me because I started to respect and love him more and more."

Monica Barbaro, Andrew Garfield and Yura Borisov at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

The conversation had its own meta moment of sorts, when Barbaro posed a question to Guiducci about his decision to profile and feature Altman on the cover of Vanity Fair’s New Establishment Issue.

"You faced heat for presenting, maybe some people would say pedestalizing Sam Altman on the cover of Vanity Fair, what is your take on that?" Barbaro asked.

“I think that the magazine is an arena where these things have to play out,” Guiducci said. “It's so interesting to me to...have the [forthcoming] feature about this film in the issue that was preceded by one where I got to ask Sam about it." Guiducci continued: "Something about [taking Sam's] picture makes people feel, ‘Oh, that's the trophy.’ But photojournalism is journalism too. And I want people to be able to look back at the magazine and see a document of the time that we lived in," he said. "And also, if the photo is what helps me get the interview where we get to know more about these people, I'm going to take it.”

Monica Barbaro at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

Other panel highlights included the subject of ChatGPT, which only Guadagnino admitted to using occasionally to ask about what’s ok to feed his dogs. He also addressed parting ways with the film's original studio partner Amazon and the fortuitous partnership that emerged with new distributor NEON.

“I think there is some kind of honor in the decision because they could have written off the movie and that's it,” he said about Amazon dropping the film from their slate. “And then they allowed us to find a partner and we found the best partner possible… They really believed in the movie.”

“They really made everything to get us to make the best movie we could,” he continued. "I only have good feelings toward my friends at Amazon. And in a strange way, I kind of understand the decision. Conflict of interest is a big thing.”

Luca Guadagnino at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

The inaugural edition of Vanity Fair’s Screening Room pairs this year’s most compelling films with a slate of programming that includes post-screening panels and conversations with actors and filmmakers. The invitation-only events are welcoming an audience from the worlds of film, fashion, culture, politics, media, and tech, much like the magazine itself.

Following the program in Los Angeles, Vanity Fair’s Screening Room will arrive in New York, where screenings and events will take place at Cherry Lane Theatre from December 4–6.

#3446. 10 Shows Like 'Cyberpunk: Edgerunners' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the dramatic conclusion of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners way back in 2022, the show has returned for a new season set in the megalopolis of Night City with a standalone story and a new cast of characters (by necessity).

Though the aesthetic and themes of cyberpunk have their roots in American science fiction of the 1970s and '80s, anime and manga of the '90s and beyond embraced the form and took it to entirely new places—so much so that a Japanese/Polish co-production of an adaptation of a video game from a Polish designer has taken its cues from a couple of decades' worth of great anime and cerebral sci-fi. Which is to say, if you're looking for more heady sci-fi series, these 10 are a good place to start.

An iconic, effortlessly cool genre classic, Cowboy Bebop is one of the undisputed GOATs of anime, blending western, noir, and crime genres and setting the resultant mash to a killer soundtrack of old-school jazz (which serves much the same purpose as Cyberpunk's propulsive electronic grooves). The title's "cowboys" are bounty hunters in a near-future in which humans have been forced to colonize the solar system after Earth became uninhabitable. Different settings, but both shows offer up ragtag crews with highly dubious fates. Former hitman Spike Spiegel leads his crew on one nearly disastrous mission after another, their standalone adventures all building to a thoroughly memorable climax. Stream Cowboy Bebop on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

This one's set in 22nd-century Japan, with a slick Blade Runner-esque aesthetic and a setup reminiscent of Minority Report. Here, technology exists to measure intentions, so crimes can be stopped before they’ve occurred, at which point the “criminals” are placed into psychological treatment (à la A Clockwork Orange)—or subject to summary execution because their threat potential is too high. That ability to predict behavior bleeds over into every aspect of life: careers and even relationships are determined in large part by the same systems that sniff out criminal intent. Obviously, this is all perfectly fine, and there’s no potential for abuse or miscalculation whatsoever...though there are a couple of warning signs. The first involves a new Enforcer who becomes a potential murderer himself when he miscalculates the extent of a criminal’s potential to do wrong, and, even more significantly, the existence of a criminal mastermind who is somehow invisible to the tech, even as his criminal actions grow more and more elaborate. Stream Psycho-Pass on Prime Video and Crunchyroll.

Created by Tim Miller and with director David Fincher as an executive producer, this animated anthology series is a grab bag of wildly diverse offerings: Each episode is produced by a different international studio, with the only link between them being one of the three words in the show's title. One episode deals with robotic gladiator fights in dystopian London, another finds us under the threat of sentient yogurt, yet another finds an ambitious cat learning to make use of a family's robot helper. Its format dictates that no two episodes are going to have the same premise, but it shares with Cyberpunk an edgy sensibility and stories set in an apocalyptic future, albeit with a dark sense of humor—its four seasons offer up a mix of tech, sex, violence, and gorgeous animation. Stream Love, Death & Robots on Netflix.

One of several completely standalone spinoffs of the wildly influential 1995 film (itself based on the beloved manga series), Stand Alone Complex requires no prior knowledge. The style is largely the draw, as the series luxuriates in its fictional Nihama City setting, a world unto itself in a future Japan in which cybernetic people hack directly into the internet. Our sympathies are more with the authorities—in this case, Public Security Section 9, a cybercrime and antiterrorism police unit—than the cyber criminals, but the show approaches some of the same themes as Edgerunners with legit punk style. Stream Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex on Tubi and The Criterion Channel.

In this adaptation of the Richard K. Morgan cyberpunk classic of the same name, Joel Kinnaman and Anthony Mackie (yes, both of them) star as Takeshi "Tak" Kovacs. In this future megacity setting, human consciousness can be transferred between bodies. The tech is widely available, but only the wealthy can afford the backups and protections that make it a form of virtual immortality. Kovacs is a former soldier turned mercenary, revived from a backup after 200 years by Laurens Bancroft (James Purefoy), one of the wealthiest men alive. His motives for bringing the man back are shrouded in mystery, but he's giving Tak a chance to solve a very cold case: his own murder. Stream Altered Carbon on Netflix.

Another popular (and Emmy-winning) game adaptation, Arcane is based on League of Legends, a top-down actioner involving online opponents shooting lasers across a map. It doesn't sound like fodder for a show this impressive, but here we are. The League of Legends lore forms the backdrop for the show, but the pull is in the narrative involving two sisters caught up in the growing conflict between a utopian city and its oppressed underclass, without whom it couldn’t exist. The painted animation style is truly something special—not a stylistic match for Cyberpunk, but the two shows both go far above and beyond to create striking visual worlds. Stream Arcane on Netflix.

Vash the Stampede is a hunted outcast with a dark history that slowly comes to light over the course of the series. He’s got a reputation as a human wrecking ball, bringing destruction wherever he goes, and seemingly just for fun—but in reality he’s far more respectful of life than his pursuers. Still, cities evacuate at the mere possibility of his arrival, and a huge bounty sits on his head (no matter that the bounty hunters do far more damage than Vash). He and his friends—actually a couple of insurance agents—find themselves in a series of misadventures on the planet Gunsmoke, building to a final showdown that caps the series with finality. Visually, it’s probably one of the defining ‘90s shōnen-style action series, with elegantly choreographed gunfights that never get old. Tonally similar, Trigun also shares with Cyberpunk 2 the work of legendary composer Tsuneo Imahori, his music being crucial to both shows. Stream Trigun on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

Another from animation studio Trigger, Darling in the Franxx leans heavily into the mecha sub-genre, set in a post-apocalypse where children are bred and indoctrinated into piloting the title's massive Franxx to defend the remnants of humanity. Adults are pretty much immortal, so the kids simply don't have any other utility. Two of these teens begin to develop romantic feelings for each other, potentially complicating their usefulness to society and leading to an explosive, bittersweet finale. Stream Darling in the Franxx on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

What starts out as a relatively straightforward action show about space bounty hunters (the title's “Killjoys”) develops surprising depth over the course of its five seasons. As officially sanctioned Killjoys, the trio at the show’s heart (Hannah John-Kamen, Aaron Ashmore, and Luke Macfarlane) are bound to remain politically neutral at any cost. Initially, that’s a way to get them right into the heat of a fight, but as they develop ties of friendship and family in an exploited community, they come to understand the high cost of unchecked wealth and greed, and the ways in which neutrality always benefits the oppressors. The show’s creators make exceptionally good use of a limited budget and offer up some impressive queer rep along the way, a rarity in pop sci-fi. Stream Killjoys on Tubi or buy it from Prime Video and Apple TV.

Another great cyberpunk metropolis: here it's Kansai, an increasingly lawless city run by elite criminals known as Akudama. An ordinary girl, quite inadvertently, becomes caught up in a major planned heist and is forced to fake credentials as a master swindler in order to stay alive. Like Cyberpunk, the show tackles anti-authoritarian themes among a diverse crew of outsiders. Stream Akudama Drive on Cunrchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

While it’s been over three decades since the final Full House episode aired, DJ Tanner actress Candace Cameron Bure still feels her TV “family” is important to her. So, you can only imagine how emotional the TV actress’s tribute was for her TV dad, Bob Saget, on the fourth anniversary of his death this year. If you want to get more in your feels, Bure shared her sweet reaction to BTS footage showing her and Saget on set. Fans, prepare to bring out the tissues.

Since Bob Saget died in 2022 due to accidental blunt head trauma, Candace Cameron Bure said it’s been hard watching Full House clips. But after ET showed her throwback clips from 1994 of her and Saget together on the set of the sitcom (as well as an earlier joint interview with John Stamos), it brought out all kinds of emotional, nostalgic feels:

A post shared by Entertainment Tonight (@entertainmenttonight)

I just want to cry seeing the late stand-up comic introduce the former child star as his “TV daughter” as their arms are wrapped around each other. The emotions were already present when the Great American Media actress honored Saget through a series of photos. With each picture, it was clear that Saget didn't need to be Danny Tanner to show affection to his co-stars.

But seeing old clips of Saget with Bure reminded me why they made a great TV father/daughter duo on their show. Their familial chemistry on the ABC series was evident through every heartfelt talk, laugh and of course, hug.

As the former Hallmark Channel star was watching these clips, an emotional Bure revealed it was the first time she had ever seen them. While being “teary-eyed,” the Some Kind of Wonderful alum shared more about what she was thinking while reflecting on the good old days:

That was great! That was so fun to see. [...] Yeah, that was really emotional to see Bob. I just have so much love for him. I really do. He was such a good friend, such a loving person, and loved everyone so well. I miss him. I miss those hugs and the jokes.

The Full House alums truly appeared to have a friendship that stood the test of time. In fact, you could have called their friendship unlikely, as Bure couldn’t get into Saget's raunchy stand-up material. However, she said it was easy to be her TV dad’s friend, as she told herself to separate the comedian’s material from the "kindness" and "love" he brought out. Because the talented actress had known Saget since she was 11, it was no wonder they were still so close by the time the latter passed.

I’m glad that Candace Cameron Bure got to see her younger self with Bob Saget. As heartbreaking as it may be for me to watch those throwback clips, I’d like to believe it strengthens the love and memories she has with her old friend that’ll never go away. You can watch DJ and Danny navigate life together on Full House, which is streaming now with Disney+ subscription or an active Hulu subscription.

#3444. Stephen King Named This Alfred Hitchcock Thriller As One Of His Favorite Scary Movies

Back in 2017, IndieWire amassed a list of Stephen King's favorite scary movies based on the titles he had either previously recommended on social media or written about in his 1981 non-fiction book "Danse Macabre." Among the many, many films included were Ridley Scott's "Alien," Mario Bava's "Black Sunday," Brian De Palma's "Carrie" (itself based on King's own litany of feminine rage), and George A. Romero's "Dawn of the Dead."

Somewhat surprisingly, Alfred Hitchcock's 1972 serial killer "Frenzy" made the cut as well. "Frenzy" was Hitchcock's penultimate film and is famously the only one of Hitchcock's movies to receive an R rating in the United States. Indeed, one might be startled to see actual on-screen nudity in a film from The Master of Suspense. The murders in "Frenzy" are notably brutal, too, and the movie, quite shockingly, contains scenes of sexual assault. This was clearly an attempt by Hitchcock to push the envelope, and one can only speculate if he was drawn to the film's twisted serial killer mentality, the sweatiness of the overall picture, or its sheer amount of on-screen violence.

"Frenzy" tells the story of Richard Blaney (John Finch), a sad-sack and impoverished London-based former military man who is accused of sexually assaulting his ex-wife, Brenda (Barbara Leigh-Hunt), and using a necktie to strangle her to death. However, the necktie is connected to a string of other murders that have been committed all over the city, as the real killer is Richard's creepy friend Bob Rusk (Barry Foster).

As with so many other Alfred Hitchcock movies, the main character in "Frenzy" becomes a falsely accused man on the run (see also: "The Wrong Man," "Stage Fright," "The 39 Steps," "Young and Innocent," "North By Northwest," "Saboteur," "I Confess"), and he has to elude capture to clear his name. Along the way, Richard ends up finding an ally and lover in his former co-worker Babs (Anna Massey) ... although, with Rusk still engaged in his murderous shenanigans, that doesn't bode well for her.

Hitchcock films excel at making audiences unwittingly root for the bad guy (see "Dial M for Murder" and "Psycho" for two better-known examples), and "Frenzy" includes a sequence where Rusk has to retrieve a personal item of his from a victim whose body he has already disposed of. Because of this, viewers are forced to watch as he struggles with the tension of having to retrieve the incriminating evidence, and while we might not feel sympathy for Rusk, we do become involved in his plight. (It's one of the most noteworthy scenes in Hitchcock's filmography.) You can see, then, why Richard turns to Rusk for help at one point, not knowing that his friend is the murderer.

The final act of "Frenzy" gets a little involved and maybe spins a little too far off with its trials and prison sentences, but know that the ultimate conclusion is very satisfying. It's a tonally unique movie as well, feeling very loose and 1970s-y. And where many of Hitchcock's previous films felt mannered and polite despite involving murder and fetishes, "Frenzy" is comparatively casual, focusing more on Rusk's overcooked murderous mindset and the sexual element of his killing spree.

What many cineastes saw as the sexual subtext of Alfred Hitchcock's previous movies becomes text in "Frenzy." By the 1970s, the filmmaker could afford to be a little more frank. The murder scenes, more so than in any other Hitchcock movie, "Psycho" included, are brutal and unsettling. There's even one particularly memorable shot in "Frenzy" of one of Rusk's victims, freshly dead, with her eyes wide and her tongue lolling out, that will remain in your nightmares for quite some time. This is not the balletic, aesthetic, obfuscated violence of Hitchcock's earlier movies. This is disturbing.

Many critics responded very positively to "Frenzy" at the time. Roger Ebert gave the film four stars (out of four), writing that it was both a departure for Hitchcock and a return to form. As he put it:

"This is the kind of thriller Hitchcock was making in the 1940s, filled with macabre details, incongruous humor, and the desperation of a man convicted of a crime he didn't commit. The only 1970s details are the violence and the nudity (both approached with a certain grisly abandon that has us imagining 'Psycho' without the shower curtain). It's almost as if Hitchcock, at seventy-three, was consciously attempting to do once again what he did better than anyone else."

Ebert added that "Frenzy" possesses a nice macabre sense of humor, another feature Hitchcock's fans appreciate from the Master. Vincent Canby, writing for the New York Times, listed "Frenzy" as one of the 10 best films of its year, and it was a hit at the box office to boot. (There's a reason we here at /Film once listed it as one of Hitchcock's 20 best movies.) Clearly, Hitchcock hadn't lost his talent for snagging audiences.
