#3443. David Tennant Officially Returns to Doctor Who in 2027

Doctor Who — The Tenth Doctor and Rani is officially confirmed

The future of Doctor Who is uncertain, but at the very least, the universe has heard the pleas of fans who are in desperate need of more of David Tennant as the Tenth Doctor. That's right, there's even more time and space adventures for Tennant on the way, as he'll be reprising his role in a new audio drama from Big Finish — a British production company known for producing Doctor Who audio dramas and shorts.

However, instead of being joined by his well-known companions like Rose Tyler, Martha Jones, or Donna Noble, Tennant will be joined by a companion who may not be familiar to fans who have only watched Doctor Who. Enter Anjli Mohindra, who is reprising her role as Rani Chandra. The Big Finish 12-episode audio drama series will be released in August 2027, and is titled Doctor Who — The Tenth Doctor and Rani.

Mohindra first stepped into the world of Who in the 2008 Doctor Who spinoff, The Sarah Jane Adventures. Rani, alongside Luke Smith, Clyde Langer, and the robot dog K9, helped former Doctor companion Sarah Jane Smith in protecting Earth from alien threats. Curious and passionate, Sarah Jane took Rani under her wing and helped her learn journalism. After Sarah Jane's death, Rani would go on to become one of the best journalists in the world.

The audio drama will reunite the Doctor and Rani, brought together by their connection to Sarah Jane. According to the official Big Finish news post, the three new adventures following the duo will see them investigate cryptids in modern-day Cumbria, crash the set of a 1970s sci-fi show, and even deal with a huge crisis at the coronation of Elizabeth I. It's never a slow day if you travel with the Doctor.

This isn't the first time that the Doctor and Rani have met. The Tenth Doctor also made an appearance in "The Wedding of Sarah Jane Smith" from The Sarah Jane Adventures, though Rani was much younger than she is now. Whether that meeting will have any significance remains to be seen.

Tennant's return to Doctor Who might not be the triumphant return to the TV series as some fans might have hoped, but for Whovians who want more of Tennant before he first regenerated, this 12-episode series is a new epic adventure that provides just that.

Doctor Who — The Tenth Doctor and Rani will be released in August 2027.

#3442. Five Smartwatch Heart Rate Zone Hacks Every Runner Should Know

If you've spent any time in or around running culture over the last few years, you've undoubtedly encountered someone preaching the gospel of Zone 2 cardio. Legend has it that easy, conversational effort cardio—also known as cardio that takes your heart rate into "Zone 2"—is the secret to unlocking everything from a bigger aerobic engine to faster race times and even a longer life.

To train by heart rate, you aim to keep your heart rate in the "zone" that gives you the desired workout. The catch is that Zone 2 is easy to get wrong, especially since no one can agree on what it actually means.  Your smartwatch can show you your heart rate, but many recreational runners will still drift into a “gray zone” that's too fast to be truly easy, and too slow to give them a real workout. If you're struggling to hit Zone 2 consistently, there are a few smartwatch hacks that can help.

Pace can be a distraction during easy runs, especially considering all the different variables that affect your effort, like hills, humidity, and general fatigue. A 9:30 mile might be Zone 2 on a flat, cool day and Zone 4 on a hot, hilly one.

Dig into your watch's activity settings (on Garmin, it's Activity > Data Screens; on Apple Watch, the Workout app's metrics layout; on Coros, Polar, and Suunto, similar menus) and put live heart rate zone front and center, ideally as a zone number or colored gauge rather than just a raw bpm figure (though this assumes these zones are accurate—more on that below).

Create an alert when your heart rate goes above or below a target range, delivered as a vibration pattern, a beep, or both. Set the alert for the upper boundary of Zone 2, and you've essentially hired a mini coach who taps you on the wrist whenever you get overzealous. Whenever you hear or feel that buzz, you’ll know you need to ease into a slower jog until your heart rate settles.

Instead of free-running and checking your numbers afterward, build structured workouts that carry the targets for you. In Garmin Connect, TrainingPeaks, Apple's Custom Workout feature, Coros Training Hub, or similar platforms, you can create sessions like "10-minute warm-up in Zone 1, 40 minutes in Zone 2, 5-minute cooldown" and sync them straight to your watch.

During the run, your watch displays the current step, the target range, and whether you're above, below, or in the pocket. Many will automatically advance between intervals and alert you when it's time to shift gears.

Heart rate-based intervals, like 4 x 4 minutes in Zone 4 with Zone 1 recovery, where you don't have to do mental math or check the clock.

Progressive long runs that start in Zone 2 and finish in Zone 3.

Hill repeats, where pace is meaningless but effort matters.

Most watches calculate default zones using a generic formula like 220 minus your age, which can be off by 10 to 20 beats for any given individual. If your zones are wrong, your Zone 2 training isn't Zone 2 training.

Here’s how to fix your watch’s heart rate zones:

Find your true max heart rate. The informal way is to just notice what number you see on your watch when you can no longer speak comfortably; the more formal way is this treadmill test. You can also look through your recent hard efforts, like races, hill repeats, or all-out intervals, and see the highest sustained heart rate you've recorded.

Use lactate threshold heart rate instead. Many watches can estimate this automatically after a few hard efforts, and zones built from threshold tend to be more personalized than ones built from max.

Customize the boundaries. Dive into the heart rate zone settings and input your own numbers. Some runners prefer the "MAF" method (180 minus age, with adjustments) for aerobic base building, and most watches let you set that as a custom range.

Recheck every few months. Fitness changes, and so do your zones.

A screen crowded with cadence, vertical oscillation, ground contact time, running power, and lap pace is a recipe for second-guessing.

Create a dedicated Zone 2 data screen with just two or three fields: current heart rate zone, elapsed time, and maybe distance. Turn off auto-scroll so it doesn't flip to a screen full of numbers you don't need. If your watch supports multiple activity profiles, make a separate "Easy Run" profile with this stripped-down layout and keep a different profile for tempo days and races.

A chest strap (or a forearm or upper-arm optical band) is generally more accurate and responsive than the wrist-based sensor on your watch. For heart rate training, where a few beats can mean the difference between Zone 2 and Zone 3, I recommend buying one. This COOSPO heart rate monitor is one of my favorites, and it's only $31.99.

The bottom line: Your smartwatch can make heart rate training far easier, but only if you set it up to support you rather than overwhelm you.

#3441. Tallulah Willis: I Stayed Out Past My Bedtime to Celebrate My Mom at the Baby2Baby Gala

The whole endeavor began as it usually does, with a search for the perfect dress. Turns out it would be a yellow Carolina Herrera column-shaped confection (if you care), teetering on yellow satin pointed peekaboo-toe platforms, with my first press pass thudding around in my corresponding yellow duchess satin clutch.

Stylist Brad Goreski and his assistant Clarke, who work with my mother, Demi Moore, sourced the ensemble after finding Mom’s beautiful black ruffled two-piece (adorably also Carolina Herrera).

Around 6:50 p.m. on Saturday, my older sisters, Scout (in cocoa-brown beaded Elie Saab) and Rumer (in whimsical archival Vera Wang), florist Eric Buterbaugh, Brad, my mom and I are about to leave her house for the Baby2Baby Gala, an annual fundraiser for the non-profit that dedicated to providing diapers, clothing, and other basic necessities to children and families in need across the country.

Demi is taking photos against a pale brown backdrop when I hear her say, marginally worried, “Yes, the outfit is amazing, but they didn’t give me pockets.” I cannot fault her. A pocket, particularly in an evening gown, creates an entirely different architecture for one’s night.

When we make it to the Pacific Design Center in West Hollywood, Rihanna is blasting and a gorgeous electric General Motors car, part of the silent auction, is parked out front. I’m holding the bottom of my dress to avoid any “yard sales” on the carpeted floor when I hear, “Is it you? I hope it’s you!” It’s my very new, lovely friend Jackie Tohn, whom I met at a Nobody Wants This premiere party.

Inside, beautifully dressed people laugh and chat. I spot Miranda Kerr, who is both a Baby2Baby board member and major donor, and pass Nara Smith leaning over a dolled-up Elsa Hosk while “Espresso” blasts from overhead speakers.

Table 4 is front and center. Some could say the best seats in the house. Fitting, as Baby2Baby is honoring my mother with the Giving Tree Award tonight. The scene around our table is a frenzy of joyful energy. I make a beeline for Paris Hilton to thank her for the facial I received at her spa this week, while Dancing With the Stars alums Rumer and Jenna Dewan immediately pull out their phones to compare pictures of their kids.

Then I spot Sofia Richie Grainge and her husband, Atlantic Records CEO Elliot Grainge. I snake through throngs of elegant people and poke Elliot’s back twice. “Elliot, it’s Tallulah! We went to Wildwood together!” He instantly remembers me. “Tallulah was the cool girl in class,” he tells Sofia. I blush, but don’t feel the need to correct him.

Scout approaches and says, almost incredulously, “Hi, I’m Scout…you guys just signed me at Atlantic Records.” Elliot grabs her shoulders. “We’re so happy to have you. Are you happy with us?” She can’t say “yes” fast enough.

The program begins with Keke Palmer, who completely owns the stage, telling hilarious stories about her son before shifting into heartfelt candor about the gift of watching him grow. Kerry Washington thanks the sponsors and announces Baby2Baby’s new permanent headquarters, “a promise to millions of children. Not just for today, but for decades to come.”

Then Kelly Sawyer Patricof and Norah Weinstein, the organization’s CEOs, come to the stage, sharing the work—no, the magic—they have created over 15 years. Their first gala in 2012 raised $1 million. Last year’s raised $18 million. To date, they’ve distributed an astonishing 850 million essential items to people in need across all 50 states, responded to over 150 disasters, developed their own diaper production line during COVID, and expanded into mental health support for new mothers. The mission remains the same, but the scale is impossible to comprehend.

Now Rumer, Scout, and I are all crying during a short video about two families impacted by Baby2Baby. The feeling is palpable for the rest of the room.

As the live auction begins, I catch my mom discreetly reading over a printout of her speech. I don’t feel nerves coming off her, but a desire to match the elegance and integrity surrounding us.

Andrew Garfield takes the stage and speaks directly to my mom about the woman he knows. “She is a miracle,” he says.

Then it’s Demi’s turn. Holding her gleaming award in two hands, she thanks Andrew for carving out time amid his Artificial press tour. My mother adores Andrew, a feeling shared across our family.

Alone on stage in her Carolina gown (sans pockets), she asks everyone to breathe. “Inhale. Exhale.” That breath, she says, is the relief Baby2Baby provides when a mother no longer has to choose between dinner and diapers. “Your child matters, you matter, and you are not alone.” She leaves us with the idea that the essence of this work is to be remarkably human. Baby to baby, mother to mother, soul to soul.

Then Cardi B takes the stage and the atmosphere shifts with a jolt. Everyone is on their feet dancing. The official after-party begins, but I’m turning back into a pumpkin in towering satin stilettos. It was a remarkably beautiful night, and I’m left with the overwhelming desire to do more—to show up for someone who may not have the ability to show up for themselves or their precious loved ones.

But for this on-scene reporter’s inaugural correspondence, it was ultimately Baby2Baby2Bedtime.

#3440. If You Liked Colleen Hoover's Verity, Watch Dakota Johnson's Acclaimed 2025 Movie Next

If you liked seeing Dakota Johnson starring in a twisted psychosexual drama like "Verity," which is based on the novel by Colleen Hoover, you might want to check out the more adult romantic drama "Materialists," Celine Song's acidic essay on modern dating from 2025. /Film's Bill Bria said in his review of "Materialists" that it was structured like a typical rom-com, but more heartfelt, full of yearning and depth.

More than anything, though, "Materialists" deals with a deeply cynical approach to romance, just as the title would lead you to believe. It's about how modern matchmaking has become a painfully specialized industry because modern adults have become all too fixated on the superficial qualities — and the earning power — of their potential mates. Johnson plays a cold-hearted matchmaker-for-the-rich named Lucy who has trouble weaning her male clients off of the idea of dating younger women exclusively. The movie itself seems to wince whenever one of Lucy's clients says they desire a woman who is "fit"; those characters might as well be yelling "no fat chicks."

Over the course of the film, Lucy finds herself torn between two potential boyfriends who have both appeared — or reappeared — in her life. On the one hand, she can pursue Harry (Pedro Pascal), an unbearably handsome, unfathomably rich, and suitably tall man who ticks all the boxes on the average dating profile requirement list. On the other hand, she has reconnected with her ex-boyfriend John (Chris Evans), a struggling actor who was always disorganized and never wealthy, but who loved her deeply. Does Lucy choose a life of poverty undergirded by true love, or does she follow her more cutthroat, materialistic instincts, and pursue the wealthy man who can give her a life of luxury?

For long portions of "Materialists," Lucy's choice seems obvious. Harry may not have the same kind of passion as John, but he is definitely interested in Lucy, and he is happy to share his wealth. There is a coldness, however, to his well-moneyed lifestyle, and something vaguely transactional about his love affair. She also becomes startled when she learns a secret about Harry that we won't spoil here. She begins to question if her attraction to him is genuine, or if it just checks the right boxes on a typical dating profile.

As "Materialists" unspools, however, it begins to skew away from the acidic nature of its opening act and begins strolling toward a drama about romantic truthfulness. Lucy is also thrown for a loop when she unwittingly matches one of her long-single clients Sophie (Zoë Winters) with a man who sexually assaults Sophie. Lucy subsequently doubts her every romantic instinct, and a portion of "Materialists" becomes about Lucy trying to reach out to Sophie to make amends. Perhaps she can mitigate her bad romantic instincts by being a genuine friend to this woman.

The ultimate answer is perhaps a little treacly, but Lucy finds herself drawn back to John. The pair had previously broken up over his incapacity for amassing wealth and her frustrations with the boring everyday financial struggles they went through. Now, however, she is beginning to appreciate the nature of human connection, and John looks more and more romantically alluring.

Of course, one could argue that Dakota Johnson, in being torn between Chris Evans and Pedro Pascal, is hardly in an unenviable place. We should all be so lucky to have two devastatingly handsome movie stars equally eager to court us.

"Materialists" was a pretty big hit, making almost $108 million worldwide on a relatively small budget of only $20 million. When the movie hit streaming, "Materialists" became a hit for HBO Max. The film isn't terribly deep in its commentary on the foibles of modern romance and the shallowness therein, but it's at least about something, and it features multiple beautiful people alternately romancing one another. It also, according to our exclusive interview with writer/director Celine Song, was modeled on a film noir, giving the film an alluring, mysterious quality. All those elements put together seemingly were what drew people out in such numbers.

Critics largely liked "Materialists," as evidenced by its 77% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, based on 307 reviews. Angelica Jade Bastién, writing for Vulture, felt that the movie didn't delve deeply enough into its own thesis that modern romance is directly tied to capitalism. Indeed, she wrote that, in its last act, the film "pivots to a more conventional romantic narrative of the kind it had promised to upend, if not outright critique."

Stephanie Zacharek, writing for Time Magazine, was more generous, writing that Celine Song is speaking very much to the moment, analyzing what romance means in an ego-driven and money-driven world of Instagram and an easily reduced sense of personal value. "That's the world 'Materialists' takes place in," Zacharek writes, "and Song sees what's funny and what's terrible about it at once—even as she acknowledges that it's human to yearn for beautiful things, and for comfort. She's chosen the perfect actors for this enterprise."

If you want a romance that mixes acid with some thoughtfulness, check out "Materialists."

Spoilers for Season 2, Episode 6 of Marshals are ahead! You can stream the series with a Paramount+ subscription and catch new episodes on CBS every Sunday.

The episode of Marshals that just aired on the 2026 TV schedule is inspired by a tragedy that actually happened to one of its stars and American Indian Affairs Coordinator, Mo Brings Plenty, and his family. In 2024, his nephew, Cole Brings Plenty, died, and a coroner ruled out foul play. His family disagreed with that, and they’re still looking for answers. In this week's episode of Marshals, Mo’s nephew, Troy, is found dead, and he and Kayce work to prove that it was a murder, not suicide. Ultimately, the case is left unsolved, and according to Mo Brings Plenty, that was a very important detail to include.

Knowing that “Roughstock” was inspired by his own experiences, I asked Mo Brings Plenty, who plays Mo in Marshals and Yellowstone, about details in the episode he was happy to see included. He immediately noted that he was glad the case was left unsolved, because that kind of outcome happens in real life, often, as the actor explained:

Oh, I was happy to see that when the police officer said he just kind of blew it off, because that's really the case. And so I was happy that we showed that legitimate part of it. Not every officer is that way, but in some cases, in some states - primarily states that have a high American Indian population - that occurs.

When I spoke to Mo in March this year about an episode of Marshals having to do with missing American Indians, he told me they “haven’t got any answers for” what happened to his nephew, Cole.

In this episode of Marshals, it’s made very clear that while Troy’s case will stay open, it will likely go unsolved. It’s obvious that it’s not being prioritized by law enforcement, and despite the marshals best efforts, there is no solution as to who killed Troy by the end of the episode. When I asked Mo why it was important for this episode to go without a solution to Troy’s case, he said:

Because the wheel of justice doesn't turn for us as American Indian people, and of course we're tax-paying people as well. And so, you know, first responders get their funding through taxpayers, tax funding, and so when it doesn't work for us, then it's so frustrating. It's like, ‘Well, why are we even paying taxes?’ And so that's one of the things that is impactful for me, and that I need to continue to speak about because it is occurring.

In the case of Mo’s real nephew, Cole, he was found dead a few days after he was reported missing and named as a suspect in a domestic violence case. Two years later, Mo spoke to THR and claimed that his nephew’s death had gone “uninvestigated,” while the Lawrence Police Department said there was “no foul play involved in Cole’s death.”

When I spoke to Mo about this topic recently and how it was represented on this Yellowstone show, he said:

It's sad for me and my family, especially when I hear the cry for other nationalities and in foreign countries, when the very same thing is occurring to us as the original inhabitants within this country, we're basically flying over mission fields to get to mission fields.

According to the U.S. Department of the Interior Indian Affairs, there are “approximately 4,200 missing and murder cases that have gone unsolved.” And when I asked Mo Brings Plenty if Marshals could ever circle back to Troy’s unsolved case, he said:

Absolutely, it could definitely happen. But you know, there are so many stories. I mean, my family is not the only family. This isn't the first time something like this has occurred in real life. You know, there are many stories, many families, different situations, different circumstances that are going through the same thing.

Overall, he was clear that there are lots of stories like his that should be shown on Kayce’s Yellowstone spinoff. He’s not the only one who has lost a loved one in this way and was left without answers, and he’s hoping to see more of those stories depicted on Marshals.

Now, to see how Mo’s story continues, you can watch the next episode of Marshals on November 22 at 8:30 p.m. ET, and you can stream it the next day on Paramount+.

#3438. These Early Black Friday Ring Camera Deals Start at $24.99

If you’re browsing home security options, Ring has one of the best early Black Friday deals that should be on your radar. Right now, you can add an indoor camera and another one at your front door for less than $65. The Ring Indoor Cam 2K is 58% off at $24.99 (originally $59.99), while the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is 60% off at $39.99 (originally $99.99)—both at their lowest-ever price.

Both offer features like 2K video and two-way talk, but the indoor cam is the simpler purchase if you mainly want to check on a pet or kids and see what’s happening near an entrance. It plugs into an outlet, so there’s no battery to recharge, and its low-light color video helps preserve detail when lights are off or dimmed. However, since it’s a fixed-view camera, keep in mind that you’ll need to position it carefully.

The Battery Doorbell is the better pick if alerting you to visitors, deliveries, and potential intruders is your priority. It has a 140-degree horizontal and vertical field of view that provides head-to-toe framing, plus up to 6x zoom for better detail. You can install it without wiring, though you’ll need to recharge its built-in battery. It also requires a 2.4GHz wifi network.

The main catch with both devices is the ongoing subscription cost: Live viewing, two-way talk, and basic real-time notifications all work without a subscription, but reviewing saved footage requires a paid plan, starting at $4.99 per month or $49.99 annually for one device; coverage for multiple devices at one location starts at $9.99 monthly or $99.99 annually.

At these prices, the Ring Indoor Cam 2K is perfect for occasional live check-ins, while the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is better suited to monitoring your front entrance. Buying both makes sense if you already have a Ring plan that covers extra devices.

#3437. Penélope Cruz Says She and Husband Javier Bardem are “Very Careful” About Choosing When to Work Together

Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem are very selective about when they work on a project together, but the opportunity to costar in director Florian Zeller's timely psychological thriller Bunker was too enticing to pass up.

"When [Zeller] came to us with this powerful, very necessary story to tell, we looked at each other and there was no way to say no to this," Cruz said during a post-screening discussion at Vanity Fair’s Screening Room on Sunday. "I'm very, very happy that we did it."

Bunker revolves around a married couple, Miguel (Bardem) and Sofia (Cruz), whose 17-year marriage is tested when Miguel, a famous architect, is presented with a life changing work opportunity.

“I really wanted to work with them because I truly believe they are [two] of the greatest actors working today,” Zeller said during the panel discussion moderated by VF's West Coast Editor John Ross. “I was also very excited and interested to have them together onscreen because they are also a real couple. I thought it would be an interesting and unique opportunity to approach something that has to do with authenticity, with the truth. Not to say that this is their story, because of course this is not their story.”

Florian Zeller at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 15, 2026

Cruz said she felt a kinship with her character's concerns. “We have so many things in common in terms of this sadness and frustration and anger that you feel in terms of where is the world going if we don't wake up soon,” she said. “I hope it's not too late, but especially the experiment that is being done on younger people, children, teenagers, it just makes me very furious.

“It's something that affects me so much as an actress, as a mother, as a citizen of the world, that I felt completely a need to play Sophia,” she continued. “And of course it was not the only reason, but it was a big privilege to be able to say those lines. And [Zeller] is such a master of writing and I am a fan of all his work. And same for Javier, who is not here with us today, he's doing theater, but we are very careful in terms of choosing when to work together.”

Pénelope Cruz, Florian Zeller and John Ross at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 15, 2026

Cruz praised Zeller’s ability to provide a supportive, safe working environment and his strong point of view. “We felt really, really safe with him, he's so talented. He doesn't need any kind of manipulation and he never treats the audience as not intelligent because the audience can feel everything,” she explained. “And that has become really the most important thing for me. Don't over-explain, don't underestimate the audience ever because the thermometer is really working. And also with young people more and more and more. That is my hope to continue to go to see films on a big screen. They're coming back thank God. So let's create more possibilities so they can keep doing that.”

Cruz also said that she and Bardem have similar approaches to their work and the preparation it requires. “It's true that we share the same passion and we have done this since we were teenagers,” she said. “We love exploring and studying and feeling that healthy fear of the unknown because every time you begin a project, in a way, it's really starting from zero. So it's a really good thing to share.”

Zeller called his collaboration with the couple “a fascinating journey. It takes a lot of courage or fearlessness to do that, I think, for actors.” He also revealed that he initially referenced Stanley Kubrick's seminal thriller Eyes Wide Shut as a point of reference for Bunker, but realized it might not be setting the proper tone, given the circumstances.

“I remember that the first time I spoke with [Cruz] and Javier about this project, I mentioned a film that was somewhere in my mind, Eyes Wide Shut. Not to say that there is any kind of connection between the two films, but as you remember, Eyes Wide Shut at the time, Tom Cruise and Nicole Kidman, they were together," he said. "And I remember as a viewer that it was so interesting to be in a position where you do not know exactly what you're invited to watch… but Javier [later] told me, ‘You should not mention this film too often because remember at the end of the shooting they broke up.’ And then I realized that the director, Kubrick, died soon after. So I was like, ‘Okay, I'm going to stop mentioning this film.’ But the real difference I would say is that we knew that the destination of that film was the last image of the painting that you saw, which means that it was about how to reconnect with the other.”

Pénelope Cruz, Florian Zeller and John Ross at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 15, 2026

The invitation-only events are welcoming an audience from the worlds of film, fashion, culture, politics, media, and tech, much like the magazine itself.

#3436. Ms. Marvel Star Iman Vellani Believes This Is The Perfect X-Men Story (And She's Right)

Whatever role Kamala Khan has to play in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, Marvel Studios needs to keep actress Iman Vellani on its payroll. A genuine comic book expert and enthusiast, Vellani is currently flexing her knowledge as co-host of Marvel's "Countdown to Avengers: Doomsday" podcast, running through all 15 films on the official "Doomsday" prep list. On the "X-Men" episode covering the original 2000s "X-Men" film trilogy, Vellani got into her love for the source material of "X2" — Chris Claremont and Brent Anderson's 1982 graphic novel, "X-Men: God Loves, Man Kills."

"If I had to recommend a single 'X-Men' comic that kind of encapsulates, like, it's the purest distillation of what these characters represent, it's 'God Loves, Man Kills,'" Vellani said, echoing common consensus among "X-Men" fans. The book's villain is Reverend William Stryker, a televangelist who believes mutants are demonic. When Stryker's "Purifiers" abduct Professor X in a plot for mutant genocide, the X-Men ally with Magneto against their common foe.

"Stryker's speaking for God, but he's preaching hatred and murder. It's so dark and explores how a lot of people's beliefs are often more dangerous than the people themselves," said Vellani. ("X2" left out the comic's religious themes and is a lesser story.)

Claremont wrote "X-Men" for 16 years and almost 200 issues. It's a soap opera, and it's so hard to pick a single story that stands out as ideal for new readers. Except for "God Loves, Man Kills," which, as Claremont told Vox in 2017, was the entire idea: "If you never read an issue of ['X-Men'] but wanted to know what the series, the concepts, the characters, the reality was all about — and to do so in a way that had, and sadly still has, relevance to the 'real world' — this was the story."

To this day, "God Loves, Man Kills" is one of the few books in Marvel's library that reaches true literary prestige, and which can compare to the great works of their rival publisher DC, like Frank Miller's "The Dark Knight Returns" or Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons' "Watchmen." It runs over 60 pages, three times as long as a typical "X-Men" issue. The art is also moodier and more down to earth than other Chris Claremont-written "X-Men" comics; heavier shadows and no flat coloring reflects the less fantastical tone.

The comic also adds more texture to how humans hate and fear mutants. The opening scene is Stryker's Purifiers gunning down two mutant children and stringing their bodies up. (Adding to the lynching imagery, both children are Black.) There's no robotic Sentinels hunting mutants here, only hateful human beings. "Genocide in the name of God. A story as old as the race," Magneto bitterly observes of the Purifiers.

The rest of the comic remains bracingly political. Claremont wrote "God Loves, Man Kills" in response to "the rise of the evangelical movement across the United States and their insertion into the political process" during the 1980s. Reverend Stryker would fit right in with the Moral Majority. (It's worth noting that one of the evangelical movement's casus belli in those days was opposition to school desegregation.) While "God Loves, Man Kills" remains a clear product of the 1980s, its themes are timeless; you would only have to change the allegory's specifics to set it today. Perhaps in 2026, Stryker would propagate mutant hatred with social media and podcasts instead of television.

But while "God Loves, Man Kills" remains Claremont's masterpiece to most, it's not without controversy — for one scene in particular.

Kitty Pryde gets in a brawl with a boy who calls her a "mutie lover" (unaware she is a mutant). Her Black friend Stevie Hunter tries to calm her, so an enraged Kitty asks Stevie if she'd be preaching tolerance if the slur had been the N-word instead of "mutie." In the original printing, the slur was written in full, though modern printings censor it.

I've never forgotten reading that when I was about 13-years-old: a Marvel comic was allowed to print something like that? The shock value has a point to make; it's easier to say "stick and stones" about bigotry if you're not its target. It makes the racism against mutants feel real and harmful, yet it tests allegory's limits: Mutants aren't real, but anti-Black racism is.

Chris Claremont more elegantly tied mutants' oppression to reality a year earlier in 1981 when, in "X-Men" #150, he revealed Magneto as a Holocaust survivor. (Claremont is Jewish himself.) "God Loves, Man Kills" comes off of that then-fresh reinvention and was pivotal in cementing Magneto as no longer a megalomaniac. Throughout the story, Magneto urges the X-Men to make their alliance permanent, but on his terms. When Kitty instead asks Magneto to join them, he refuses: "For all our sakes — mutant and human — I hope you [succeed]. But should you fail, it will be my turn."

Magneto and the X-Men both believe Stryker's hatred will endure even with his defeat. Stryker's claim that mutants are made in the Devil's image also hits especially hard for Nightcrawler, who does look demonic despite being a practicing Catholic. Later works, including "X-Men: The Animated Series," would explore that religious conflict inside Nightcrawler, pushing on the boundaries that "God Loves, Man Kills" tested first.

Warning! The following contains spoilers from the 90 Day Fiancé: The Other Way episode "Out Of The Frying Pan, Into The Family." Stream the episode with an HBO Max subscription, and read at your own risk!

Niles Valentine has kept his wife, Matilda, in the dark since the start of the 2026 TV schedule about his plan to move to Ghana. He finally decided to drop the bombshell in this latest episode, and predictably, she was pretty upset to learn he was no longer working toward bringing her to the United States. Given her anger, there was a possibility this married 90 Day couple could split at the end of the season.

With various rumors floating around the internet about their status, I decided to do a bit of digging to see what I could find on whether series veterans Niles and Matilda are still together. While I didn't expect either of them to break their contract agreements and explicitly say one way or another, I think it's safe to say it looks like they're still together, with some predictable updates.

Niles posted a photo on Instagram of what appeared to be the inside of an apartment in the United States back on November 13th. Readers can take a look at the post below, in which he showed the difference someone's posture can make. Take a look:

A post shared by Niles Valentine (@roman_cupid_95)

That doesn't look like any room in Matilda's apartment, which has me guessing he's back in the United States at this point. I can't claim to be an expert on apartments in Africa, but I've lived in a good deal of American ones that have that exact same look when it comes to the bathroom!

Niles returning home feels like the most obvious outcome in this season of 90 Day Fiancé: The Other Way. Matilda married him in the hopes of coming to the United States and not just having a better life for herself but for her family back in Africa as well. She's obviously mad that Niles couldn't make it happen as soon as he promised, but that doesn't mean she wants him to give up.

If Niles has returned to the US, I think it's fair to speculate that he and Matilda are still together. The pair still follow each other on Instagram, which usually feels like an obvious sign that 90 Day couples are still together and married.

Why 90 Day Fiancé's New Florida Spinoff Has Me Questioning If We've Lost The Plot

If we get to the end of 90 Day Fiancé: The Other Way and learn that Niles is still working to bring Matilda to the United States, I won't be surprised. That's been the goal from the start, and I think he made a rash decision to move to Africa without looking into how difficult it would be for him to start a life in the country.

Niles may not be incredibly wealthy, but his earning potential in the United States is likely higher than it would be in Ghana. Even if she doesn't have her husband with her, I can understand wanting to wait as long as it takes for him to find a way to bring her to the United States rather than changing the plan.

90 Day Fiancé: The Other Way continues on TLC on Sundays at 8:00 p.m. ET. We'll see how things shake out for Niles and Matilda down the stretch, and keep an eye on the other couples taking part as well.

He graduated from the University of Southern Indiana with a degree in Journalism and a minor in Radio and Television. He's great at hosting panels and appearing on podcasts if given the chance as well.

#3434. Apple Won't Make a Small Phone so This Company Is Stepping In

Big smartphones have long been the norm. It seems many, if not most, of us prefer our smartphones to be akin to tiny tablets. Even Apple's smallest iPhone isn't that small, with a 6.1-inch display. (Compare that to the 5.4-inch iPhone mini it used to sell.) But just because a lot of us like it that way doesn't mean all of us do.

Despite what companies like Apple would lead you to believe, there are plenty of people out there who want their smartphones to be smaller. For some, the iPhone mini was perfect, featuring a design that most could use comfortably with one hand. While the sales might not have been steady enough for Apple to continue producing the mini line, anecdotally, I know quite a few people who would happily keep using iPhones this small, if only Apple would make more of them. Perhaps you know people like this too; maybe you're one of them.

While the rumor mill does not suggest that Apple plans to make a new iPhone mini, that doesn't mean the dream of the tiny smartphone is dead. Enter "Enough Phone," a new device with a humble goal: to create a "small, modern smartphone that's enough."

Enough Phone really does seem small. The company says its upcoming device is 133mm by 64mm, and less than 12mm thick. That's the equivalent of 5.24 inches by 2.52 inches, and less than 0.47 inches thick. It's remarkably similar to the iPhone 13 mini, at 5.18 by 2.53 inches, and 0.3 inches thick. While the Enough Phone might be a tad larger overall, and perhaps noticeably thicker, it's still reminiscent of that "mini" footprint.

The Enough Phone's 5.3-inch display isn't particularly modern, however. While we don't know the display type, we do know that it has a resolution of 1520 x 720, which may look less sharp to anyone coming from the 2340 x 1080 resolution of the iPhone 13 mini. I'd wager that most people interested in a device like this aren't looking for an ultra-sharp OLED display anyway, but it's worth noting here.

As for the Enough Phone's other specs, the company says it plans to pack in a 2.4GHz MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chip with 8GB of RAM, 128GB of built-in storage, though you can expand that with a microSD card (something you don't see on many smartphones these days). The current plan is to ship with a single 50MP Sony IMX766 rear camera, and a 32MP selfie cam, which would be amongst the highest-resolution front-facing cameras on any smartphone. It supports 5G, Wi-Fi 6, and eSIM, with the option to use a physical SIM as well.

Enough is also aiming to make its smartphone more repairable than the competition. While smartphone OEMs have made slight improvements to repairability in recent years, few phones are made to be opened up by the user, and their components replaced. While Enough Phone isn't fully modular, it is designed with easy-to-open screws, and comes with a fully replaceable 3,500 mAh battery. Combined with promised software support through 2032, Enough says this device "should last you into the next decade."

Now, all of these specs are targets, as the phone is currently in the prototype stage. Enough says that final details may change "slightly" during testing. I would at least hope that the dimensions, particularly the screen size, remain the same by launch. What will likely stay the same, however, are the ringtones: Enough says they hired composer Brian Squillance of LAANDS to produce the jingles for its phone, which is a neat touch.

Unfortunately for Apple fans, however, Enough Phone isn't an iPhone. That said, it doesn't have to be an Android phone, either. While you can buy the phone with Android 17 installed, you can also choose to run OdysseyOS, a minimalist "de-Googled" operating system made by SLEKE. Enough says OdysseyOS is meant for "intentional phone use," which might appeal to anyone looking for a phone that's "dumb" as well as small.

Of course, neither operating system is iOS. Unfortunately for Apple users, the only true iPhone options here are to continue using an old iPhone mini, which Apple does still support, or to opt for an iPhone 17e, the smallest iPhone the company currently makes. It's pretty easy to find a used and refurbished iPhone 13 mini for reasonable price; but while they can still run the latest version of iOS, you won't be able to take advantage of all of Apple's newest features. Plus, while there's no telling how long Apple plans to support the 13 line for, it won't support it forever—by iOS 28 or iOS 29, your phone might lose support entirely.

If the promise of a modern mini smartphone entices you, you can back the Enough Phone on Kickstarter today. While the company's $399 "Super Early Bird" reward is already sold out, as of this article, the "Early Bird" reward is still up. That reward costs $449, and includes a glass screen protector pre-installed, a protective case, a USB-C cable, a USB-C to 3.5mm headphone adapter, a hex screwdriver, and green "Founders' Edition" backplate screws. Enough says that the retail price for its phone will be $599 after the campaign, so you can save $150 by backing the phone today—if you're serious about small phones. The Enough Phone is slated for a May 2027 launch.

#3433. All 10 Zelda: Ocarina of Time Bosses, Ranked From Worst to Best

Explore the top 10 bosses in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, ranked by challenge, design, and excitement.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time brought every great aspect back from the original version — including its iconic boss fights. From fire-breathing dragons to giant spiders to wicked witches, Ocarina of Time features a diverse lineup of boss battles that adds to every dungeon's unique charm, making this one of the best games in The Legend of Zelda series.

Many of the bosses force players to use the items obtained in their respective dungeons in Ocarina of Time. But overall, many of them feature such clever designs and battles that have made exploring the dungeons worthwhile. In fact, the bosses are so great that Nintendo has allowed players to fight them again in the remake’s Hall of Fallen Foes.

No boss in this game is the same, and some are far better than others. While Zelda fans may be familiar with them from the original game, some of the bosses have been given some enhancements in the remake. So now, here are all the bosses in Ocarina of Time ranked from worst to best.

Nintendo made the Water Temple in Ocarina of Time much easier and enjoyable for gamers in the remake, but the aquatic boss fight still feels dry. There’s nothing visually noteworthy about Morpha, as it’s essentially a giant blob of water with an amoeba inside it. The player simply has to use the Longshot to pull out Morpha’s core and strike it repeatedly. Though the remake gives Morpha some more dynamic attacks, many can agree that Dark Link was a much more interesting battle in the Water Temple.

This giant, fire-breathing dinosaur takes over the cavern in which Gorons harvest their rock roast, forcing Link to go in and take it out. Though it is a fearsome presence, King Dodongo loses points for being just a bigger version of the regular Dodongo. At the same time, the boss battle is very straightforward, as Link must repeatedly throw bombs into the beast's mouth before hitting its weak spot. At least it features its own theme song rather than the traditional boss music.

Lord Jabu-Jabu has some truly weird things in his stomach, from a giant octopus to electric jellyfish to fleshy elevators. But what really takes the cake is the dungeon's boss, Barinade: a giant, tentacled blob that shoots lightning bolts. To defeat it, Link must use the boomerang to sever its tentacles and strike its core, all while avoiding its giant jellyfish and electric blasts.

Barinade is one of the wildest battles in Ocarina of Time and the remake improves the experience by putting it in a dark, neon-lit chamber. It also adds another bit of protection for the boss' weak point, making the fight a more challenging test of the player's skill, timing, and patience.

Deep inside the Deku Tree, Link encounters his first boss in the form of Gohma. The buildup to this fight is straight out of a horror movie, with Link noticing dirt falling from above before seeing a giant, one-eyed spider crawling above him. The fight itself is pretty simple, as Link must use the Fairy Slingshot to shoot the monster's exposed eye. Given that it's the first boss fight of the game, it doesn't offer a huge challenge. Nevertheless, it serves as a strong preview to the other horrors Link must face throughout Hyrule.

This ancient lava dragon was revived by Ganondorf to eat the Gorons of Death Mountain. Link faces Volvagia in the heart of the Fire Temple, and their battle is nothing short of glorious. With the Megaton Hammer, Link must break open the dragon's skull as it pops out from the lava pits, turning this boss fight into a fiery game of Whac-A-Mole.

Volvagia poses an especially challenging fight, spewing fire at Link and sending boulders crashing down from the ceiling. At the same time, the game doesn't make this a linear battle, as the player can also use the Fairy Bow to shoot the dragon's exposed skull. Ultimately, this boss fight cranks up the heat with a thrilling environment and concept that allows players to get creative.

Despite its silly name, Bongo Bongo is no laughing matter. This phantom shadow beast scorched Kakariko Village after escaping its prison at the Bottom of the Well. After Link chases it into the Shadow Temple, the Hero faces him on top of a giant drum in the middle of a toxic lake.

This boss fight builds an eerie atmosphere with Bongo Bongo’s monstrous moaning and spooky lair. It also forces the player to use their resources wisely in order to come out on top. They must evade and shoot the demon's giant hands, wear the Hover Boots to move steadily across the beating drum, and use the Lenses of Truth to see and strike its head.

In the first boss as Adult Link, the Hero of Time faces Phantom Ganon, an evil spirit that resembles the Demon King. The boss of the Forest Temple cleverly hides inside multiple paintings in its chamber, forcing Link to shoot the right Phantom Ganon with the Fairy Bow.

But after a few hits, the boss changes tactics, challenging Link to a game of Dead Man’s Volley, in which he must use his sword to knock an energy ball back at him. It’s a thrilling and inventive boss battle that culminates in a haunting cutscene where the real Ganondorf threatens Link, building up hype for the game’s final boss.

The surrogate mothers of Ganondorf, Komue and Kotake, known collectively as Twinrova, take control of the Spirit Temple after Young Link retrieves the Silver Gauntlets. Seven years later, after making Link fight one more Iron Knuckle, the two witches grow in size and battle him using their powers over fire and ice.

The age of Ganon is over. It's Twinrova's turn to rule

The boss fight features an incredibly cool concept, in which Link deflects magic lasers back at Twinrova using the Mirror Shield. Also, unlike most of the game’s bosses, Twinrova actually transforms, with both witches fusing into one giant, superpowered sorceress. It feels especially rewarding taking down Twinrova after seeing them brainwash Nabooru for seven years. The remake also adds another intrguing layer to this fight by having the witches spare Young Link beforehand, thinking he wouldn’t be worth killing, making their defeat a result of their own arrogance.

After lowering the barrier around Ganondorf’s Tower and battling several monsters, Link comes face-to-face with the Demon King himself at the top of his castle. However, Ganondorf's magic prevents Navi from reading his weakness, forcing the player to figure it out for themselves. Ultimately, this fight makes the player use what they learned fighting Phantom Ganon and deflect Ganondorf’s magic back at him, all before shooting him with Light Arrows.

After everything Ganondorf made Link and his friends endure throughout the story, the game pays off this build up by letting the player give the villain an incredible beatdown. The remake heightens the challenge by having Ganondorf remove more portions of the floor during the fight. It seems as though Nintendo knew many veteran Zelda players would be playing this game and wanted to make things more exciting for them. And boy, did it work.

Ocarina of Time saved the best for last. After Link and Zelda escape Ganondorf’s Castle before its collapse, the duo see the Demon King has survived the wreckage. Then, in a blind rage, the villain transforms into his final form, a giant, hulking pig demon with two massive swords.

The final boss is perfect based on atmosphere alone. The game fills the player with incredible dread and excitement as Link fights Ganon in the ruins of his castle, all while a dark storm hangs over them. The player can feel the weight of Hyrule on their shoulders as it seems like they're fighting at the end of the world.

The remake makes some clever deviations from the original game by giving Ganon new weak points and new attacks during the second phase. It also features more gripping cinematics that give Zelda a more active role during the battle. Overall, the remake's final boss delivers a much more epic climax to Link and Zelda's war with Ganon.

#3432. How Starship Troopers Author Robert A. Heinlein Really Felt About His Hollywood Experiences

Robert A. Heinlein wasn't fond of working as a screenwriter in Hollywood, and he definitely hated working in TV.

The famed sci-fi author loved the movies, but was always more comfortable sticking to his preferred medium of the printed page. Heinlein was quoted in a 1994 issue of Cinefantastique Magazine saying that working on a Hollywood screenplay meant a great deal of stress, but also that seeing a completed movie he had worked on was a rewarding experience. Heinlein, however, was pretty negative about his experience working on 1960s TV. That, he recalls, was totally miserable.

Movie fans may know Robert A. Heinlein's name best for writing the 1959 novel that provided the source material for Paul Verhoeven's 1997 sci-fi war satire "Starship Troopers," a movie full of disturbing details. He was also behind the short story " '—All You Zombies—' ," which was adapted into the wibby-wobbly time travel movie "Predestination." Sci-fi fans, however, know him as a giant of the genre, having written books like 1951's "The Puppet Masters," 1961's "Stranger in a Strange Land," and many others besides.

In the '50s, Heinlein was also tapped by Hollywood to write a few screenplays, and the famed author is a credited screenwriter on movies like Irving Pichel's 1950 film "Destination Moon" (which adapted elements of Heinlein's 1947 teen novel "Rocket Ship Galileo") and Richard Talmidge's 1953 film "Project Moonbase." About "Destination Moon," Heinlein noted that he was actually pleased with the results.

It was when he was approached in the 1960s to write the pilot for an unmade TV series called "XXII Century," however, that Heinlein's experience in Hollywood turned sour. That show, it seems, was a huge headache.

To give you an idea of how well "Project Moonbase" was received by the public, it was featured on an episode of the bad-movie showcase program "Mystery Science Theater 3000." Robert A. Heinlein didn't comment on that movie directly. But "Destination Moon" has been recognized by Steven Spileberg as the movie that taught him about cinematic suspense, and Cinefantastique quoted Heinlein about his rewarding experiences working on it:

"[I]t had cost me eighteen months work, my peace of mind, and almost all of my remaining hair. Nevertheless, when I saw the 'rough cut' of the picture, it seems to have been worth it."

Heinlein wrote his masterpiece, "Stranger in a Strange Land," several years after his experiences working on "Moonbase" and "Moon," so Hollywood started looking at him again. A producer named Howie Horowitz called Heinlein about making a TV pilot, and the result was a script called "XXII Century" (also called "Century XXII" various places online). The script can be purchased on the Heinlein archive website, and that edition contains pages and pages of notes, seemingly requiring that Heinlein repeatedly alter his work.

"[I]f the series is never produced, I hope I have sense enough to stay home and write books in the future, and leave the movie never-never land to those who enjoy the rat race."

It seems those pages of notes didn't leave Heinlein in a good mood. It was the last time he would be directly involved in any major Hollywood production.

The basics behind the pilot of "XXII Century" can be found on the Libertarian Futurist Society website. "XXII Century" was to take place in the year 2163, and followed the plight of a secret society of powerful superhumans who had the ability to think rationally at all times, even if it pained them. They had cordoned themselves off from the rest of society, and developed a benevolent dictatorship.

The LFS website notes that this premise was culled from Robert A. Heinlein's 1949 novella "Gulf." In the pilot episode, called "The Man Who Wasn't There," it was explained that the United States, Russia, and China engaged in a devastating war in the year 1984. Thereafter, the former two affected authoritarian governments founded moon colonies, and eventually began sending criminals and undesirables there. Fast forward a few centuries, and "XXII Century" can begin. The moon colonies were matriarchal in nature, as there were far fewer women than men, and were also meant to reflect a post-racism future, where prejudice was left behind. And all of this was written before "Star Trek" ever made it to the air in 1966.

Why did the show fall apart? The Space Review has some commentary on "XXII Century" from noted Heinlein scholar Bill Patterson, and he said that the script was way too daring for its own good, and that there was no way it could have ever made its way to the small screen. The project was abandoned, Heinlein lost interest in television, and he went back to writing hit novels. The TV show sounds great, but Heinlein was likely better off in his preferred medium.

#3430. This '90s Crime Thriller Has One Of Samuel L. Jackson's Most Underrated Performances

Samuel L. Jackson stars in F. Gary Gray's 1998 police thriller "The Negotiator" as Danny Roman, a Chicago police negotiator said to be the finest in his district. He's clearly very good at his job, and right from the jump, audiences get to see Danny's charisma and confidence at work as he talks down a desperate situation. Indeed, Jackson is such a forceful and badass actor that it's quite easy to believe that he'd be a good police negotiator.

The plot of "The Negotiator" involves a twisty scheme perpetrated by a hidden cadre of dirty cops to frame Danny for embezzling money from a police disability fund. As a result, Danny comes under the scrutiny of a potentially shifty Internal Affairs officer named Niebaum, played by the great J.T. Walsh. When Danny begins to discover that he is being set up, he storms into Niebaum's office and takes him, along with three other people, hostage. He wants justice.

Of course, being a police negotiator, Danny knows exactly how hostage situations work, and he insists on talking to another crackerjack negotiator named Chris Sabian, played by Kevin Spacey. (I know, I know.) At the time, seeing Spacey and Jackson play opposite one another was very exciting, and the best scenes in "The Negotiator" are when Danny and Sabian interact. The two of them have to somehow find the truth about the embezzlement scheme while under the scrutiny of the Chicago PD. There are many moments of characters being put in imminent danger.

"The Negotiator" was a modest hit in 1998, and I, alive at the time, recall it having many fans, as several of my peers ended up buying the film on home media. These days, though, it tends to be overlooked.

1998 was a good time for both lead actors in "The Negotiator." Samuel L. Jackson had caught everyone's attention in the early 1990s in films like "Jurassic Park" and, more importantly, was widely lauded for his performance in "Pulp Fiction," which netted him an Oscar nomination. This was in addition to piles of credits that he merrily racked up with expedience. Meanwhile, Kevin Spacey, many years before being ousted for a pattern of sexual assault, had gotten a lot of attention in 1995 for his performance in "Seven" and won an Oscar for Best Supporting Actor for his turn in Bryan Singer's "The Usual Suspects." By 1998, when "The Negotiator" came along, they were both riding high.

On paper, "The Negotiator" sounds like a pretty rote police thriller. There's corruption in the Chicago PD, run by a network of unscrupulous cops, and only honest cops can find out the truth through extreme measures and rid the world of injustice. The screenplay, credited to Kevin Fox and James DeMonaco (the guy who would go on to create "The Purge"), is tight and efficient, but it's not Oscar-worthy or super-original. The film sings because it features some great performances from some notable actors. Jackson is great, as he always is, but one should also give credit to the ever-reliable J.T. Walsh for playing tightwads with such aplomb. (Walsh tragically died several months before "The Negotiator" was released.)

In addition, the movie's cast includes great character actors like David Morse, the reliable Ron Rifkin, a pre-"CSI" Paul Guilfoyle, John Spencer (who's better known for having played Leo McGarry, one of the best characters on "The West Wing"), and a just-then-kind-of-becoming-famous Paul Giamatti. That's a lot of character for a standard police thriller.

As noted, "The Negotiator" was a modest success, and it was liked well-enough by critics. Director F. Gary Gray, who had previously made "Friday" and "Set It Off," proved to be capable with the more "Hollywood" material and would go on to helm giant blockbusters like 2017's "The Fate of the Furious," which was most certainly a big-ol' "Hollywood" picture.

Roger Ebert gave the film three-and-a-half stars out of four, declaring it a triumph of style over story and of acting over characters. He admitted that it wasn't until he sat to write his review that he realized how clichéd the movie actually was. That's how swept up he had become in the drama. Ebert added that he liked how the movie managed to be talky while skipping to the next plot point without being too obvious, writing:

"Yes, there are clichés all through the movie, including the obligatory role of Roman's new wife (Regina Taylor), who wants him to stop taking the dangerous assignments. Yes, the TV news crews supply the usual breathless bulletins and obnoxious questions. Yes, the action scenes are unlikely [...]. But 'The Negotiator' works because it takes its conventional story and jacks it up several levels with Gray's craft and style. And because [Samuel L.] Jackson and [Kevin] Spacey are very good."

"The Negotiator" is hardly a lost classic, and many might stay away from it because of Kevin Spacey's presence. Still, it should be reiterated that Samuel L. Jackson gives a very good performance in the film, which F. Gary Gray directed the heck out of.

#3429. One Chicago Officially Breaks Tradition With Its Fall Schedule

It feels like just yesterday that the official 2026-2027 TV season began, but shows are already preparing for their fall finales. With Thanksgiving and the winter holidays right around the corner, networks are gearing up to wrap up their autumn runs with major cliffhangers. While most scripted hits like the One Chicago franchise will simply pause for a midseason hiatus before returning in January 2027, several shorter-order series like RJ Decker have already wrapped up. However, some shows will sign off earlier than others.

One Chicago returned for another historic season, with all three shows continuing to occupy their Wednesday time slot. On NBC, Chicago Med Season 12 leads off at 8/7c, followed by Chicago Fire Season 15 at 9/8c and Chicago P.D. Season 14 at 10/9c. The new seasons have seen some shakeups, as more cast members have left the shows, with notable departures from Chicago Fire's Joe Minoso in the 300th episode and LaRoyce Hawkins in Chicago P.D. However, plenty of characters remain, and some new ones have joined, making Wednesdays on NBC one of the best nights in television.

Fans still have a few weeks of drama and thrills left before the franchise airs its fall finales, which will break tradition this season and stretch into the final month of the year. With episode counts reduced across all three shows, fall finales in recent years have aired in late November, but this season all three shows sign off on Wednesday, December 9, 2026, before returning for their winter premieres on January 6, 2027. #3428. Three Ways to Avoid CAPTCHA Prompts When Using a VPN

VPNs make it harder to track your online activity across websites, but it also makes them suspicious about your origins. When you borrow an IP address that hundreds of other people are also using for any number of reasons, you’re much more likely to get repeat verification requests from online firewalls.

CAPTCHAs are simple puzzles that websites use to filter out bots and spam. They’re supposed to be easy for people but hard for robots, such as simple object recognition tasks or audio-visual challenges. However, they can still disrupt your browsing experience if they happen too frequently.

Most modern CAPTCHA providers, like Google's reCAPTCHA v3 or Cloudflare Turnstile, start working long before they give you a puzzle to solve. It usually starts with a risk score that studies your IP address, browser and device signals, or recent online activity.

If the CAPTCHA provider can’t confidently identify your request as human based on those signals, it requests that you complete a puzzle before deciding if the request should be blocked. That means when you get repeat CAPTCHA requests, there’s something affecting your browser’s risk score. For example, popular VPN servers spread the same IP address across any number of users, which can easily make a website mistake you for a bot farm. If you change your IP address frequently by switching servers often, that might look suspicious too.

Luckily, there are ways to deal with frequent CAPTCHA requests using tools and services available with your browser and VPN. Cloudflare has already cut its CAPTCHA requests by 91% using its Managed Challenge platform. Apple has also been shipping token-based verification on devices since iOS 16 and macOS Ventura. In June 2026, Cloudflare even announced a joint effort called the Private Access Control Tokens (PACT) standard with Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Shopify.

While there’s no direct off switch for CAPTCHAs, you can use different fixes to improve your browser’s trust signals when using the internet. That way, you’re less likely to be hounded by verification requests.

The easiest fix for repeat CAPTCHAs is to stop connecting to whichever server your VPN app picks automatically. Proton recommends choosing servers with lower traffic load. In fact, its apps display load as a percentage to help you avoid the most crowded options. I'd also skip big traffic hubs like New York or London, since that's where most traffic originates from. Servers in smaller cities located nearby are often just as fast but never as populated.

You should also avoid changing IP addresses too frequently, which can look suspicious on its own. Pick a server that seems to behave well, then continue using it for at least one session. Also remember you’re more likely to get premium server options if you’re on a paid VPN plan. Major platforms like ExpressVPN, Surfshark, Proton, and Nord are particularly likely to have a larger server collection to pick from.

Costs nothing more than your current subscription

Hopping between servers often can backfire

Private Access Tokens (PAT) let you verify the authenticity of your request using your device rather than an IP address. Apple calls it Automatic Verification, where an Apple server validates your device and Apple Account to assign you an anonymous token.

To enable Automatic Verification on an iPhone or iPad, go to Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification. On a Mac, open System Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification.

Unfortunately, there’s no equivalent feature for Windows, Android, and Linux users. That said, Cloudflare offers the Silk extension for Chrome, Firefox, and Edge that serves a similar function. A quick look at the ratings will tell you it’s not as effective, but Cloudflare’s upcoming cross-browser standard called PACT seems promising once it is released.

Doesn’t share personal details with websites

Chrome and Firefox extensions can be unreliable

If you pay a bit extra for a dedicated IP add-on, VPN providers can assign you a unique IP address that isn’t shared with anyone else. For example, NordVPN offers dedicated IPs in 30 countries for $2-5 a month and Surfshark charges $3.75 a month for it.

There are also dedicated providers like Private Internet Access, which charges $3.99 per month for a zero-trust setup so not even their employees know which IP address is assigned to you. On the other hand, Proton VPN offers dedicated IPs only to business plan users, so you’ll need to be on the Workspace Standard, Premium, or Enterprise plans to get one.

That said, there is a trade-off here too. NordVPN itself admits that a dedicated IP makes it easier to link online activity back to a single user. Also, many websites can still tell that the IP address originated from a VPN data center rather than a consumer’s device.

Get unique IP addresses with pristine reputation

Works across desktop, mobile, and even smart TVs

Also functions as an allowlisted address for work

Add-ons cost more on top of the VPN subscription

Offers less anonymity than shared VPN servers

#3426. Star Trek: Picard Started As A Pitch For An Underused Original Series Character

Over the course of its three-season run, "Star Trek: Picard" took viewers along for the final voyage of the legendary Starfleet captain played by the equally legendary Patrick Stewart. But while the series was heavily rooted in Picard's history, referenced storylines in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," and even spent its final season giving us the "TNG" crew getting back together for one last ride that viewers really wanted all along, the original idea for the show was apparently very different.

According to an interview with Trekcore, "Picard" co-creators Alex Kurtzman and Kristen Beyer started out with an idea that would've featured another character from the "Star Trek" universe that arguably deserved the spotlight even more than the famous captain: Nyota Uhura, the groundbreaking communications officer of the original "Enterprise," originally played by Nichelle Nichols.

Early in the development of what would eventually become "Picard," Beyer and Kurtzman started with the idea of bringing Nichols back to play her iconic role for the first time since 1991. Beyer recalled the initial idea:

"We were actually beginning with an Uhura story, and the idea was that we very much wanted to see we could bring Nichelle [Nichols] back in at this point in time, and then see what kind of stories [Uhura] might tie in to. And then Patrick's name came into the mix, and could we get him, would he be interested ... so the very first idea was a meeting between Uhura and Picard — a very, very young Picard."

Kurtzman gave a few more details about the idea, indicating that at one point, Uhura's role may have been more of a cameo than as the driving force of the show:

"The original idea was that a young Picard had been called to a hospital where Uhura had a mission for him, and it was related to the Borg."

It's an intriguing idea for a lot of reasons. From a real world perspective, it would've rectified a glaring oversight in how Nichols' legacy has been overlooked. Despite the fact that her portrayal of Uhura, which featured television's first interracial kiss between Nichols and costar William Shatner, was praised by no less than Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and inspired real-life astronaut Mae Jemison, among others, Uhura was extremely underused in the original series, even having her scenes rewritten to minimize her role. She's also the only member of the original series' bridge crew to never return for another appearance after "Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country." Nichols was offered and turned down a small cameo role on "Star Trek: Voyager," but sadly, since she passed away in 2022, her return will always be something fans never get to see.

There are also a lot of fascinating questions from the nerdier in-universe view as well. Considering that "Star Trek: The Next Generation" takes place nearly 100 years after the events of the original series, any meeting between Uhura and Picard might seem pretty unlikely. That said, "Star Trek" has always found a way to keep its classic characters in circulation, whether it was through the transporter trickery that allowed Scotty (James Doohan) to come back in the "TNG" episode "Relics," the extended Vulcan lifespan that saw Spock still traveling the universe well into his second century, or just the extended lifespan of the utopian future that gave us a 137-year-old Dr. McCoy wandering around the "Enterprise-D" in the pilot episode of "TNG."

The bigger question is about the Borg, who did wind up being a major element of "Picard." They were a completely unknown species when the "Enterprise" first encountered them in the second season of "TNG," so Uhura knowing about them well before Picard took command of the Federation flagship, and telling him about them, is certainly a surprising development. Then again, the Borg are no strangers to time travel. It's entirely possible that Uhura's long career in Starfleet could've seen her encounter them, even if she probably should've given everyone else a heads up before all that stuff where they captured Picard and then blew up half the fleet. The Borg may have given us some of the best moments in "Trek," but a warning could've saved the Federation a lot of trouble

We're also left wondering whether this meeting between Uhura and a young Picard would've been a prelude to Patrick Stewart's return, or if we'd have seen another actor taking over the role, much like Celia Rose Gooding did with the role of Uhura herself on "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds." There are a couple of obvious choices for the role, of course, but it seems unlikely that they could've gotten Tom Hardy (who played Picard's younger clone Shinzon in "Star Trek: Nemesis"), and that kid who played a young Picard in the "TNG" episode "Rascals" has to be pushing 50 by now. Sadly, we'll never know.

#3424. Bill Pullman Starred In This '90s Neo-Noir Drama That Tried Suing The Oscars

Before we discuss John Dahl's "The Last Seduction" starring Linda Fiorentino and Bill Pullman, let's set the table. In the indispensable documentary "A Personal Journey With Martin Scorsese Through American Movies," the legendary director discusses the concept of artistic smuggling. The idea is that clever filmmakers can slip subversive themes past unsophisticated producers who are more focused on making a tidy profit than crafting a movie that means and says something.

Back in the B-movie heyday of the 1950s, this practice was common, particularly in genre pictures. Film noir offered a particularly fertile ground for such felonious messing around. Tales of compromised characters doing the wrong thing to get over or simply survive resonated in the wake of the Great Depression and World War II. People knew hard times and found cruel catharsis in watching folks trying, and typically failing, to game the system.

Noir never went away. It mutated with the ever-troubled times, as any fraught moment in American history could serve as the backdrop for a sexy, politically charged thriller. Then third-wave feminism hit in the 1990s, and femmes fatales became protagonists. And we were rooting for them.

It's hard to top the great Sharon Stone as Catherine Tramell in Paul Verhoeven's "Basic Instinct," but I think the best third-wave femme fatale is Fiorentino's Bridget Gregory in "The Last Seduction." From the minute her dirtbag husband, Clay (Pullman), slaps her for insulting him, she begins spinning a complex web that will lead to his undoing. Fiorentino is magnificent every step of the way, and she would've waltzed into a Best Actress Oscar had the film been treated with the respect it deserved. Alas, despite a lawsuit to get her into contention, the Academy refused to budge. And this is a case where smuggling might've hurt a film noir.

In a 2015 interview with Creative Screenwriting, "The Last Seduction" screenwriter Steve Barancik explained the film's creatives pitched the movie to ITC Entertainment as standard-issue Skinemax sleaze. John Dahl, of course, aspired to make a high-quality neo-noir, and once the film's actors read Barancik's script, they knew the project had a chance to be something special. That's how the movie attracted respected names like Linda Fiorentino (who demanded Dahl cast her), Bill Pullman, Peter Berg, Bill Nunn, Dean Norris, and the dearly missed J.T. Walsh.

When an ITC executive panicked early on, the filmmakers got a tongue-lashing. "He shut down production and called the principals of the movie on the carpet, and they all had to pledge that they had no artistic pretensions," Barancik recalled. After the film was completed, ITC sold it off to HBO before it could get theatrical distribution. Unfortunately, if a movie doesn't get an Oscar qualifying run in theaters, it's ineligible for consideration. Again, the distributor October Films brought a suit against the Academy on Fiorentino's behalf, but the organization's rules were clear: no qualifying run, no nomination.

Fiorentino did earn Best Actress prizes from the Independent Spirit Awards and the New York Film Critics Circle, but she likely would've won the Best Actress Oscar if she'd been allowed to compete. (Instead, the prize went to a deserving Jessica Lange for making a meal out of her role in Tony Richardson's film "Blue Sky.") I don't blame Dahl and company for their smuggling gambit, but ticking off ITC was a costly mistake.
