#3423. 30 Best Cartoon Network Shows From The 2000s, Ranked

Although Cartoon Network started becoming popular in the '90s, it was in the 2000s when its shows really took off. The network had some great cartoons that started in the 2000s, and many of these series carried over into the 2010s, proving that this was the best network on TV at the time for cartoons. Not only did the network have some great shows carrying into the decade, but it introduced some seriously memorable cartoons in the 2000s as well, giving Cartoon Network an entire decade of animated dominance.

Alongside the launch of Adult Swim in 2001 — the network's spinoff block of programs aimed at adults — Cartoon Network's regular programming simultaneously pushed the boundaries of animation for children. Today's more limited lineup presents a totally different landscape for the network, and so many continue to look back to the best Cartoon Network shows from the 2000s for next-level content and a hit of nostalgia from what was considered the Golden Age of Cartoon Network.

With several spin-offs and a revival, it's not too far-fetched to say that Total Drama continues to be one of the best Cartoon Network shows from the 2000s. The Survivor-like animated series is essentially a satirical depiction of reality TV, with each season revolving around a group of teenagers who join a competition and try to avoid elimination. It's certainly a show with more mature themes, as the competitors (much like on regular reality TV shows) develop relationships, fight, and backstab each other to stay in the game.

Total Drama was created by Jennifer Pertsch and Tom McGillis, premiering initially in Canada before moving over the US Cartoon Network channel a year later in 2008. While it takes most of its inspiration from Survivor when it comes to its satire, it parodies many conventions found across the wider genre of reality TV — and the results are hilarious.

Mexican wrestling is one of the country's most famous cultural exports, present in everything from WWE, thanks to wrestlers like Rey Mysterio, to Hollywood with movies like Nacho Libre. In 2002, Cartoon Network did its own spin on the sport with the animated show Mucha Lucha, which was also the first ever series created with Macromedia Flash. It's set in the town of Luchaville, where almost every resident wears a Lucha Libre costume and has a signature move.

Not only is Mucha Lucha among the best wrestling TV shows, but it's also the first Western animated series focused on pro wrestling. Mucha Lucha stars Rikochet, Buena Girl, The Flea, and El Rey — students at the Foremost World-Renowned International School of Lucha. Though not as well-remembered as many of the other best Cartoon Network shows from the 2000s, Mucha Lucha's over-the-top depiction of the Mexican art of Lucha Libre makes it a must-see.

The 2000s were an interesting time for animated kids' shows, as the genre was moving away from some of the risqué humor of '90s offerings like Ren & Stimpy and into safer territory. This is what makes Chowder, released in 2007, feel like such an oddity. Chowder isn't about the popular soup, but it does involve an aspiring young cook named Chowder. Chowder is an interesting character that's a mix between a cat, bear, and rabbit. Despite wanting to be a chef, he gets involved in comical scenarios due to his impulse control issues.

He often eats customers' meals due to being always hungry — but that's not all. Chowder can also regurgitate items, and his stomach is basically its own storage unit. Considering Chowder's sexist jokes and oftentimes inappropriate material, there are some parts that haven't aged well, and it's more of an adult cartoon than one that's aimed at children.

Dorothy, Horace, and the other colorful residents of Soap City serve as supporting characters to the conflicts between the nerdy and nature-loving Lucien and the aggressive and blue-skinned scrap rat Wayne. While The Cramp Twins is one of many forgotten Cartoon Network shows from the era, that doesn't stop it from ranking among the best 2000s Cartoon Network shows. It has all the hallmarks that made the network's original content so popular during the decade, and almost every episode hits the mark when it comes to including laugh-out-loud humor.

From the lovable Otto Osworth to the excitable Larry 3000, the titular Time Squad is tasked with maintaining the flow of time and ensuring that the future remains a flawless utopia. Undoubtedly one of the best Cartoon Network shows from the 2000s, Time Squad served almost like an after-school history class in the best ways possible, as the team of travelers meet figures like Abraham Lincoln and Sigmund Freud on their adventures.

The squad had to correct history's course by guiding these significant people down the right paths. Notably, while the comic book debut of Marvel's Kang the Conqueror far predates Time Squad, the cartoon aired over two decades before the Time Variant Authority debuted in Loki. Time Squad portrayed a far more lighthearted take on the idea of guardians of history, however, and while it's not as popular as some other Cartoon Network shows from the 2000s, it is certainly among the most imaginative.

Xiaolin Showdown was a 2000s Cartoon Network show that capitalized on the popularity of anime thanks to series like DragonBall Z, Sailor Moon, and Pokémon. In a world where martial arts and magic have become the norm, it's up to a group of Xiaolin warriors to make sure that evil forces don't steal the mystical artifacts known as the Shen Gon Wu, which can change everything in a good or terrible way, depending on who wields them.

One of the best Cartoon Network shows from the 2000s, Xiaolin Showdown shows the struggles of brave characters like Omi and Kimiko Tohomiko as they travel the world to look for powerful artifacts and take on formidable enemies along the way. The series also raises some surprisingly mature questions about morality, with some of its heroes being tempted to use the artifacts for their own benefit.

With original series creator Craig McCracken already working on the Foster's Home for Imaginary Friends reboot, there's no better time to rewatch what many consider one of the best 2000s Cartoon Network shows. Foster's Home represents the onset of truly surreal storytelling in Cartoon Network's regular programming. In this world where imaginary friends are physically real and coexist with humans, a young boy named Mac is pressured by his mother to abandon his imaginary friend, Bloo.

They soon discover a foster home for abandoned imaginary friends. As long as Mac visits Bloo there, he is safe from adoption, a heartwarming premise that gives way to hilarious narratives. Foster's Home for Imaginary Friends was also notable not just for its hilarity and incredibly unique animation style (even by Cartoon Network's standards), but also because it had more tear-jerking and genuinely emotional moments than any other show on the network.

Few Cartoon Network shows from the 2000s, or any other decade for that matter, feature a trio of characters as memorable as Billy, Mandy, and Grim. Echoing Ingmar Bergman's The Seventh Seal, Grim, the personification of death, loses a limbo match against the dim-witted and cheerful Billy and his ego-driven and cynical best friend Mandy, forcing the Grim Reaper to be under the servitude of these children.

As would be expected from the premise, the scenarios and characters in The Grim Adventures of Billy and Mandy are incredibly horror-flavored, though the show isn't scary, instead portraying some dark concepts in an incredibly upbeat light. Unsurprisingly, many consider The Grim Adventures of Billy and Mandy to be foremost among the classic Cartoon Network shows that deserve movie adaptations. Curiously, viewers may not have realized Grim's constant desire to kill the two children at the beginning of the show.

While the majority of Cartoon Network shows in the 2000s featured original characters, the network was also host to many licensed properties with recognizable names and faces. Starring Looney Tunes characters in an even stranger setting, Duck Dodgers is a sci-fi adaptation of a short 1953 theatrical cartoon of the same name.

Featuring Daffy Duck as the eponymous protagonist, the show starts off with a humorous origin story, as Duck Dodgers finds himself in the far future after being accidentally frozen for over three centuries. He meets iconic characters in space like K'chutha Sa'am (Yosemite Sam), Witch Hazel (Leezah the Wicked), and Wile E. Coyote (a parody of the alien from Predator). The myriad references to franchises like Star Trek and even Bond films make the short-lived series even better to watch as an adult today.

No list of the best Cartoon Network shows from the 2000s would be complete without Codename: Kids Next Door. Like many original Cartoon Network programs, Codename: Kids Next Door took an established concept and put a spin on it that was beyond unique. In this case, it was spy movies and secret agents. Five kids — Numbuh 1 to Numbuh 5 — are trained by the organization known as Kids Next Door, undergoing oaths to protect children and battle adulthood.

These kids are in charge of Sector V, where their main base of operations is a high-tech tree house that's ridiculously much bigger from the inside. While the oathbound agents of Kids Next Door are typically decommissioned at the age of 13, it was later revealed that the most competent agents get recruited into Teens Next Door to spy on evil teens.

And can someone tell me where the hell is Adventure Time on this list?!?!?!!!😤 You have Regular Show, but not Adventure Time??? It should be in the Top 10 for crying out loud.😂

#3422. Forget 'Game of Thrones,' These 10 Fantasy Shows Have Perfect Final Seasons

Game of Thrones is undeniably one of the biggest television and cultural phenomena of the 21stcCentury, and its legacy is likely to be remembered for generations to come. However, the final season was rather divisive. Some fans defend it, while many others have dragged it through the mud, criticizing it for being rushed, nonsensical, and deeply unsatisfying.

It's a thing that happens sometimes: some shows just don't end on a high note, especially in the fantasy genre. On the other hand, there are plenty of fantasy shows out there that do have excellent finales, which is pretty widely agreed on. These finales didn't sow division amongst the fanbase; they satisfied long-time viewers and did everything they were supposed to.

Like it or not, franchise creator George Lucas says that Star Wars is more in line with fantasy than with sci-fi. Star Wars: The Clone Wars was the first animated TV show to be produced within the current canon, and it lasted seven seasons and 12 whole years. Set between the second and third prequel films, the saga follows various Jedi knights, Sith lords, bounty hunters, politicians, and clone troopers across engagements in the galaxy as the Republic faces off against the Separatists.

The sixth season aired much earlier than the seventh, due to Disney acquiring the brand around 2014. However, Disney still made the effort to release the final season during the height of the COVID pandemic, which is exactly what fans needed. The final season was amazing, too, featuring a climactic confrontation and wrapping everything up in a nice little bow, providing a smooth segue into the third film. This final season is one of the finest efforts Disney's Star Wars has undertaken.

The Dragon Prince is an animated series set on the magical continent of Xadia. The land has been divided in half following a catastrophic war, with humans segregated to the West and the Elves to the East. Dividing the two is a massive river of magma, overseen by the king of dragons. However, humans assassinate the dragon king, along with his egg, using dark magic, throwing both realms into chaos. In the West, two human princes team up with an elf when they discover that the dragon king's egg was actually not destroyed at all, which makes them embark on a quest to take it to the elves and remaining dragons.

The animation on this one is absolutely gorgeous and jam-packed with vibrant colours and detailed environments. The Dragon Prince also has a fascinating world, a simple but effective magic system, a grand sense of adventure, and some highly emotional moments. The seventh season wrapped everything up perfectly and proved that the showrunners never lost their mojo throughout its run, not even for a second.

His Dark Materials is the second attempt at adapting the novel trilogy by Philip Pullman, following a disastrous movie effort in 2008, which halted all chances of a sequel. This modern HBO effort was much better and was far more faithful to the book. Playing into themes of the multiverse, magic, and mythological creatures that impressed long-time fans of the original work.

The plot concerns a young girl living in an alternate version of England, who is the key to undermining and dismantling a shadowy corporation that runs much of the known world. She is accompanied by her dæmon, a small shape-shifting creature who serves as a sort of animal companion for her. His Dark Materials is clearly crafted with love, as the showrunners hid a ton of Easter eggs that only book readers will pick up on. The final season was not a cancellation, but rather the point that there was no more source material left to cover: all three books had been adapted. This means its conclusion is well-rounded and complete, as well as utterly amazing.

Shadow and Bone is based on the novels by Leigh Bardugo, which have a sizable fanbase. Unfortunately, it wasn't sizable enough to sustain the multi-million-dollar budget, resulting in the show's cancellation just two seasons in, ending on a cliffhanger, no less. This cancellation was not received well by fans, who actually adored it for how it embodied the atmosphere and humour of the original novels.

Rather than being a Medieval-themed fantasy, which the genre tends to favour, it went a little more steampunk, feeling more like Victorian England, instead. This ensured the show had a distinct identity separate from other fantasy TV shows. It's full of witty writing, heartfelt moments, and a shockingly detailed world for what was originally a YA series. The second and final season cranked things up to 11, doing everything just right, even if it didn't attract the numbers it needed.

Avatar: The Last Airbender is a classic Nicktoon that completely threw out the typical Nickelodeon formula. Instead of being a comedy with zero continuity, it was a distinct, beginning-to-end adventure, although it definitely had its comedic moments. As many know by now, the story is about four nations, each representing the elements of air, fire, earth, and water, which are in turmoil following a widespread invasion from the Fire Nation.

It is prophesied that an Avatar will rise, learn to "bend" all the elements, and bring harmony to the land. With an aesthetic inspired by Japanese anime and Medieval East Asia, the series was acclaimed for its profound moral wisdom, light-hearted humour, and action-packed antics. This show had everything going for it, including an explosive finale that never gets old, no matter how many years have gone by.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

Arcane is an animated series based on the popular MOBA video game League of Legends. The universe of the game has always blended elements of sci-fi, fantasy, and steampunk, and the show tends to follow in its footsteps. Ordinarily, video game adaptations are seen as shameless cash grabs, though Arcane was quite the opposite. It was actually created by some of the game developers and was crafted with such care that it even won multiple Emmys.

Arcane is only two seasons long, but it still became a major television event, with its final season becoming a highly anticipated entry in Netflix's library. Don't be fooled by the two seasons thing, though--it didn't get cancelled, and it was willingly brought to a proper close by the showrunners. This meant the final season wasn't rushed, and was crafted just as carefully as the first, making for an action-packed adventure that was surprisingly moving.

What We Do in the Shadows is a series created by Taika Waititi, based on his 2014 movie of the same name. Filmed in a mockumentary style, the idea is simple: what if a bunch of classic Gothic European vampires were abruptly thrust into 21st Century New York City? The result is every bit as absurd and horrifying as you could possibly imagine.

Concluding after six whole seasons, the horror/fantasy/comedy reached a proper conclusion that left very few, if any, loose ends. As it ended, it retained much of the same flair and quirky humour that made fans fall in love with it in the first place, proving that its final season could be just as good, if not better than its first.

The Twilight Zone is one of the most revolutionary television series ever made. Created by Rod Serling, this anthology series describes itself as featuring ordinary people in extraordinary circumstances. It tends to blur the line between genres, featuring episodes that stray into sci-fi, fantasy, and horror. Some are about aliens or robots, while some feature ghosts or demonic entities. Each episode has its own unique concept, cast, plot twist, and self-contained storyline, so no two episodes are alike.

After five seasons, the show came to an end, yet it felt like it could have gone on forever. Whether the writers were running out of ideas or not, The Twilight Zone maintained its momentum throughout its five-year run, never once dipping in quality or producing anything short of perfection. As such, the final season for this show is just as brilliant as the rest of it.

Kingdom is a South Korean Netflix series based on a webtoon-turned-graphic novel. Set at the end of the Middle Ages, the show features the historic kingdom of Joseon as it is plunged into chaos. This is due to the tyrannical Haewon Cho Clan making a violent bid for the throne by using a mythical resurrection plant, unleashing a zombie horde in the process. Now, the current royalty has to fight with their competitors on top of an army of the undead.

Kingdom received two full seasons plus one feature-length special episode before being soft-cancelled. Even though it's doubtful it will ever come back at this point (which is made even more infuriating by the fact that it ended on a cliffhanger), that doesn't change the fact that each and every episode is flawless. This fantasy/horror is absolutely singular in atmosphere, and brought a whole bunch of interesting concepts to the table. The final season is even better than the first, and is pretty much perfect in every sense of the word.

Based on the novel series by the late Robert Jordan, The Wheel of Time was unceremoniously cancelled right as it hit its stride. The first season was average, the second was good, but not great, and the third was absolutely stellar. This is probably why its abrupt cancellation prompted a massive online fan campaign to try and save it, which is a response that was quite unexpected.

Story-wise, the show is about a chosen one named the Dragon Reborn who is destined to either save the world or destroy it. The show had its own distinct identity, bringing Jordan's fascinating world to life in a way that nobody had seen before, and absolutely nailed the casting. It had such a unique vibe too, one that is completely unmatched by other fantasy shows. It's honestly such a shame that The Wheel of Time never got to see a proper conclusion, but at least its third and final season ensures it went out on a high note.

#3421. Samsung’s Newest Flagship Soundbar System Is $500 Off Ahead of Black Friday

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Samsung’s flagship soundbars have reached the point where the yearly upgrades are more about refinement than reinvention, and that is pretty much the story with the Samsung HW-Q990H—and with Black Friday approaching, this 2026 model is already seeing a $500 discount, bringing its price down to $1,497.99 from $1,997.99. That's its lowest price to date.

Samsung kept the same 11.1.4-channel setup from the older HW-Q990F, including the soundbar, wireless subwoofer, and two rear speakers, but leaned harder into software this time around—features like the SpaceFit Sound Pro automatically adjust the sound depending on your room layout, and unlike some auto-calibration features that barely change anything, this one reportedly shifts the audio balance in noticeable ways. Sometimes it improves dialogue clarity and bass response. Other times, you may prefer tweaking things yourself with the built-in seven-band EQ.

The system also handles basically every major audio format, supports wireless Dolby Atmos with compatible Samsung TVs, and includes 4K 120Hz HDMI passthrough for people gaming on a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X. That said, while the bass is strong for a compact subwoofer, it compresses when you push the volume near maximum, so it's not perfect for huge spaces or people who want nightclub-level output. More importantly, if you already own the HW-Q990F or even the older HW-Q990D, upgrading probably will not feel dramatic enough to justify the cost. But for someone starting from TV speakers or an entry-level soundbar, this system can completely change how movies, games, and even sports feel at home.

But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by Dec. 2, 2026.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

#3420. 6 Upcoming Sci-Fi Movies, Ranked by Hype

The next wave of sci-fi TV is looking out of this world

Science fiction has always been one of the most exhilarating genres to experience on the big screen, and today we’re entering another massive era for theatrical spectacle. Studios like Warner Bros., Disney, and Legendary have given filmmakers, VFX artists, and visionary directors the canvas to explore everything from humanity's distant future to planets in galaxies far, far away. Fortunately, the next few years of sci-fi cinema look just as — if not more — promising.

As studios double down on high-stakes bets, pouring absurd budgets into sprawling worlds and complex narratives like Dune: Part Three and Avengers: Doomsday, speculative fiction remains Hollywood’s ultimate proving ground for event-sized storytelling. To see what’s most exciting on the near horizon, here are the biggest upcoming sci-fi movies ranked by hype.

It’s always a gamble betting on a mid-budget sci-fi concept in a release calendar dominated by legacy IP, even with Keanu Reeves at the center of it. Directed by Deadpool’s Tim Miller, Shiver has been pitched as Edge of Tomorrow meets The Shallows. Reeves plays an as-yet unnamed smuggler who gets trapped in a deadly time loop in the middle of the shark-infested Caribbean Sea after a job goes sideways.

Even in the age of original sci-fi spectacles like Everything Everywhere All at Once and Severance, the lack of any built-in franchise awareness or even a massive marketing blitz behind it makes Shiver sit outside almost everyone’s hype level at the moment, especially in the face of such massive juggernauts on the horizon. Still, watching Miller pair R-rated action choreography with a high-concept time-loop premise in the same vein as Looper, all while letting Reeves carry the story, makes Shiver one of the more fascinating wildcards on the slate, especially if you’re a John Wick fan.

At this point, Legendary's MonsterVerse has settled comfortably into its wild identity, built primarily on ridiculous kaiju matchups. Following the events of Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire, the next installment looks ready to take things past the stratosphere, both literally and figuratively. Director Grant Sputore, who takes over for Adam Wingard this go-around, is gearing up to steer the franchise into cosmic territory. Even with the limited amount of story details, it’s clear SpaceGodzilla will emerge as the franchise's next big bad, which would mark a significant escalation for the sixth film in the series.

The MonsterVerse isn’t exactly the most cerebral science fiction franchise around, and nowhere close as jaw-dropping as Minus Zero, but it has become one of Hollywood's most dependable sources of blockbuster entertainment. You can’t deny there’s something undeniably exciting about seeing kaiju go toe-to-toe, wreaking havoc across some of the world’s most beautiful cities. The idea of a threat from the stars crashing into the MonsterVerse makes Godzilla x Kong: Supernova particularly intriguing, though not quite Star Wars-level intriguing.

It’s not an overstatement to say Star Wars is in rough shape right now. Following the poor reception of The Mandalorian and Grogu, the franchise is in dire need of structural reinvention before one of cinema’s most beloved sci-fi properties falls into full-blown creative obsolescence. At least Star Wars: Starfighter looks like a promising breath of fresh air, bypassing the Skywalker Saga to jump five years past The Rise of Skywalker.

Set to hit theaters on the 50th anniversary weekend of the original 1977 film, Shawn Levy’s standalone entry stars Ryan Gosling as a cynical rogue pilot alongside Mia Goth, Amy Adams, and Matt Smith. The story sees Gosling's character taking a young Jedi child under his wing, giving the film a chance to explore a more personal mentor-student dynamic set against a galactic adventure. In the wake of countless Disney Plus spin-offs that never quite stuck the landing, Levy has his work cut out for him, especially with the film carrying the weight of the much-maligned sequel trilogy with it.

After spending nearly three decades stuck in development hell, The Incredibles director is finally bringing his long-gestating passion project to the silver screen. Set in an alternate retro-futuristic megacity as imagined from 1939, the animated sci-fi noir follows Raymond Gunn (Sam Rockwell), the last human private investigator as he is pulled into a murder conspiracy involving extraterrestrial visitors and multimedia superstar Venus Nova (Scarlett Johansson).

Director Brad Bird has tapped a laundry list of additional stars to back the voice ensemble, from Alan Tudyk to Michelle Rodriguez, and it looks like the exact kind of stylized swing mainstream animation rarely takes anymore. It already reminds me of Satoshi Kon’s unfinished final project, Dreaming Machine, which was also set in a retro-futuristic society like Ray Gunn’s Metropia. Watching Bird blend hard-boiled detective fiction with mid-century pulp sci-fi is an exciting prospect, and you won’t have to wait long to see it. Ray Gunn releases in theaters on December 4 ahead of its debut on Netflix later that same month.

Denis Villeneuve has already pulled off what filmmakers thought was impossible by turning Frank Herbert’s dense prose into twin modern sci-fi classics. Dune: Part Three is poised to ring in even more hype and acclaim as it pulls in new players and villains into the overarching conflict. Adapting Dune Messiah, the third installment picks up with Paul Atreides (Timothée Chalamet) sitting on the Golden Lion Throne, forced to reckon with the fanatical fallout of his holy war across the imperium.

Jason Momoa returns as the ghola Hayt, a resurrected clone of fallen Atreides swordmaster Duncan Idaho, and is joined by Robert Pattinson as the shape-shifting conspirator Scytale. Villeneuve's closing chapter on Dune is undoubtedly one of the most ambitious and exciting sci-fi events of the year, but it lands on the same day as Marvel’s Avengers suit up to take on one of their toughest foes yet.

Opening on the same "Dunesday" weekend, the Russo brothers’ return to Marvel isn’t pure hard sci-fi in the traditional sense, yet its multiversal stakes make it the loudest pop-culture collision on the calendar. Built around reality-bending incursions and a crossover that pulls the Avengers, The Fantastic Four, and the Fox-era X-Men into one universe-shattering event, Avengers: Doomsday is easily one of the most anticipated comic book blockbusters in years. Bringing Robert Downey Jr. back into the fold as Victor Von Doom is a swerve unlike any other, but one that will prove the most exciting to witness as he collides with Marvel’s pantheon of heroes on-screen later this year.

The multiversal saga has had more than its fair share of missteps, leaving plenty of skeptics wondering if Marvel can actually recapture its Infinity War and Endgame momentum. Love it or hate it, nothing else on the release schedule commands a bigger mainstream footprint than watching Marvel’s architects try to pull off the biggest crossover event Hollywood has seen yet. And, in the wake of that surprise VisionQuest post-credit scene, the hype is at a fever pitch.

#3419. ’12 12 12′ Review: Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan’s Ticking-Clock Heist Thriller Runs on Broken Time

Every episode of “12 12 12” opens with the same explanation of its title: Citing the fictitious law enforcement manual, “Principles of Crime, FBI Research Center, 4th Edition,” Anthony Mackie explains, “A high asset robbery, professionally conceived, is 12 months in planning, 12 hours in execution. A bank robber who’s not caught within 12 days is not caught at all.” Then the screen splits horizontally to reveal images from the 12 months of preparation, the 12 hours of execution, and the 12 days when thief extraordinaire Paul Galvin (Jamie Dornan) does his best to elude Mackie’s obsessed FBI agent Jack Strickland. And then, we’re off to the races. Related Stories ‘The Good Daughter’ Review: Rose Byrne Sizzles in Peacock’s Brutal Trauma-Drama About Crime-Solving Sisters ‘American Doctor’ and ‘You Can See Everything’ Lead 2027 Cinema Eye Honors Film Nominations

The heist genre, in theory, seems ripe for this kind of temporal manipulation. A game of wits between cops and criminals typically involves plenty of twists, many of which pull the rug out by flashing back to show where, when, and how it was placed so stealthily underfoot. Also working in “12 12 12’s” favor is the genre’s familiarity: There will be “getting the team together” montages, there will be unexpected hiccups in the days and hours during the robbery, there will be chest-thumping meetings between our confident cop and the equally confident con artist. Throw in the complex heist itself and the tense escape soon after, and there appear to be enough recognizable pieces that jumbling them up shouldn’t prove too confusing.

And “12 12 12” isn’t confusing. It is, however, convoluted. Taking a serpentine route through well-trodden territory does more to undermine our enjoyment of an otherwise well-mounted chase than it does to liven things up. Heists are inherently exciting. They’re exciting in conception (when master thieves can wow us with their slick plans), they’re exciting to see carried out (when the shit hits the fan and even the most astute architects have to think on their feet), and they’re exciting to get away with (when safety is within reach, but it could be snatched away at any moment). Anticipation, suspense, and anxiety work to form a natural arc, and disrupting that arc over and over, every hour for eight hours, in service of a few extra twists — and to extend what’s obviously a movie-length story across eight hours — simply isn’t worth it.

On that note, let me get this minor but essential point out of the way now, quickly and clearly: Jamie Dornan needs more weird roles, not more conventional ones. We saw what he can do in “Barb and Star Go to Vista Del Mar” (a modern comedy classic). Let the man cook — or sing or dance or all three at once! He can do it! Honestly, I believe he can do anything. (Remember the bee movie?! No, not that bee movie — the other one.)

Anyway, here his character’s only unique attribute is his brilliant… planning. He’s got a mind for details, and he uses it to map out every possible contingency before embarking on his elaborate heists. Caught in a bind with his dumbass brother (Jack Kesy, doing his best Travis Kelce impression), Bobby lays it out in aptly blunt terms: “Paul, you’re the fucking plan guy, so plan me a plan.”

But the only plans Paul wants to make these days are for his family: He’s happy working on fishing boats off the coast of France and coming home to his wife, Severine (Agathe Rousselle), in their little apartment above a bar. He’s bonded with his father-in-law, Serge (José Garcia), who’s the Marxist papa Paul never had, and he’s got a kid on the way.

Unfortunately, Bobby can’t stop being Bobby and winds up indebted to the wrong people; people who don’t just want their money back, but who want more money to make up for the inconvenience. And since Bobby already owes more money than either brother could ever pay back, Paul has to take on one last job to free his brother — and himself — from their lives of crime.

Too bad that puts him back on Jack’s radar or, I should say, squarely on Jack’s radar, since Jack is nursing a (secret) grudge against Paul from years earlier. Ever since, he’s been obsessed with catching the one criminal who’s eluded his grasp. He wants revenge, he wants “respect,” he wants to win — “12 12 12” throws out a number of motivations for Jack early on that clearly don’t paint the full picture. They’re placeholder reasons until the show deems it time to dig into what’s really driving him to move to Zurich, hole up in a shitty police station, and wait for Paul to try to steal something.

Mackie, who’s reunited with his “Falcon and the Winter Soldier” director Kari Skogland, gives great determined face, and Dornan is the softest, sweetest guy on the FBI’s most-wanted list. Thankfully, co-creators Dudi Appleton and Jim Keeble don’t ask their lead characters to betray their core identities amid all the twists and turns, shading Jack as more of an antagonist (all-consumed and, thus, single-minded to a fault) and Paul as more of the protagonist. (He doesn’t want to steal, but now that he must, he’s going to do it the right way.) That helps keep our rooting interests in line, which goes a long way toward a satisfying emotional payoff, even when the momentum ebbs and flows with every flash-forward, -back, and -sideways.

With slick locations and clever-enough problem-solving, “12 12 12” should satisfy die-hard heist fans (but not “Die Hard’s” heist fans). It just takes a circuitous route to scratching that itch, and that’s almost as aggravating as not scratching it at all.

“12 12 12” premieres Friday, November 13 on Apple TV with two episodes. New episodes will be released weekly through the finale (Episode 8) on December 25.

#3418. I Played Wendy's RPG, and It's Actually Worth It for the Free Food

November is a huge month for video games. Nintendo dropped its remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Switch 2 last week, and the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI is right around the corner. But the game we've been waiting for most of all also launched this month: WendyQuest, the free RPG from Wendy's. (No, this is not a joke.)

Despite the absurdity of a hamburger chain making a full video game (complete with Wendy's-themed puns), the thing is, this game is pretty solid—even if it is a promotion at the end of the day. WendyQuest's main purpose is to offer customers coupons they can use toward purchases in real life, though it's a bit of a commitment. It took me just under an hour of gameplay before I earned my first coupon, and Wendy's says it takes roughly 15 hours to beat. All that to say, this is a pretty unique marketing campaign.

I was surprised booting up WendyQuest on my iPhone. This doesn't necessarily feel like a thrown-together product. On the flip side, the production quality is quite high. The music is solid and very much traditionally RPG; there are even three save slots, in case you plan to return to this RPG again and again.

There's even a story, albeit cheesy (no pun intended): As the game explains, the "Four Great Spirits of Flavor" created Savoria, "a food-rich paradise." All was well until Mech Corp, led by the evil Dr. MechBorg, built robots to take over Savoria. The plot is far from compelling, and the writing can be a little over the top, but hey, I'll give them credit: They thought through a full story here.

You play as Wendy, the "representation of true culinary excellence and taste as dictated by the four ancient spirits of flavor." Wendy (or The Wendy, as some call her) is tasked with saving the world, traveling between villages and picking up new characters along the way. The game world even has "real" Wendy's locations you can visit. These act like inns and shops in other RPGs, giving you a chance to heal while also buying equipment.

Like other RPGs, WendyQuest uses turn-based combat. You have to charge up your attacks, but stop before they hit 100%, or you'll miss. (It took me a while to master the timing.) I'm pretty impressed with how challenging some of these battles can be, though you are quickly given the option of an amulet that gives you a huge leg-up in combat. You don't have to take it, but it makes fights easier if you're only in it for the coupons. That, combined with the spatulas the game encourages you to buy, lets you mow down enemies. You can also utilize your companions here: "Frygor," for example, can either attack enemies with a barrage of fries, or use those fries to build a shield to protect you.

While there are tons of enemies to fight, the key baddies are the "mechs." There are five in total, and after you defeat each, you get a coupon. Spoiler alert: The first mech drops the "Fry Stone," which nets you a coupon for a free order of medium fries—though you need to buy something in tandem, as well as use the Wendy's app. While I stopped my gaming here for this article, the other four coupons are:

Free biscuit or croissant (I didn't even know Wendy's sold biscuits and croissants)

Again, it's wild that WendyQuest has a 10+ hour campaign, with over 1,000 lines of dialogue to boot. I'm not sure this is a game I'm going to see through to the end, but I'll admit, it's a fun marketing approach from Wendy's. Sure, they could have run a promotion in the Wendy's app to give people coupons, but instead, they built an entire RPG. I respect it. You can download the game for iOS, Android, or Steam.

#3417. Ridley Scott's 44-Year-Old Blade Runner Mystery Won't Be Answered In New 2099 Spinoff

Blade Runner 2099 will keep one lingering question a mystery.

Since Ridley Scott adapted the sci-fi thriller in 1982, Blade Runner has become a cult classic and remains one of the most underrated movies from that era. However, the classic didn't develop into a franchise until 35 years later, when Denis Villeneuve directed the critically acclaimed sequel, Blade Runner 2049. Now, the universe is expanding with the first television sequel Blade Runner 2099, set to premiere on Prime Video this month.

With so much rich lore expanding through sequels and spinoffs, one of the most debated mysteries is whether Harrison Ford's protagonist, Rick Deckard, is a replicant. Unfortunately, it appears that the question will remain unresolved even with Prime Video's new series. In a recent issue of Empire Magazine (via The Direct), Blade Runner 2099 showrunner Silka Luisa confirmed that the script doesn't mention Deckard at all, saying, "Why would you ask?" That lack of reference means that the series won't address his humanity.

Furthermore, she also argued that the lack of clarity about who is human or a replicant is built into the world's lore, exclaiming: "Not knowing is part of what makes the world so disorienting."

The upcoming 2099 series will take place 80 years after Scott's original movie and 50 years after the sequel. While the two epic movies saw Ford and Ryan Gosling's protagonists hunting down rogue replicants, the show turns the tables, as replicants become the ruling class after winning the war against humans. Nevertheless, the story is similar to Blade Runner's search for rogue replicants. This time, the main players are a Replicant Blade Runner, Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), and her partner, Cora (Hunter Schafer), a human posing as a replicant.

Luisa's recent comments track with updates about the show's connection to the movies. Despite being in the Blade Runner universe, the showrunner previously said watching the two movies wasn't required, and that Ford won't appear in the series. In September 2026, she told Collider that she structured the show so that "you would understand because of the way the story evolves." The 50-year time jump from Blade Runner 2049 may be the key reason to avoid mentioning Deckard and keep the show standalone since he may be long dead.

Unfortunately, that also means the question of Deckard's humanity will continue to linger as a cold case. Although Philip K. Dick's novel, Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, made it clear that the protagonist was human, Scott introduced more ambiguity about his humanity in the film.

In fact, the legendary filmmaker has argued that Deckard is indeed a replicant, with the unicorn dream sequence and Gaff's original origami serving as proof. Meanwhile, Ford countered that notion, intending for his character to be human to provide the emotional resonance as he develops romantic feelings for the replicant Rachael (Sean Young).

Blade Runner 2049 ended with Gosling's K helping Deckard reunite with his daughter after faking his death, and the sequel never took a direct position on his humanity. Now, that ambiguity will linger, allowing the debate to persist even after the 2099 series drops.

The remaining main cast includes Dimitri Abold and Lewis Gribben, while Tom Bruke, Daniel Rigby, Johnny Harris, and Amy Lennox have recurring roles. Scott is an executive producer. Luisa also confirmed that Blade Runner 2099 won't have a season 2 because it has a contained beginning, middle, and end.

Blade Runner 2099 will drop all eight episodes on November 25, 2026, on Prime Video.

#3416. HBO's 'Harry Potter' Has the Perfect Opportunity to Fix the Movies' Biggest Mistake

Greer Riddell is a London-based film and television journalist writing about comedy, streaming and the evolving media industry in the UK and USA. She works at Collider, covering the latest in film, television and entertainment through interviews, features, reviews and industry coverage.

Her recent brand collaborations include HBO, Warner Bros., Netflix, Hulu, Sky, Disney+ and DC Studios. She has covered titles including Saturday Night Live UK, Rivals, Scrubs, Stuart Fails to Save the Universe, Ludwig, Supergirl and Stranger Things.

Her recent interviews include Florence Pugh, Mike Faist and Christopher Abbott for Netflix's East of Eden, Taika Waititi and Jenna Ortega for Klara and the Sun.

One of the biggest advantages of HBO's Harry Potter adaptation over the original films is the amount of time it has to explore Hogwarts. A feature film has to prioritize the main storyline, meaning many details about the school's history, traditions, and everyday life were cut from Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone. The upcoming TV series can give these elements more attention, depicting Hogwarts not just as the setting for Harry's adventures but as an established institution with its own curriculum, residents, and history.

HBO has already offered glimpses of how the series will restore details from the books, including changes to Hogwarts' iconography. One example is Ravenclaw's crest design, which returns to the book-accurate eagle mascot and blue and bronze colors. Although these may seem like small details, the houses are central to Hogwarts' identity, and their distinct symbols and traditions help establish the school's history.

There are also several customs from the books that the films had little time to explore. When new students arrive at Hogwarts, for example, the Sorting Hat performs lengthy songs that describe the houses and their histories. The books also establish house points, common rooms, and dormitories as important parts of everyday school life. For many international audiences, particularly those unfamiliar with the British school system, the films made these details seem like magical inventions specific to Hogwarts. In reality, the school is modeled in part on traditional British private schools, with their established customs and institutional histories. The HBO series can make that connection clearer, presenting Hogwarts as a prestigious boarding school with traditions comparable to those of Eton or Wycombe Abbey, rather than treating every aspect of its organization as something exclusive to the wizarding world.

Hogwarts is getting some very familiar ghosts.

The series also has more time to explore Hogwarts' curriculum. The films showed a relatively small number of lessons, focusing on those that contributed to the main storyline. Audiences saw Professor Flitwick, played by Warwick Davis, in two very different costumes, Snape's (Alan Rickman) Potions lessons, and just one flying lesson with Madam Hooch (Zoe Wanamaker), which introduced Harry and the audience to Quidditch. However, the books feature a much wider range of subjects, teachers, and magical skills. An episodic format gives the adaptation room to show more of these classes and follow Harry and his classmates as they develop their abilities throughout the school year.

One omitted teacher who seems to be receiving more attention in the HBO adaptation is History of Magic Professor Binns, played by Richard Durden. Binns died while sitting at his desk but did not realize it, so he continued teaching as a ghost. Most students consider his lessons boring, but History of Magic provides important background on the wizarding world's past and makes Hogwarts seem much more like a real school, as there’s always going to be a class that is universally disliked!

Beyond its traditions and school curriculum, Hogwarts is also home to magical residents and creatures who contribute to its everyday life. The films omitted several of these characters or only gave them passing mentions. Gryffindor's ghost, Nearly Headless Nick, appeared, and Ravenclaw’s Grey Lady was played by Trainspotting’s Kelly Macdonald. However, the books feature several other ghosts associated with the different houses — the Bloody Baron, Slytherin's house ghost, and the Fat Friar, who represents Hufflepuff. According to Variety, the HBO series will feature both, played by Andrew Brooke and Daniel Fearn respectively.

One of the most significant supernatural omissions from the Harry Potter films was Peeves the poltergeist. Unlike Hogwarts' ghosts, Peeves has a physical form and spends his time causing trouble throughout the castle, dropping heavy objects, smashing items, and disrupting lessons. He’s regularly supported by Fred and George Weasley, united in their hatred of the Ministry of Magic official Dolores Umbridge. Peeves was originally intended to appear in the films, with British comedian Rik Mayall (The Young Ones) filming scenes as the character; however, they were cut during editing. The HBO adaptation will finally bring Peeves to life, with comedian Peter Serafinowicz (The Tick) cast in the role. His inclusion, alongside the other Hogwarts ghosts, will give the series more opportunities to show the characters who continue to inhabit the castle outside of term time.

The series can also look beyond The Philosopher's Stone to introduce parts of Hogwarts that become important in the later books. In Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, Hermione discovers the school kitchens and learns about the house-elves responsible for cooking, cleaning and maintaining the castle. This leads her to establish S.P.E.W., the Society for the Promotion of Elfish Welfare, to campaign for house-elves' rights and freedom. The storyline also introduces Winky, Mr. Crouch's former house-elf, who Harry and his friends meet after the Quidditch World Cup. Dobby eventually finds work in the Hogwarts kitchens, too. Including this subplot would show another part of how Hogwarts operates beyond the students and teachers. The house-elves carry out much of the work that keeps the school running, and their presence introduces wider questions about the wizarding world's social structure. It would also give Hermione's full personality room to develop, rather than cutting her screen time to prioritize Harry alone.

By including more of these details, HBO's Harry Potter can establish Hogwarts as an institution with its own ecosystem independent of Harry's adventures. The school existed long before Harry arrived and will continue long after he leaves. Its teachers, students, ghosts, house-elves, and traditions all contribute to its identity, and the upcoming series can finally depict Harry as only one part of Hogwarts' much larger legacy.

HBO's Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone is scheduled to premiere on December 25, with streaming available on HBO Max.

#3415. In Shana Feste’s Films, Gender-Flipping Cinema’s ‘Tradition of Celebrating Damaged Men’ Is Its Own Reward

Shana Feste knows her filmography might be a bit tough to pin down. Some directors like to stick to a certain genre. Not Feste. Some only like to work with certain stars. Not Feste. Others enter a franchise and never look back. Not Feste.

But over the course of nearly two decades behind the camera, Feste has carved out a particular sweet spot, regardless of the genre or the cast or the wider world her stories fit inside: She likes complicated women. Not unlikable women, but messy women, contradictory women, women who get things done their own way. It’s a signature unto itself.

“My filmmaking, my history, people have not really known what to do with me. I’m making a comedy, I’m making a horror film, I’m making a genre thriller,” Feste told IndieWire during a recent interview. “But I do find that they’re all starting to build into each other, especially the trajectory from ‘Country Strong’ to ‘Run Sweetheart Run’ to ‘Heartland.’ I’ve always been drawn to women who don’t behave correctly. I’ve always been interested in women who don’t grieve correctly, who mother incorrectly, who love incorrectly. I just want women to have the freedom to behave in this contradictory, destructive, funny, selfish way and be given the same freedom that male characters are given.” Related Stories Box Office: ‘Club Kid’ Scores Best Limited Expansion of the Year as Younger Audiences Embrace Jordan Firstman’s Oscar Hopeful Box Office: ‘Ebenezer’ Opens to Modest $19 Million, Showing Johnny Depp Is Still a Draw for the Right Price

Another shared characteristic between Feste’s complicated women: They may be messy or unexpected, but they tend to get shit done. In her new film “Heartland,” getting shit done is at the center of the story, as the Nashville-set drama follows Jessica Chastain as Misty Jones, a former country-singing superstar who left the business after her designation as the, ahem, “cunt of country” became too much to bear. She’s thrust back into that world after her niece, rising star Charlie Heart (Carter Faith), goes missing. Misty, being Misty, takes it upon herself to get to the bottom of an increasingly dark and twisted mystery, no matter what it takes.

“I am a mom of three, 51, and I’m like, ‘Let’s write about some women who get shit done,’” she said. “I find a lot of those women exist. I’m living in the South now that I see those women every day and am inspired by them. We have this long-established cinematic tradition of celebrating damaged men. But when women behave similarly, they could be labeled as hysterical or dramatic or that word, unlikable. I want to prove that wrong.”

For the (complicated, messy, extremely capable) character of Misty, Feste said, she initially tapped into her longtime love of film noir. She always gravitated toward the Humphrey Bogart types, she said, but wondered what might happen if they gave those sorts of roles to women. That also fed into the dark underbelly of the Nashville scene that the film interrogates, a perfectly noir-ish idea.

“It could have been any city, but specifically this dark underbelly had to do with the music world,” Feste said. “Sadly, it was a common experience for a lot of artists that I spoke with. It was an experience that I’ve experienced in our industry, and it was all too relevant. When we were making the movie, a lot of conversation around Diddy was happening. He had just been arrested, and things were coming into light. We thought, oh wow, this is such a topical moment. And I’m like, it’s always topical, sadly. Whether we’re Epstein, Diddy, Weinstein, this is always going to be in the world, sadly.”

But Feste is also someone who loves this world and wants to celebrate what’s good and true about it. “Country Strong” was about making it — and maybe even making it again — even at great personal cost. “Heartland” just ratchets that sensibility up.

“I wanted to lean into the secrets and the dark corners and the underbelly, but I also will always celebrate the artistry and the storytelling of country music,” she said. “Misty says one line that really speaks so much to me about what the film is: ‘You don’t deserve country music.’ It takes a lot to deserve country music in my eyes. Country music is like the apex of storytelling. So to point out someone who doesn’t deserve country music, I mean, that’s a big insult for me.”

Feste started writing “Heartland” around four years ago, mostly because she was really missing the world of country music that framed her 2010 music drama “Country Strong.” “My father died about eight years ago, and I found myself listening to a lot of country music when he died,” she said. “In the years after he died, going back to the music that he loved, that he used to play for me in the car when we were driving on road trips, I realized that when you’re a writer, you don’t know quite why you write something until years later. And I realized, oh, I’m really missing my father.”

She was also eager to reteam with her “Country Strong” collaborators Jenno Topping and Randall Poster, two people who Feste said have believed in her the most over the course of her career. (Topping and Poster both produced “Heartland,” with Poster also serving as music supervisor, as he did on “Country Strong.”) “When I’m having my darkest days about, I don’t know, me and what I create and my career, knowing that they believe in me has always been such a huge lift,” Feste said. “So having them help me tell this story was just monumental. It was being with someone that you knew had your back the entire time.”

If “Heartland” sees Misty feeling ill at ease in the very spaces that used to celebrate her talent, Feste had the opposite experience. Six films into her directing career, she said “Heartland” let her approach her work in an entirely new way. And it felt good.

“What was really valuable with this experience is that I felt completely comfortable saying, ‘I don’t know,’ and I don’t know if I’ve ever felt that way,” she said. “Certainly not with my first few films, feeling like as a woman, I had to know every answer from every head of department immediately. It was only working with this group of filmmakers, Jenno and Randy and [production designer] Naomi [Shohan], some of my heads of production, that I knew that they saw my vulnerability not as a weakness, but as a strength. I was able to say, ‘I don’t know, what do you think?’ That’s where a very new form of collaboration happened that I haven’t experienced in my career, and with Jessica as well.”

Casting Chastain was an easy call for Feste. She wanted someone who could sing and who was admired in this space, but Chastain’s way of working and approach to on-set life gave Feste more to work with than she could have dreamed.

“I always want my films, especially when we’re shooting a movie that takes place in Nashville, to feel authentic, and I knew Jessica already had a huge buy-in from this audience. The South, they love her from ‘George & Tammy,’” Feste said. “And Jessica can sing, and that is another qualifier. Whenever I’m making any kind of movie with music, I want the actors to be able to sing their own material. But I think most of all, Jessica is one of the biggest champions of other women that I’ve ever met.”

It was freeing for Feste to say “I don’t know,” but Chastain also made it clear that she was there to support Feste’s vision and leadership.

“There were certain times on set where it would get a little loud or kind of disorderly, and people would be talking and having opinions, and no matter what, she’d be like, ‘Shana, sorry, I couldn’t hear you,’ and it was like this just gentle reminder, ‘This is who is leading the ship right now for me,’” the filmmaker recalled. “It was done in the classiest, most polite way.”

That approach turned the collaboration into more of a partnership. When Chastain had an idea, Feste was eager to listen. Even a decade ago, she said, that might not have been so easy for her.

“If I had been the director that I was 10 years ago, it would’ve scared me to death, because Jessica is not afraid to come into a scene and say, ‘OK, wait, that might not be serving us. Let’s throw that idea out of the window. What if we did this?,’” Feste said. “As a director, I’m planning, and every shot is in my head, and I’ve done the work, and I’ve done the homework, and I’m the A student. And to be able to relinquish control and admit when my idea wasn’t the best idea and she’s coming in with a stronger idea because she is Jessica Chastain? She has done the work. She has made this character so rich. This wasn’t a scary experience. It was actually going to elevate the scene and make it work even better.”

It was always the plan for Feste’s stars to also sing their songs to add to the film’s deeper authenticity. “When I’m watching movies that feature performing artists, and there’s so much hype, and they’re playing this celebrated musical performer, and then they come on, and we hear them sing and we’re like, have they been re-voiced? It’s just kind of mediocre? You just kind of lose your authenticity. You lose the ownership of the movie,” she said.

Casting Jennifer Nettles was something of a no-brainer for Feste, and so was actually directing the country superstar. “I didn’t know how to direct someone how to move on stage. That is something that’s not in my repertoire of directing. I can direct someone talking about their divorce in a bedroom, but how to command a stage and move your body? That is something that she learned over 20 years of experience being a superstar,” she said. “Most of the time I said, ‘Just speak to the audience like you are at the Opry, like you’ve done a thousand times. Make it your own.’ She did so much heavy lifting for me.”

So too did Carter Faith. In early discussions about the five characters in the film who are musical artists, Feste said she and Poster were constantly trying to figure out who they would sound like in the real world. Was Misty an Emmylou Harris? A Miranda Lambert? And who was young rising star Charlie Heart? Was she a Taylor Swift type? Poster had an easy answer: She sounds like this actual rising star, Carter Faith. And when it became clear that Faith was able to and interested in auditioning for the role? Serendipity.

“She was like a breath of fresh air,” Feste said. “I remember asking her, ‘Carter, what do you think you have in common with Charlie?’ And she said, ‘Well, we both have boy names.’ My heart exploded. It was the most non-Hollywood endearing response. Then I heard her story of how she was eating red beans and rice, crashing on couches, calling all of these places on Lower Broadway just to get an audition to be the performer at 10:00 AM on a Monday morning. She is someone who really moved to Nashville the day she graduated from high school to make it. She was Charlie. So much of her experience was exactly what the character was going through. So it was only the question of, are you brave enough to access all that trauma of how you got here? And she was absolutely, she said yes, and she trusted me, and it makes me emotional thinking about it because that’s an incredible trust to have.”

Faith also wrote the lyrics to the song that plays at the end of the film, which Feste sees as “dialogue that I could never write.” All the songs in the film and on its soundtrack, including the ones Feste simply imagined as titles first, like “Texas Land,” or that her stars like John Hawkes wrote or that Poster commissioned, add to the film’s incredible authentic feeling and sound. “Working with musical performances in film, it is so additive because it just takes the storytelling to another level. It’s beyond the dialogue. It’s beyond physical blocking. It tells story in this just purely emotional, raw, beautiful way,” she said.

Next up: In true Feste fashion, she’s working on or thinking about a variety of other projects next, including the next chapter of the “Dirty Diana” story, which she first cooked up during lockdown, a TV series about a Southern family, and her “dream project,” which is about Texas bank robbers. Mostly, she said, “I really want to continue working in this space. I want to continue telling stories about messy, complicated, vulnerable Southern women. I think that’s my bread and butter.”

#3413. Netflix's Award-winning Dark Sci-fi Series is Officially Returning

Netflix's dystopian sci-fi show is in production

Get ready for more dystopian science fiction because an eighth season of TV series Black Mirror is in production for Netflix. Variety reports that the show began filming this summer, but has no confirmed release date. Series creator Charlie Brooker is back, and he will write and executive produce the series alongside Bisha K. Ali.

“Black Mirror will return, and hopefully it’ll be more Black Mirror than ever,” Brooker said in an interview with Netflix’s Tudum when the series was renewed this January. “I can confirm that Black Mirror will return, just in time for reality to catch up with it. So, that’s exciting. That chunk of my brain has already been activated and is whirring away,” he added.

Black Mirror is an anthology sci-fi series that began in 2011 on the British network Channel 4 before moving to Netflix. The show largely focuses on near-future dystopian scenarios, tapping into contemporary anxieties about our relationship with technology; "black mirror" refers to phone and computer screens. The series currently spans 33 episodes and a special across seven seasons. There’s also the experimental interactive film Black Mirror: Bandersnatch (which was admittedly more interesting in theory than practice).

Over the years, the show has divided critics, with some praising its trenchant observations on modern society while others find its messaging ham-fisted and numbingly cynical. The series' anthology format certainly adds to these divided opinions, since it is easy to hold both views at once: some episodes are definitely better than others.

Black Mirror has won multiple times at the Emmys, and “San Junipero,” “USS Callister,” and (somehow) Black Mirror: Bandersnatch took home the Outstanding Television Movie award for consecutive years from 2017 to 2019. Since then, some argue the series has declined with its fifth and sixth seasons. Considering that the phrase “It’s like we’re living in a Black Mirror episode” has become increasingly common, it will be interesting to see if the series can stay ahead of the times.

The first seven seasons of Black Mirror are now streaming on Netflix.

#3412. David O. Russell’s ‘Madden’ Biopic Is Out Next Week — Does Anybody Know or Care?

Once upon a time, a new David O. Russell movie would be a must-see cinematic event. The writer/director earned three consecutive Best Picture Oscar nominations with “The Fighter,” “Silver Linings Playbook,” and “American Hustle,” all of which scored at the box office and are roundly regarded as generational classics of their era and even holiday fare. But did you know Russell has a new movie opening next week from Amazon MGM Studios? That would be “Madden,” his biopic starring a physically distended and hair-pieced Nicolas Cage as the iconic NFL commentator. When I told an IndieWire colleague about this story, they had heard of “Madden” the movie, yes, but had no idea that Russell directed it. Doesn’t bode well. Related Stories Box Office: ‘Club Kid’ Scores Best Limited Expansion of the Year as Younger Audiences Embrace Jordan Firstman’s Oscar Hopeful Box Office: ‘Ebenezer’ Opens to Modest $19 Million, Showing Johnny Depp Is Still a Draw for the Right Price

The film co-stars Russell perennial collaborator Christian Bale, strapped back into the hair and makeup chair for another grotesque transformation, as Oakland Raiders owner Al Davis, receding bleach-blond hairline and all, plus a wigged-out Kathryn Hahn as Madden’s wife Virginia, and poor Sienna Miller as Davis’s wife Carol. Reports have claimed the sports biopic carries a $75 million budget, making it one of the “Spanking the Monkey” director’s most expensive movies next to the critically flayed COVID release “Amsterdam,” which, not adjusted for inflation, cost a reported $80 million and earned a paltry $14 million domestically. That’s a movie that entirely vaporized from the cultural imagination — though you may recall a much-memed excerpt of a blink-and-you’ll-miss-her Taylor Swift being thrown under a car to her doom.

The “Madden” release strategy does not inspire confidence, either, suggesting a classic case of bag-and-tag on the part of Amazon MGM Studios: a day-and-date release on Prime Video globally with a perfunctory, subterranean-level theatrical bow, both on Wednesday, November 18. The critics’ screening takes place Monday, November 16, with the embargo lifting about 15 hours later. Muted marketing only further intimates Amazon wants to take the latest Russell joint gently into that good night — but why? Is it that bad? The trailer has more than 8.6 million views and counting, though that’s largely explained by the prolific fanbase behind Madden, who died in 2021, and the NFL. Less so by any fanbase of Russell’s.

To be fair, the studio has its hands full trying to position “Project Hail Mary” in the Oscar race and back into voters’ consciousness after opening theatrically six months ago. Amazon MGM’s social media heist movie “How to Rob a Bank” opens in theaters this Friday, while another awards hopeful, “I Play Rocky,” is in limited release. While “Project Hail Mary” was a box office juggernaut for the company, the tech giant has yet to master juggling multiple tentpole-scale projects theatrically at once — though they’ve had a banner year with considerable successes “Verity” and “The Sheep Detectives” spread out throughout 2026.

Co-scripted by Russell and Cambron Clark, “Madden” centers on Madden’s Super Bowl-winning partnership with Al Davis and the Raiders that led to the “NFL Madden” games. The film wrapped production well over a year ago, in late spring 2025 in Atlanta. A TMZ report from May 21 claimed several actors walked off set after Russell allegedly used a racial epithet during a scene. A reputation for volatility has followed Russell across projects, from the widely seen behind-the-scenes footage of the filmmaker chewing out his “I Heart Huckabees” star Lily Tomlin, to Amy Adams’ confessional interviews in which she revealed the filmmaker made her cry throughout the “American Hustle” shoot. George Clooney has called Russell “a miserable fuck” and swore never to work with him again after his experience making “Three Kings.”

The five-time Oscar nominee has built a career on quirky, sprawling ensembles and pushing actors toward extreme physical performances, like Christian Bale, who went gaunt (again) to win an Academy Award for “The Fighter,” then put on the pounds for “American Hustle.” Back in October, Russell and producer Todd Black appeared at the Virginia Film Festival in Charlottesville to present four clips from “Madden” — which showcased Cage in prosthetic padding that’s more January Jones in “Mad Men” Season 5 than Kazu Hiro Oscar-level effort, plus an exasperatingly accented Bale with bleached eyebrows, and the women, including Hahn and Miller, in insane wigs. Clearly, this is Russell operating at an 11, with characters, based on these clips, squawking over each other like the most strident ensemble scenes out of “Silver Linings.”

During the panel, Russell described the casting process as “trippy,” noting that Cage gained weight for the role along with the prosthetics.

“We were scared because we weren’t telling a documentary, but we were honoring John Madden and honoring Al Davis,” Black said. “We were trying to make it an entertaining story without making it a documentary. So some stuff was inspired by, some stuff was true, and a lot of stuff we made up, not wildly, but just for entertainment value.”

The producer added, “I think when you see the movie, you’ll see it really is an incredibly positive film that when you watch it at Thanksgiving time, I think you’ll watch it with your family, hopefully, and you’ll walk out feeling really happy about it and telling people it’s such an inspiring film.”

He might be onto something. With three NFL games scheduled for Thanksgiving — including the Kansas City Chiefs at the Buffalo Bills on NBC and Peacock — “Madden” could prove apt counter-programming to sports spectacle. That’s if enough people know where to watch it, or that it’s available at all.

#3410. 50-Episode Sci-Fi Masterpiece Boasts One Of The Greatest Performances In TV History

It is a no-brainer that a sci-fi show is only as good as the performances of its cast. A sci-fi show can boast everything from high production value to compelling conceptual foundations. However, if its ideas are not driven by grounded performances and rootable characters, it is almost always bound to fail.

Fortunately, one 50-episode sci-fi thriller perfectly understands this and delivers one of the greatest performances in TV history. Created by Graeme Manson and John Fawcette, Orphan Black has an incredibly compelling opening hook. It begins with a scene where a character, Sarah, witnesses the death of her own doppelgänger. This prompts her to assume her identity.

With what follows, Orphan Black turns into a harrowing exploration of identity as it unfolds a grand conspiracy involving human cloning. From a thematic and conceptual standpoint alone, Orphan Black is brilliantly written. The show is packed with enough twists and turns and narrative highs and lows to keep viewers glued to their screens.

However, the Canadian sci-fi show's true appeal lies in the phenomenal performance of its lead, Tatiana Maslany. Throughout the show's runtime, she plays multiple characters and ensures that each has a distinct identity. If it wasn't for her, the near-perfect sci-fi show probably would not have been half as successful.

Tatiana Maslany plays a total of 17 clones in Orphan Black. Instead of purely relying on their distinct physical appearances to highlight their differences, Maslany fully embraces their mannerisms and personalities. She immerses herself so deeply into every clone's identity that a viewer can take one look at even a still frame from the series to tell who she is playing.

For instance, when she plays Helena, everything from her demeanor to her expressions turn feral and predatory. Meanwhile, she seems more warm when she appears as Cosima. Alison is another memorable clone from the series because Maslany perfectly projects her clipped hand gestures. In some of the best story beats from the show, Maslany also plays meta clones.

Instead of portraying a specific cloned variant, she captures how one cloned character in Orphan Black is pretending to be another. In this feat of meta-acting, she intentionally allows some nervousness and hesitance to bleed in. This ensures that viewers know they are looking at an impersonator.

Every time actors play multiple characters in the same movie or show, it is hard not to notice overlaps in some baseline mannerisms.

Maslanay's performance, in contrast, is exceptional because almost every clone seems to have a completely distinct identity. As a viewer, it becomes hard not to routinely forget that you are watching the same actor play so many different roles. With every clone's story, Orphan Black also switches genres. Such wild swings in tone could have easily turned the series into a disjointed mess.

However, it is Tatiana Maslanay's performance that single-handedly holds the show's tonal shifts together. Orphan Black's story makes massive pivots where it is a suburban black comedy in some story beats while a sci-fi family drama in another. Each pivot feels like a compelling journey in the overarching story because Maslanay carries every character with ease.

This explains why Tatiana Maslanay even won a Primetime Emmy Award for her performance in Orphan Black and the show is still considered a timeless sci-fi masterpiece.

Orphan Black follows a streetwise hustler who becomes entangled in a complex conspiracy after witnessing the suicide of a woman who bears an uncanny resemblance to her. As she assumes the deceased's identity, she uncovers a secret that places her life in jeopardy.
