#3409. Russell Brand Was Sentenced for Rape and Sexual Assault on Monday. By Friday, Netflix Had a Sleazy Doc Ready to Go

The term that comes to mind most is “ambulance-chasing.” Earlier this week, just one week after Russell Brand was convicted of rape and sexual assault and two days after he was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison for his crimes, word spread that Netflix was prepping a documentary on the comedian-turned-criminal.

Olivia Isaacs’ documentary has been in the works for a while. Deadline’s initial story on the project even noted that it “was referenced during the trial” and that while “giving evidence at London’s Southwark Crown Court, Mark Pinheiro, a former friend of Brand, said he had been approached by a producer about the Netflix show.” Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

But that the project — “Russell Brand: Open Secret,” a slim and unfocused documentary feature that clocks in at just under 90 minutes — was being dropped on the streamer to ride the wave of interest after Brand’s conviction and sentencing felt distasteful. How essential, after all, could this be? And what could it tell us about Brand’s actual trial, sentencing, and conviction?

Turns out, not much. Isaacs’ film doesn’t get into the trial until its final five minutes (counting its end credits to boot), when it uses title cards to share the conviction news, note that all of the allegations contained in the film itself “pre-date” those that led to the conviction, and make clear that Brand’s legal team was contacted after the Monday conviction and chose not to respond. That’s perhaps the most interesting part of the film’s literally tacked-on final moments: a desire to show its work when it comes to the journalism and attendant standards behind Brand’s long-simmering takedown.

Other elements are far less successful, as Isaacs’ film leans hard on tired tropes and cloying conventions. Captions frequently mention “[unsettling music playing]” or “[dramatic music playing]” during the most benign moments. Old footage of Brand, from home video to early stand-up gigs, is played slowly, all the better to maximize the sense that something is wrong with this man. Far more effective are interviews with those who were allegedly victimized by Brand, but those are often drowned out by played-out techniques.

The film opens with a typical “rise and fall” style montage, charting Brand’s humble beginnings, meteoric rise to fame, profound injection into the cultural consciousness (he met the queen! and also Tom Cruise!), stumble into right-wing ideology, and eventual criminal convictions for horrific acts the film posits everyone knew about forever.

It is, after all, called “Russell Brand: Open Secret.”

Isaacs’ film lacks a thesis beyond the general idea that everyone knew Brand was a creep from the jump. She assembles a hodgepodge of talking heads to hammer that home, including fellow comedians, some genuinely freaked out ex-girlfriends, a handful of accusers (including one who, reticent to appear on camera, is replaced with an actress, one of the film’s most thoughtful choices), and some bizarrely starry-eyed commentators (journalist George Monbiot comes across particularly badly here, zipping from talking about his early delight in Brand and his now-held belief that Brand’s far-right switch is the most horrifying aspect of all of this, oof).

Most compelling are Times journalists Rosamund Urwin and Charlotte Wace, who worked tirelessly to investigate myriad accusations against Brand for years (Urwin first began to look into Brand in January of 2019). Even smushed up against a herky-jerky timeline and a loose sense of purpose, the way that Urwin and Wace talk about the precise nature of their work, what they can and cannot report, the women they spoke to, and the ways in which they were nearly shut down (and, in fact, many other investigations of its ilk were allegedly turned off) is both gripping and necessary.

With more time and better access, the film could have focused more on the police and legal minds that helped build the case against Brand, but in the rush to get this out in the world, that was surely not a major aim.

By its midpoint, Isaacs’ film turns its lens on the culture that helped give rise to Brand, the wild “noughties” when “ladette culture” ruled and being overtly sexy and crude was de rigueur. Women were into Brand! Being ruthlessly unfunny and breathlessly boorish was hot! Also, his dad was mean to him! Diddy and David Walliams jump scares! These are some of the insights on offer in “Open Secret,” and the only thing truly revealing about them is how huge of a mistake it was to let someone as outwardly disgusting and deeply unwitty as Brand get into a place where he could pick and choose his “damsels” or his “whores,” depending on who is talking about them.

The film speed-runs through the last few years of Brand’s life and career, as he pivots into far-right shock politics and Christianity just as the walls are starting to close in on him. Brand may have alleged that his former cadre of famous friends and stalwarts won’t “touch him with a barge pole” these days, but the film’s distinct lack of bigger talking heads stands out. That could stand some further interrogation, too, but there’s simply no time for that. (Well, there is, but not if you want to be a part of this news cycle.)

The four-day gap between Brand’s conviction and the film’s release is zippy, even for Netflix, which has gotten progressively speedier with its true crime joints. In July of 2024, it was announced that Netflix would release a multi-part Karen Read documentary, just days after her first murder trial ended in a mistrial due to a hung jury on July 1, 2024. Three episodes dropped earlier this month.

In January of 2026, the streamer announced a Lucy Letby project with “unprecedented access” after the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) announced it would bring no further criminal charges against the former nurse, who was sentenced to life imprisonment for a slew of charges of murder and attempted murder of infants in her care following a review of additional allegations. “The Truth and Tragedy of Moriah Wilson” was first publicly announced in February of 2026, almost three years after Kaitlin Armstrong was convicted of first-degree murder of the cyclist in November of 2023.

“Russell Brand: Open Secret” will surely capture lots of eyeballs as this part of the news cycle winds down, but what the film trades for immediacy, it more than loses in actual insight. Part two can’t be far behind. Let’s just hope it takes far more time to make and far more consideration to craft.

“Russell Brand: Open Secret” is now streaming on Netflix.

#3408. 'Tracker' Is Finally Giving Colter What He Needs After 2 Seasons | Review

It's wild to think that after three seasons on the road, Tracker Season 4 is the first time we see Colter Shaw (Justin Hartley) united with the entire cast. Seriously. Even in the first season, Colter's former handlers never appeared on-screen alongside our favorite rewardist, and the one time Colter met up with one of them in Season 2, his former tech expert was still further east in the Windy City. But now that the rest of the cast has consolidated to Denver, "Blind Spot" offers Colter the opportunity to share some screen time with everyone currently on his roster — and it's about time.

At a nice home somewhere in Denver, Colorado, a man we later learn is named Emelio Chavez (J. Anthony Pena) leaves his wife, Marie (Mercedes Colon), indoors to meet two guys named Hector Cruz (Rafael Cabrera) and Freddie (Mike Miller) in his garage. They speak briefly about a car before Chavez invites his buddies inside for some dessert his wife made — of course, they're only welcome after they dispose of a dead body wrapped in a sheet on the floor. The next day at Reenie Greene's (Fiona Rene) law office, Colter arrives and reunites with his lawyer in the flesh. It's been a while since they've seen each other, and nothing is said about her date with Russell (Jensen Ackles), so those hoping for answers will be disappointed. Colter also meets Mel Day (Cassady McClincy Zhang) for the first time, who awkwardly steps over herself during the introduction. However, Colter is there to work, and he's soon brought before Reenie's mentor, Judge Gail McGill (Amy Aquino), whose daughter, Erica (Daniela Nieves), appears to be missing. Although they haven’t spoken in years, Gail’s terminal diagnosis has led her to make amends.

Tracker works because the case changes every week and the four people solving it never do. Here is which of them you are, what it says about you, and the case for yours being the best of the four.

You would rather handle it yourself and you are usually capable of doing so. Colter is a survivalist who lives in an Airstream and takes reward money for finding missing people, which is a premise that only works because he is clearly running from something of his own.

You know somebody, and that somebody owes you a favour. Reenie is the lawyer Colter calls when a case needs a door opened legally, and she is the only person on the show who can get further with a phone call than he can on foot.

You are two steps ahead and you rarely mention it. Bobby is the one who finds the thing that unlocks the case, usually from a desk, usually about ninety seconds before anybody realises they needed it.

You turn up, change the temperature of the room, and leave people arguing about you. Russell is Colter's brother, ex-military, and the show has never once let the audience settle on whether he is a help or a problem, which is exactly why he keeps coming back.

Speaking to Gail, she admits that she wasn’t really there for her growing up after Erica's father died. Colter asks about what led to their estrangement, and Gail reveals that it was a combination of her own stubbornness and cutting her daughter off. It's been three years since they've spoken, thus far, but she hopes to rectify that. With no social media or current contacts, there's little to go on, but Gail offers Colter a letter to pass to her daughter if he does find her. “I’m going to do everything I can to find her for you.” Meeting with Randy (Chris Lee), the hacker reveals he’s unable to find literally anything — credit cards included — on Erica. The only thing that may give them an edge is an old photo from a deleted social account that leads them to Mile High Taproom, a local brewery where Erica once worked alongside a friend, Ashley Cox (Carina Conti), who appears in several photos.

Arriving at the brewery, Colter speaks with Ashley, who reveals that she thought Erica just wanted a clean break from life. However, the two have since had a falling out of their own after a dispute regarding a guy Erica had been seeing named Jeb Boyd (Jesse Luken). “I have no idea where they landed,” she tells Colter. This gives Randy some extra material to work with, however, and leads Colter to a towing company Boyd owns across town. When he arrives, the door is ajar, and Boyd has been knocked out on the floor. Upon waking up, he tells Colter that three guys beat him up over a Cadillac that Erica had repossessed the night before. Of course, when they try to call her, they have no luck.

Instead, Colter heads over to Erica's place and looks around. Randy calls to reveal that the car itself belongs to a woman named Paloma Nava, a local churchgoer with a clean record. Poking around inside, Colter doesn’t find much other than the fact that her bed comforter is missing, as is a missing curtain. That leads him to a bullet hole in the window frame and, given that the place smells like bleach, it doesn’t look too good for Erica. That's when he has Randy hack into the neighboring camera, where he sees Erica gunned down and her body taken by several goons. Later, when the cops show up, Detective Zahn (Rolando Boyce) reveals that they believe the man involved is Emelio Chavez, who headlines a mean narcotics operation in town. After being told by the detective to stand down for the time being, Reenie shows up and asks what she should tell Gail — Colter asks for more time. He just wants to find answers for her before they tell her that Erica is dead. For a minute here, it really looks as if Colter has failed, but there's, of course, more to the story.

Just then, Randy calls to reveal that Hector Cruz, Nava’s nephew, would have had access to the Cadillac. He further connects Hector to Chavez by linking him to a construction company owned by the outlaw. Colter believes that they probably have Erica’s body in the car, and so heads out to the last spot where Hector's phone pinged — which just so happens to be one of Chavez’s construction sites. Colter comes upon the goons involved, creates a distraction, and takes him out. Looking around, he finds the breach and bloody materials but not the body itself. Breaking into the office, he holds a gun at Hector and starts firing off both questions and bullets — anything to get answers. Apparently, the body they have in the car is a federal agent named Mark Sutton, an undercover DEA agent who was killed by Chavez. But Hector messed up. Having left the car long enough for Erica to repo it, they took the fight to her. Hector tells him that they took the bodies to the gas fields ten miles north, and he won't have enough time to stop them. As usual, don't tell Colter Shaw the odds.

After taking out the federal agent first, Freddie goes back for Erica's body, only for her to fight back. She survived her gunshot wound and does all she can to escape, though Chavez tackles and strangles her. Barely beating him with a rock, she runs off, still wounded. By the time Colter arrives, however, he finds the scene empty. The car is there (trunk open) and Freddie is dead, but Chavez and Erica are missing. When Colter sees the bloody handprint on the car and a trail leading away from the scene, he realizes that Erica is alive. Unfortunately, he's not the only one following her trail toward the nearby power plant. Although she flags down some help, Chavez kills the worker before he can do anything but slow him down, which signals Colter to their location.

With Chavez on her tail, Erica escapes into the plant and hides. Chavez's other men show up, and they invade the plant, looking everywhere for their loose end. Fortunately, Colter arrives in the nick of time to help, dressing Erica's wound and leading her toward the roof. When Chavez and his men enter, he takes out one of the guys and a firefight ensues. Colter beats down Chavez in a one-on-one fight, but before he can take him out to the police, Erica shoots and kills her captor. When Zahn and the rest of the reinforcements arrive, the detective thanks Colter for his help, though notes that the prints on the gun that killed the drug lord have been wiped clean.

That night, Colter visits Erica in her hospital room, who has been reading over her mother's letter. After everything, she decides that she wants to see her mother after all, prompting Gail to walk in. The pair have a heartfelt reunion as Erica finally forgives her mother, and Colter slips out to let them reconcile. Back at Reenie's office, Colter enjoys a few drinks with Reenie, Randy, and Mel. For the first time, the Tracker cast is all together, but, as per usual, Colter does his best to skip out before things get too personal — this was the same technique he used to get out of spending time with Reenie and Randy's cousin Bobby (Eric Graise) back in Season 1's "Chicago."

But before he can perform his Irish goodbye, Colter is cornered by Mel, who asks him to look into what happened to her mother. She still has questions about how exactly her mother died, and Colter agrees to take a look. It's a bit strange that Reenie hasn't brought up what she found to Colter before, but the reward seeker will no doubt be clued in soon enough. “It was nice meeting you,” he says, taking off without looking back. Far be it from Tracker to allow Colter to bond with his allies...

Colter Shaw reunites with the Tracker cast for a one-off episode with some sudden twists.

#3406. 5 Funniest 'Peanuts' Comics About Dogs

Starring Schroeder! (I kid, they’re all with Snoopy)

Broadly speaking, there are three types of Peanuts comics. There are the funny ones, the sweet ones, and ones that are both funny and sweet. (And, let’s be honest, there are a good number of boring ones too.) But, very generally speaking, those are the three types of good Peanuts comics: funny, sweet, and the ones that do both of those things.

I bring this up because my goal here is to find the five funniest Peanuts comics about dogs. Not like, just Peanuts comics “starring Snoopy,” even though all of them do, but comic strips that are actually about dogs and the nature of dogs in general, if that makes sense. So that means no Flying Ace or Joe Cool stuff. I love those, but I wanted to define this one pretty narrowly about “dogs” (which, I guess, is still pretty broad).

I also wanted to just go for the funny ones. These aren’t the sweet “go hug your dog” Peanuts comics, or even the sweet/funny ones that check all the boxes for Snoopy fans. I was determined to just find funny, dog-themed Peanuts comics which illustrate Charles Schulz’s impressive abilities as a joke-writer.

Dogs do live a pretty enviable life. They have no jobs, people bring them food for free, and simple pleasures like stick-throwing are entirely fulfilling. A lot of people wish life was that simple for them — I know I do. Here, Snoopy addresses those feelings of jealousy many humans have towards dogs and basically says “Yeah, being a dog is pretty great.”

From Jan. 6, 1952, this is the first-ever Sunday strip of Peanuts. The comic had begun in 1950, running six days a week with its regular, four-panel daily strips, but its growing popularity brought it to Sundays.

In these early ones, Snoopy didn't really have all of his more human-like personality traits that would become his signature. Instead, he was just a regular, adorable old dog, which is evidenced here when Snoopy does something that it’s hard to imagine him doing: biting Charlie Brown. It comes during a game of tag where a bunch of kids are running around, tagging each other. One of the kids tags Snoopy, then we see Charlie Brown shout “Ow!”

Then we see Charlie Brown with the back of his shorts missing, with an angry expression as Snoopy looks on innocently. Meanwhile, a kid named Patty — this is the original Patty, not Peppermint Patty — tells Charlie Brown, “Don’t get mad, Charlie Brown…. That’s just his way of tagging!”

What I love about this one is it seems like it could be about something deeper. Snoopy is experiencing some serious malaise, feeling like his life has no meaning at all. And because we all love Snoopy, it makes us all empathize with him and worry about him. Snoopy often acts like more of a human than a dog, and in this comic strip, he seems like he is a super-depressed human. And then, after multiple panels that make Snoopy look like he’s going through a mid-dog-years crisis, Charlie Brown arrives with a full bowl of food. All of a sudden, Snoopy snaps out of it and his life has meaning again. Snoopy may act like a man, but he’s all-dog.

I love how mad Snoopy is in this one. He’s such a happy dog that we rarely see him in a bad mood, which is why this one is so funny and feels like he’s being a real dog here. Dogs hate to see their food bowls empty, and it’s hilarious to see Snoopy play that very dog-like emotion.

Is this one too sweet? It is really funny, but I fear I’m breaking my own stupid rules here. I just couldn’t resist this one. I mean, it is about “dogs” and quite literally the “nature of dogs,” with Lucy talking about the reason for a distinctive dog behavior. Yet the sleepy Snoopy on top of Linus’ head is super cute. I guess it’s impossible to entirely separate the humor of Peanuts from its inherent sweetness.

#3405. Will ‘Dune’ and ‘Avengers’ Drown Out Everything Else at the Box Office This Christmas?

Look, it’s only November, but we know we’re not the only people getting excited about Christmas already. In fact, we know that some studio executives have been thinking about the holiday season a lot for a while now. That’s because they know as well as anyone that they have two juggernauts to contend with: “Dune: Part Three” and “Avengers: Doomsday,” which open on Dec. 18 in true clash of the titans fashion.

There’s a question that if those movies take up so much oxygen, will there be room for anything else? The last “Dune” movie surpassed $700 million globally at the box office, and “Avengers: Doomsday” has already sold over $60 million in pre-sales. Those top two titles create enormous competition for everything opening on Christmas weekend itself. Those include the Dwayne Johnson threequel “Jumanji: Open World” from Sony, the football biopic “Mr. Irrelevant” from Paramount, Robert Eggers’ horror film “Werwulf” from Focus, and Luca Guadagnino’s “Artificial” from Neon. Paramount’s “The Angry Birds Movie 3” is also opening on December 23 just ahead of the rest. Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

Anyone will tell you the Christmas holiday is always crowded at the movies. And there’s usually room for multiple blockbusters to draw crowds. Despite the onslaught of new titles, U.S, distributors are confident they’ll be able to secure the screens they need to be successful. For instance, “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” this year opened at the end of July to $360 million domestic, and “The Odyssey” in its third week in theaters still made $50 million. Even during the “Barbenheimer” weekend, “Sound of Freedom” in its third week managed to bring in another $19.8 million. There’s always opportunity if the demand is there.

Recent Christmases have been similarly crowded. Last year had “Avatar: Fire and Ash,” “The Housemaid,” a new “Spongebob,” and “Marty Supreme” open the weekend before Christmas, then “Anaconda” and “Song Sung Blue” over the holiday itself. 2024 had “Mufasa: The Lion King,” “Nosferatu,” “Sonic the Hedgehog 3,” “A Complete Unknown,” “Babygirl,” and “The Fire Inside” all in a short span just before Xmas.

But this Christmas does bring some unique challenges that studios are preemptively working around for their titles that are not “Dune” or “Avengers.” Both of those films have had tickets on sale for months, and both are locked in a fight for premium large format screens that distributors would be lying to say they didn’t want, even if it’s for a family film that doesn’t need it. Warner Bros. and Legendary’s “Dune: Part Three” specifically will exclusively be on IMAX screens, which has famously left “Doomsday” without them, leaving Disney to create its Infinity Vision certification to drum up excitement.

To compete, “Angry Birds 3” is still opening in 3D if on otherwise standard format screens. “Werwulf” won’t have IMAX as Focus did for “Nosferatu,” but it has pre-sold select 35mm screenings of the film that have already done quite well (they went on sale on the full moon last month). The hope, too, is that titles like “Jumanji” and “Mr. Irrelevant” appeal to crowds that are distinctive from the male, fanboy-heavy audiences for “Dunesday.”

One source IndieWire spoke with argued that even though this Christmas is top heavy, it’s arguably lighter in sheer quantity than we’ve seen in recent years. What we’re not seeing is a movie like “Marty Supreme” or “Uncut Gems” getting a run in a more mid-size or limited number of screens. Universal doesn’t have a movie opening in that window, nor does Amazon MGM. Other awards titles like “The Debut” from A24 are going earlier in the month and aren’t doing the limited, Christmas day, qualifying run before going wide in January (GKIDS’ “Look Back” may be an exception, opening December 30).

There are some potential holdovers that could generate money well into Christmas. Rival studio execs are keeping an eye on movies like Disney’s animated “Hexed” or Universal’s “Focker-in-Law,” and Focus’ “Elsinore” will also be going wider shortly before the holidays.

The hope now is that all of these films get their flowers and collectively put an exclamation point on a stellar 2026, with the box office now projected to finish far above $10 billion domestic, a number that might’ve been a pipe dream this time in 2025. That’s reason for holiday cheer, indeed.

#3404. 5 Massive Anime Just Left Crunchyroll, Here's Where To Stream Them Instead

Vanessa Piña has been writing as a journalist for over two years. As a senior writer, she focuses on timely coverage of the latest anime releases and popular comic franchises.

Changes to the libraries of streaming platforms are not unusual, but Crunchyroll has faced significant backlash for failing to notify users which anime series are about to be removed, leaving fans with no opportunity to watch them before they disappear for good. Over the last few months, more anime series have left Crunchyroll, and while some can still be watched on other streaming services, others have vanished from the streaming landscape entirely, becoming accessible only in physical format.

It's not uncommon for anime series to leave Crunchyroll for other streaming platforms, whether due to expiring licensing agreements, high renewal costs, or another platform paying for exclusivity that leads to the series being pulled out. As @MangaAlerts shared on X in July 2026, among the recent waves of anime removals from Crunchyroll, the most notable was the departure of five major series: Blood Blockade Battlefront, Barakamon, Orange, Grimgar: Ashes and Illusions, and Rokka: Brave of the Six Flowers.

This selection of anime series was highly acclaimed for its incredible animation and profound narrative, a prime example being Grimgar: Ashes and Illusions, regarded as one of the best modern isekai series for its gritty take on the genre, avoiding the trope of overpowered heroes. Another removed title was the live-action adaptation of As the Gods Will, a work by the creator of Blue Lock that's widely said to have served as an inspiration for Squid Game.

Occasionally, there's a scenario where they might return to Crunchyroll later. However, it's worth noting that several of these titles were part of Funimation prior to its acquisition by Crunchyroll, adding to the list of series inherited from that catalog that the platform continues to remove over time.

While these anime series have sparked debate among fans due to their large followings, other lost titles have flown somewhat more under the radar. In addition to Black Lagoon, and as part of its recent content shake-up, Endride, Bem, and Sasami: Magical Girls Club were also cut from Crunchyroll in July 2026.

Crunchyroll has been hit with controversy after its store updated to remove a massive amount of anime and manga titles, leaving fans uncertain.

This trend has continued well beyond the summer. In September, Crunchyroll also removed Teasing Master Takagi-san, Kanojo ga Flag wo Oraretara (If Her Flag Breaks), Nagi-Asu: A Lull in the Sea, Pandora Hearts, and From Me to You: Kimi ni Todoke. Perhaps the most well-known anime series that the platform recently delisted is Akame ga Kill!, produced by the studio White Fox, a title that left a significant mark on fans by subverting expectations within the shonen genre with its tragedy and brutality.

While Crunchyroll is parting ways with some memorable titles, fans who haven't seen them yet (or those who want to watch them again) can still enjoy these anime series on other platforms. Here is a list of where viewers can find these anime series following their removal from the service:

Kanojo ga Flag wo Oraretara (If Her Flag Breaks)

Unfortunately, western fans will have to access titles like Grimgar: Ashes and Illusions, Barakamon, Rokka: Braves of the Six Flowers and Akame ga Kill! in physical form until they are added to another streaming platform. While the expiration of licensing agreements is a reality for all streaming platforms, which are characterized by their constant evolution and content renewal, the fact that certain anime become unavailable is undoubtedly frustrating for viewers, as some series could end up becoming "lost media."

#3403. Update Your iPhone to Prevent People From Seeing iMessages They Shouldn't

Has this ever happened to you? You add someone new to an iMessage group chat, and wonder, "Huh, can they see any of the messages from before they were added?" The answer to that question is supposed to be "no." By design, new iMessage group chat members are only privy to texts that arrive after they were added. When they join, it's essentially a blank slate, as if you just created the group for the first time. At least, that's how it's intended to work.

As it turns out, there's a bug with iMessage that may allow new group chat members to see texts from before they were added to the chat. That's a problem, and not just for the iPhone users out there talking smack about people before inviting them to join the group chat. It means iMessage, and Apple's platforms in general, aren't working like they're supposed to be. You don't have to be talking behind people's backs to not want new members seeing existing chats. Maybe you're planning a surprise party for someone, and add them to the group once everyone's in on the plan; maybe the texts in the chat aren't relevant to the current group, and the person joining simply does not need to access them.

That's not all: There exists another security flaw that could allow remote hackers to join an iMessage group and receive new messages. You might add a new user to a group chat and inadvertently invite them to read all existing messages, while at the same time being attacked by a bad actor who can then intercept all future messages. Not good.

Luckily, there's currently a fix for these problems. Apple patched (and revealed) the bugs, along with seven other security flaws, with a series of software updates on Monday for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro. Not all of the updates include patches for these two iMessage flaws—specifically, some of the updates for older Apple devices. But the rest, including iOS 27.2.1, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, macOS 15.8.3, watchOS 27.2.1, and visionOS 27.2.1, include the iMessage patches.

Each update includes its own list of patches, but, for this article, I'll take a look at the nine patches in iOS 27.2.1. You'll find the two iMessage bugs, plus seven other patches, in the list below:

AirPlay: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113968: Apple

App Intents: Impact: An app may be able to access sensitive user data. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113963: László Várady

Bluetooth: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to corrupt process memory. Description: A use-after-free issue was addressed with improved memory management. CVE-2026-113970: Apple

brotli: Impact: Processing maliciously crafted input may lead to memory corruption. Description: An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved input validation. CVE-2026-111497

CoreUtils: Impact: A malicious Bluetooth device may be able to establish a pairing without user interaction. Description: This issue was addressed with improved checks. CVE-2026-113965: Apple

CoreUtils: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts and pair with a device without user interaction. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113964: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A remote attacker may be able to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved validation. CVE-2026-113961: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A user added to an iMessage group may be able to access messages sent before they joined. Description: This issue was addressed by removing the vulnerable code. CVE-2026-113960: an anonymous researcher

Rapportd: Impact: An attacker on the same network may be able to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113969: Apple

For a full accounting of the patches included in the other security updates, check out Apple's official security releases site.

To install Apple's latest security updates, you'll simply need to update your device as you usually do. On iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro, head to Settings > General > Software Update; on Mac, go to System Settings > General > Software Update. Here, follow the on-screen instructions to download and install the latest version of your device's software.

#3401. This AirPods Feature Fixed My Biggest Problem With Listening to Podcasts to Fall Asleep

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

There's lots to recommend about podcasts (and lots of podcasts to recommend), but one of their biggest benefits—for me, anyway—has little to do with what a particular show is about or even who hosts it: They're great for dissociating. I often have a podcast playing to distract my anxious brain from whatever I'm worried about (which, in 2026, is usually slightly less than everything).

Any time I don't want to be alone with my thoughts (say, when commuting or doing mindless chores), I can put on a podcast and be entertained by a couple of goobers talking about movies rather than spinning my wheels about my son's middle school applications. And there's no time I want to disassociate from reality more than bedtime.

For years I've used podcasts as a non-pharmaceutical sleep aid, and few things are more effective at helping me drop off quickly. Unfortunately, for years this also meant that once I fell asleep, the podcast kept playing. I have my podcast app set to delete episodes once finished, so if it was a show I cared about, I'd need to do a lot of redownloading and scrubbing through to find where I left off—that is, until I upgraded my earbuds to the AirPods Pro 3.

The AirPods Pro 3 launched alongside iOS 26 in the fall of 2025 with flashy features like vastly improved noise cancellation, Live Translation, Heart Rate Sensing, and hearing health settings, all of them quite welcome on a set of $250 premium earbuds. But the best new AirPods feature was one I didn't even know about when I decided to upgrade my four-year-old Beats Fit Pro.

In the AirPods settings (accessible via your iPhone's Settings app), if you tap Audio & Routing and scroll down, you'll see an option to turn on a setting called Pause Media When Falling Asleep. I don't think I need to tell you what this setting does. I can tell you that it works great.

According to Apple, the feature works by sensing when you're drifting off using the earbuds' built-in accelerometer to track your movement (or lack thereof). Once your earbuds have determined that you're falling asleep, they will pause your audio for you. And it isn't just the 2025 AirPods Pro 3 that support it—it also works on the second-generation AirPods Pro as well as the AirPods 4 and the AirPods 5.

I'll admit that I don't really understand how the AirPods Pro 3 can tell I'm falling asleep versus just lying very still, but I've never had them pause accidentally during active listening. Conversely, whenever I go back to the podcast I was listening to the night before, I'll find that the audio paused within a minute or two of the last part I remember hearing.

The AirPods Pro 3 aren't the only earbuds with a feature like this, but you'll most often only find it in dedicated "sleep earbuds" designed specifically for the purpose. While many of those offer extra health features like the ability to track your sleep cycles, I'm not really interested in that (my Apple Watch does most of it, and I don't look at that data anyway). Pausing my audio when I'm asleep is really all I need, and the AirPods Pro 3 do it well enough that I don't need to bother with a pair of dedicated bedtime buds.

#3400. 'Game of Thrones' Meets Jack Reacher in Alexander Skarsgård's Near-Perfect Action Epic

Conor Sheeran is a Movies and TV features writer for Collider. He has a deep passion for cinema and watches everything from the biggest blockbusters to the smallest indies. While he specializes in movies and television, he has also written about politics, culture, and sports throughout his career. Based in New York City, Conor is also a massive fan of the New York Jets, Mets, and Knicks. He is still waiting for any of those teams to bring home a championship in his lifetime. A member of the National Writers Union and the International Federation of Journalists, Conor is a strong proponent of press freedom and collective action.

Few movies of the past decade have been as ambitious and as meticulous in their approach to life and combat as Robert Eggers' The Northman. Released in 2022, the Viking revenge epic combines the violence and political intrigue of Game of Thrones with the "man on a mission" brutality of Reacher, fusing what makes those shows great while improving where they may fall short. Led by a career-defining performance by Alexander Skarsgård, The Northman is a bloody and haunting journey through betrayal and Norse mythology that deserves more recognition than it initially garnered upon release.

Although the film received widespread critical praise, especially for Skarsgård's performance, it never caught on in theaters and struggled to earn back its production budget. Filmed for between $70 and $90 million, it earned just $75 million at the box office, so while it's not considered a bomb, it had enough commercial appeal to leave some feeling disappointed. However, like many hidden gems and cult classics, The Northman's reputation has only grown in the years since release, particularly among viewers searching for the historical, adult-oriented action spectacle Hollywood has become reluctant to produce. With its stunning cinematogaphy, ferocious battle sequences, and emotional story of revenge, Eggers' Viking tale remains one of the best action movies of the 2020s.

Set in the late ninth century, The Northman follows Amleth (Skarsgård), a young prince whose life is forever changed when his villainous uncle Fjolnir (Claes Bang) murders his father, King Aurvandill (Ethan Hawke), and kidnaps his mother, Queen Gudrun (Nicole Kidman). As the young man manages to escape death, Amleth dedicates his life to avenging his father, rescuing his mother, and killing his uncle.

We shan't be going to the Viking times, thank you.

Years later, Amleth has become a hulking Viking berserker, the living embodiment of vengeance and someone who is willing to murder anyone who gets in the way of his quest for revenge. He soon discovers his uncle's whereabouts and travels back to Iceland to finally accomplish his mission. There, he meets and falls in love with a slave woman named Olga (Anya Taylor-Joy), who helps him in his quest.

Skarsgård is nearly unrecognizable in his performance, delivering a physically imposing portrayal that makes Amleth feel less like a man and more like a force of nature. His sheer brutality recalls the unstoppable presence of Jack Reacher, particularly in the Prime Video series Reacher, starring Alan Ritchson. Both characters possess the intimidating physicality and an almost supernatural ability to overwhelm their enemies, often in the most brutal ways possible.

While Reacher operates by a certain moral code, Amleth is consumed by obsession. Revenge dictates where he goes, what he eats and drinks, and who he interacts with, dominating every decision he makes regardless of the consequences. His unwavering, terrifying determination makes him a monster to his enemies while threatening to destroy everything he holds dear.

Beyond its ferocious action, The Northman's DNA is thoroughly mixed with HBO's classic Game of Thrones. Both focus on the brutality of a medieval setting while blending it with the loyalty and political ambition of the day, and both exist in a world where betrayal can be as devastating as any defeat on a bloody battlefield. Much like dragons and the ancient magic of Game of Thrones, Eggers imbues his world with the supernatural elements of Norse mythology, incorporating witches, draugr, and Valkyries to create a world where the line between history and fantasy becomes increasingly blurred.

However, The Northman does not focus on the maneuvering and scheming for a throne that Game of Thrones does, but instead on the violence that exists behind the scenes in a psychologically complex story about the consequences of revenge. One of the film's greatest strengths is its willingness to challenge what Amleth believes about his family. As with Thrones, family members can sometimes become your worst enemies, which is something Amleth did not expect or prepare for.

While the movie's ambition may have exceeded its success, its lackluster box-office performance was never a reflection of its quality. Viewers who love the ruthless medieval world of Game of Thrones and the bone-crunching brutality of Reacher will certainly find something to enjoy with The Northman. It's an unforgettable combination of genres that proves a movie doesn't need to fit into a box to succeed. Most importantly, it shows that action cinema can be visually spectacular, emotionally devastating, and intellectually ambitious without sacrificing the thrills of a fantasy epic.

#3399. IndieWire Honors Film Celebration to Fête John Turturro, the ‘Artificial’ Cast, Los Javis, and More

IndieWire, the definitive outlet for creative independence in film and TV, announced on Friday, November 13 the lineup for the Winter 2026 edition of our IndieWire Honors event, featuring our largest lineup yet of film honorees. Curated and selected by IndieWire’s editorial team, IndieWire Honors is a celebration of the filmmakers, actors, and artisans key to crafting some of the most exciting cinematic works this year.

The event will take place on Thursday, December 3 in Los Angeles, starting with an intimate cocktail reception and awards ceremony. IndieWire will also begin rolling out exclusive editorial content, including honoree profiles, on Friday, November 27 through the lead-up to the awards night. Throughout the ceremony, into the next day, IndieWire will publish photos and exclusive social content from the event as well. The ceremony’s host will be announced at a later date. “It’s thrilling to be able to recognize the artists behind so many of this year’s most exciting and compelling films,” said Brent Lang, IndieWire’s editor-in-chief. “They dazzled us with their talent, inspired us with their willingness to take risks, and left an indelible mark on cinema. We are excited to celebrate their accomplishments.”

“It’s exciting to celebrate such an eclectic group of film talent for this year’s IndieWire Honors,” said James Israel, IndieWire’s SVP and Publisher. “We are also pleased to continue to celebrate top craft artisans in entertainment.”

The Winter 2026 IndieWire Honors honorees are:

The fact that he is known for being a frequent collaborator of both Spike Lee and the Coen brothers conveys just how expansive an actor Turturro is. The Brooklyn native is quintessentially New York, as most recently proven in Sony Pictures Classics’ acclaimed Sundance premiere “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” written and directed by Noah Segan. Yet, a filmmaker can still drop the performer into the corporate dystopia of sci-fi series “Severance,” or have him go on a Southern odyssey in “O Brother, Where Art Thou?,” and he just as well hits it out of the park.

With nearly five decades of film work under his belt, starting with an uncredited role in “Raging Bull,” Turturro manages to be one of the few veteran actors who continues to best himself year after year.

The pair of Madrid-based directors colloquially known as Los Javis are not shy about cluing the audience in on the shoulders upon which they stand on. They cast Penélope Cruz and Lola Dueñas, two muses of auteur Pedro Almodóvar, as the most important women within their epic adaptation of an unfinished play by Federico García Lorca, another one of Spain’s queer artist forefathers. That reverence is balanced by the confidence in their own eye for new talent, weaving together three different timelines led by three relative unknowns, including most notably, indie musician Guitarricadelafuente, who also contributed the poignant original song “La Nieve” to the project.

Made outside the Hollywood system and chosen to represent Spain in the Best International Feature Oscar race, the Netflix release “La Bola Negra” is a film of immense scale. If viewers knew nothing of the director duo before seeing the film, they come away with a crash course in everything they are about. Considering how they won both the Best Director Award at Cannes, and the coveted People’s Choice Award at TIFF, it seems to be an experience most cinephiles enjoy.

“Tallgrass” is the code word that unlocks what makes the creative collaboration between “Paper Tiger” writer-director James Gray and star Adam Driver such a feat. Though the Neon release, which premiered at Cannes, is their first time ever working together, the filmmaker imbues the two-time Oscar nominee with such a specific vision of what it feels like to realize one’s time has gone by. Though the film is another deeply personal work in the oeuvre of the Queens-born auteur, Driver adds a more broad portrait of a figure wrapped up in crime, slowly feeling the overwhelming situation constrict and constrict.

“Josephine” was not made to be an easy watch, but boasts the rare feat of winning both the Grand Jury Prize and Audience Award at the Sundance Film Festival. Written and directed by Araújo, and starring Gemma Chan and Mason Reeves as mother and daughter, the drama is a bold exploration of how little control parents have over their children being confronted by certain horrors in life that there’s no guarantee of avoiding.

An early release for new distributor Sumerian Pictures, “Josephine” has only felt more necessary as the year has gone on, and news stories like the Cornell rape case have come to the forefront. It is a conversation piece about a subject many wish to evade, that puts forth the effort to reach meaningful discourse.

The most bold artistic choice in “Artificial,” the latest film from prolific director Luca Guadagnino, is to not proffer any romance in becoming one of the Promethean figures. The repeated refrain of “Feel the AGI” rings as a benevolent threat by the time the two hours and 20 minutes of the Neon release are over. Garfield, Borisov, Barbaro, and Barinholtz, all four playing key figures in the genesis of OpenAI, play incredibly off of each other as tech titans forcing a smile as they convince their audience artificial technology is inevitable. Join or die. Their joint efforts to invoke a common sense of humanity would be funny if the reality of the situation weren’t so uncanny.

Re-teaming with her “Secret Sunshine” director Lee Chang-dong almost 20 years later, the “Possible Love” star is unmissable as a woman caught in a class divide between her blue collar, out-of-work husband, and the couple that hosts them as a means to interview them for a documentary. It is a role that she said uses “the whole entirety of her body” to push back against the weight of capitalism. The Netflix film chosen to represent South Korea in the Best International Feature category at the 2027 Oscars offers a feast of ideas, with Jeon’s layered turn as Mi-ok alone being enough fodder for many conversations to come.

All sorts of biopics enter theaters each year, but few task their leads with the difficult job of playing someone still actively in the public eye. In Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky,” from Amazon MGM Studios, newcomer Ippolito deftly captures the distinctive look and sound of a young and hungry Sylvester Stallone. But what is more impressive than that form of transformation is how the 27-year-old actor captures the spirit of the unlikely star and scribe of the 1977 Best Picture winner. How some of his best moments come when he himself plays Rocky is a meta element we are still unpacking, but add it to the overwhelming evidence that Ippolito is one to watch.

There is a standout moment in Oscar winner Siân Heder’s “Being Heumann” in which Madeley, as trailblazing disability rights activist Judy Heumann, asks a well-meaning congressman what he means by calling her “inspiring.” “Inspired to do what?,” she says. It is a moment that clarifies that the film about Heumann leading the successful protest to get the government to sign Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act is not standard fare about a woman in a wheelchair overcoming odds, but a film about her refusing to let those odds overcome her.

Madeley embodies a fight against circumstances that applies to more than just the disability community. May casting directors take notice of the limitless potential she offers as part of any type of ensemble.

As the President and CEO of Laika Studios, Knight has spent over 20 years educating audiences on the artform of stop-motion animation. And still, in his latest film “Wildwood,” a fantasy epic taking place in the forests outside Portland, Oregon, Knight directs scenes that seem inexplicable. It is hard enough to animate one bird flying, using that technique, yet the Fathom Entertainment release sees whole flocks fly off toward a war between species. The film’s commentary on parents and children is as heartrending as the craft behind how the film was made is genuinely inspiring to filmmakers of all types.

Talk about legacy. Decades after his father, noted documentarian William Greaves, hosted a party for the surviving members of the Harlem Renaissance, “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” co-directed finished the film, one of the gems of Sundance 2026. To listen to Black luminaries from the ‘20s speak about how their work has endured into the ‘70s, with the dramatic irony of watching the film through a modern lens, is a singular cinematic experience. In a year where there is so much conversation around what pushes the documentary artform forward, the Neon release delivers both necessary context and innovation.

There is humor in having puppetry, one of the world’s oldest artforms, at the center of a conversation around innovation, but come on. Ortiz’s performance as Rocky in “Project Hail Mary,” supported by the work of visual effects team leaders Scanlan, Lambert, and Sarnowska, made us fall in love with a spidery alien rock that has no mouth or face. Puppetry’s forebearers would have still found that to be an insurmountable challenge. Hence, why the artist behind the fan favorite character opposite Ryan Gosling in the Amazon MGM Studios blockbuster deserves their flowers for helping viewers go beyond their earthly imaginations.

#3398. After 50 Years, Marvel Finally Gives A Fan-Favorite Avenger Their Own Joker

Every comic book hero needs a villain to define them. It’s how an average character becomes something even greater than anyone could have expected. It’s doubtful that Batman, Superman, and Thor would be where they are without Joker, Lex, and Loki. There are exceptions to the rule, like Wonder Woman. Someone so well-written and important to a genre that they surpass what’s needed to make a god-tier character. Unfortunately, even the best-written heroes don’t always rise to the top. That’s where Marvel's Jessica Drew, Spider-Woman, comes in.

It may be hard to believe, but Jessica Drew has been around almost as long as Storm and Wolverine. Another fun fact about Jessica is that she, unlike many other Spider-People, doesn’t have a direct connection to Peter Parker. Other than being part of the Spider Totem, they aren't related in any way. Her power and skills come from having terrorist parents, being connected to the High Evolutionary, and working with Hydra. That backstory should have been enough to make her a star. Sadly, that isn't the case.

No matter how many amazing writers have worked on Spider-Woman comics, something seemed to be missing. It could be because, despite working for elite teams like S.H.I.E.L.D., S.W.O.R.D., and the Avengers, one thing eluded her. She doesn't have a major nemesis. Sure, Hydra and the Skrulls count, but everyone hates them. Thankfully, writer Dan Watters (Nightwing and Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Shredder) is about to change that.

At the end of Amazing Spider-Man/Venom: Death Spiral, it looked like Carnage would be out of the way for a little while. It was stuck bonding with rodents and insects, and without a human host, it would be aimless. At the end of Amazing Spider-Man: Spider-Versity, it’s revealed that the Carnage Klyntar bonded with Jessica Drew. She does this hoping that she could teach the symbiote a better way.

Since the Klyntar aren't inherently evil, this was possible. Sadly, it may be too far gone. In the first issue of Dan Watters’ Spider-Woman, Jessica is making jokes about murdered people and enjoying brutally hurting goons. It’s clear that the symbiote is affecting her, so she has a conversation over a flame (fire being a Klyntar’s weakness). This is to remind Carnage that she is in charge.

There’s good news for Jessica. She may not have to worry about Carnage for long. His original host, Cletus Kasady, is back and ready to take Carnage from Jessica. When that happens, there will be a struggle to see who the symbiote's next host is. Even if Kasady loses, he's still dangerous. That means, no matter how it ends, Spider-Woman has a new nemesis, and he's perfect for Jessica Drew.

Putting any random villain with Spider-Woman isn’t a good idea. It must be someone who can challenge her on multiple levels. Jessica is smart, crafty, and an amazing detective. Not to mention, she has a bunch of superpowers that make her one of Earth’s most reliable heroes. Using someone like Electro or Wrecker won’t challenge her in a way that draws readers in. However, Cletus Kasady is.

What makes Kasady special is that, as mentioned earlier, he’s a threat without the symbiote. Before becoming Carnage, he was one of the most notorious serial killers ever. Adding the Klyntar made him more creative, and the last thing a serial killer needs is something to feed their imagination. They certainly don’t need an alien suit that heals them and can make weapons with a thought.

It will be interesting to see what direction Dan Watters goes in during Spider-Woman. Considering all the amazing work he’s done, especially over the last couple of years, Marvel Comics fans can relax knowing that, whatever it is, it will be good. It will also likely be very violent.

#3396. Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

From the misty seaports of Massachusetts seaports to the otherworldly town of Twin Peaks and even the distant shores of Troy, Ruth De Jong has spent the past twenty years transporting audiences into the unforgettable worlds created by auteur directors like Paul Thomas Anderson, Terrence Malick, Kenneth Lonergan, David Lynch, Jordan Peele, and Christopher Nolan.

“My goal in my work is to always paint the most authentic pictures,” De Jong shared with IndieWire at the Virginia Film Festival, where the production designer received the festival’s Craft Award. The town of Charlottesville has a special place in De Jong’s heart.

It’s here where legendary production designer Jack Fisk, father of De Jong’s high school friend Schuyler Fisk, suggested she forgo attending the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts for grad school in favor of working on the set of Paul Thomas Anderson’s 2007 Oscar-winning film “There Will Be Blood” instead. Recalling that fateful conversation, De Jong said that Fisk told her he saw the younger version of himself in her, sharing, “I think what the world continually needs are mentors [like Fisk] showing up.” Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

De Jong fell in love with filmmaking as she continued to work with Fisk on Anderson’s “The Master,” and a handful of films by Terence Malick, including his Palme d’Or winner “The Tree of Life.” Eventually she spread her wings and took on her first film as production designer: Kenneth Lonergan’s “Manchester by the Sea.” Looking back on these early days and everything she learned on those sets, De Jong said that she believes “a body of work like that is built upon itself. I think I’m constantly pulling from the past, but also pulling from the future.”

Whether designing a fishing village in modern-day Gloucester, recreating the White House Oval Office, or crafting the iconic Trojan horse, all of De Jong’s work comes in service of the characters and story being told. While crafting a film’s world, De Jong asks herself, “How do I make this tangible and alive and real and authentic?”

To capture undertones of the real working-class people in the fishing community at the center of “Manchester by the Sea,” this meant spending time with local fishermen. “We asked if we could go into their houses. We asked if we could use their fishing boats. We asked if we could use their lobster cages and rope everything, and then we would,” De Jong recalled. All of this research helped De Jong nail the subtle nuances and layers of the region. “You’re always striving to not make it cliché,” De Jong told IndieWire.

The first step involves breaking down the script. At this phase of her process, De Jong attaches an image to each scene. “It may be a piece of art. It could be a photograph. It could be a texture. It could be a piece of cloth. It could be anything,” she shared, adding, “Then from that, I add physical locations, and we start putting the whole thing together and seeing our film.”

Sometimes these images come from the director themselves. While working on “Twin Peaks: The Return,” David Lynch gave De Jong some of his own artwork for inspiration. “He would hand me some of his paintings, his drawings, his work, and say, ‘Here, this is this set. Build that,,’” De Jong revealed, adding that even if it was “a flat 2D painting, the colors were wild and it’s textural.” These came in handy for the new worlds of the series, like the landmark Episode 8 (also known as “Gotta Light?”), in which De Jong designed the radio station and other eerier riffs on the atomic age 1950s.

For the more iconic aspects of “Twin Peaks, ” De Jong also dug up the original plans for the Red Room from the 1990s. “David remembered in his mind’s eye,” De Jong said, “and I’m there to continue to be David’s conduit on the new work. It was just a beautiful, beautiful dance.”

Along with reviving iconic sets from pop culture’s past, De Jong herself has created work that has become part of the entertainment firmament. The set she created for the “Jupiter’s Claim” theme park in Jordan Peele’s “Nope” has been added to the Studio Tour at Universal Studios Hollywood, a unique feat for an aspect of filmmaking that is often binned as soon as a production wraps. On the honor of her set being preserved in such a way, De Jong said, “It’s pretty incredible, because in the act of doing it, you aren’t thinking about what this is going to turn into.”

After receiving her first Oscar nomination for her work on Christopher Nolan‘s Best Picture-winning biopic “Oppenheimer,” De Jong re-teamed with the writer-director this year for his ambitious take on Homer’s epic poem “The Odyssey.” For this film, her process began at Nolan’s home, where she spent hours reading the script. Afterwards, De Jong asked for the parameters. “He said, ‘There are none,'” De Jong recalled.

This allowed the designer the freedom to “take the audience on the same journey that Odysseus (Matt Damon) was on,” she said. Starting with seven countries, De Jong and Nolan began searching for the film’s faraway locations, the only edict being that Nolan wanted the film to start in the Mediterranean and end in the Mediterranean. Without the barriers of realism, De Jong found inspiration in locations across the globe. “We didn’t care that we were shooting the Laestrygonians in Scotland. It didn’t matter. It just had the topography we were interested in. Same with Iceland and the same with Morocco,” De Jong said. Once the locations were determined, then came building sets that reflected the characters who inhabit them.

For the ominous stone house owned by Circe (Samantha Morton), who beguiles Odysseus’ men and turns them into pigs, De Jong shared that Nolan “was very clear about not wanting Circe’s home to be a Hansel and Gretel in the woods type cottage. She’s so peculiar and unique and bizarre and a witch.” With this in mind, the duo decided she should live on the edge of a cliff, finding the perfect craggy rocks in Scotland. Soon, a whole backstory informed the building of her dwelling. “She formed her house out of those craggy rocks,” De Jong said, adding, “We just made up all these stories and created the sets from there.”

The same attention to character informed the creation of the iconic Trojan horse, an imposing image of which opens the epic film. Nolan envisioned a rearing horse, telling De Jong that “it has to be iconic and it has to be larger than life.” For Nolan, De Jong said, the question at the center of this opening scene is, “Are the Trojans going to accept the gift?” Thinking about what kind of horse would be accepted, Nolan wanted their horse to be “the antithesis” of the one in Wolfgang Petersen’s 2004 film “Troy.” “We didn’t want the clunky wheels,” she said, adding that “these were master shipbuilders.”

“They’re master craftsmen,” De Jong insists, “If they collected all this wood, why don’t we shiplap the entire body, shiplap the tail? They hand-carved the legs and the head. That leaves the body all hollow like a ship, so all the men could all go inside and cut a trap door.” Once they agreed on the backstory for the building of the horse, the next step was figuring out how to make multiples out of fiberglass (and later out of plastic as one of the summer’s hottest collectible popcorn buckets).

As “The Odyssey” marches its way into awards season, De Jong is looking towards her future – and her next gig. With every project she takes, De Jong is looking to push herself as an artist. “It’s that space of being uncomfortable that is how you know you’re in the right place,” she said, adding, “The minute I find comfort, I realize I’m in the wrong place. So I’m always pushing to get back into that area of discomfort.”

Thinking back to her conversation with Fisk all those years ago, De Jong feels that what he taught her was “The act of physically doing and going and staying in momentum,” adding, “That’s something that Christopher Nolan has. All of these directors; They don’t stop producing work. They don’t do it in vain. They do it because that’s their language and their medium. They’re all artists at heart.”

Although De Jong looks back at her past fondly, she doesn’t regret forgoing art school to join the movie business. What she learned after all these years is that, “You need to go forward, and even if you go forward and you hit a wall, then just keep pivoting a little bit. Stay open and don’t be fearful. You can’t fear. I’d rather screw up royally and have tried than not tried at all.”

#3394. After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

With Cannes entry “Bitter Christmas,” Oscar-winning Spanish auteur Pedro Almodóvar (“Talk to Her”) is back making movies in his native language. Since his debut “Pepi, Luci, Bom and Other Girls Like Mom” in 1980, Almodóvar has written singularly identifiable, heightened, rhythmic, and mellifluous Spanish dialogue.

While Tilda Swinton and Julianne Moore adeptly wrangled his translated English in Golden Lion-winner “The Room Next Door,” which deployed his usual bright Almodóvar colors and exacting mise-en-scène, the director did not enjoy dealing with the unions in New York. “In Spain everything is much more immediate, and also it is my language, it’s my culture,” he told me during the New York Film Festival. While he doesn’t rule out making another English-language movie, it would have to be small-scale. “I don’t find myself, anymore, capable of dealing with a production that is chaotic with a lot of people and a lot of characters.” Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

Now he’s back in Spain in self-referential, meta autofiction mode in full force. The results are exhilarating. “Bitter Christmas” offers a movie within a movie, as writer-director Raúl (Leonardo Sbaraglia) crafts a script that lifts some key story points from his friends’ experiences. Even though Almodóvar considers the movie one of his riskiest, it’s the filmmaker’s biggest hit in Spain since “Volver.”

Almodóvar considers “Bitter Christmas” to be “twins” with Oscar-nominated “Pain and Glory,” which starred his old favorite Antonio Banderas as his alter ego. “‘Pain and Glory’ is more about the physical pain, right?,” he said. “The character [Raul] has had a lot of surgeries, and his fear is about that the fact that he’s not going to be physically able to to handle another another film shoot. Whereas in this film I deal with a different pain, which is the pain of writer’s block, of the blank page, or writing something that doesn’t quite come together for you. The character of Aitana in the film says to Raul, ‘you know we are all losers, you have lost grace.’ And by grace it means inspiration, something that is equally painful to that writer-director as the physical pain was to the writer director in ‘Pain and Glory.'”

Mostly when Almodóvar sits down to write, he’s making things up. He’s gotten into trouble in the past for raiding his friends’ stories. “There is not any law that creates the limits of the autofiction,” he said. “There is no law that’s going to define the limits of what you can appropriate and what you can’t appropriate. But if I’m inspired by the life of someone who’s close to me, who’s going through a difficult time, as a writer, you are selfish, because what propels you is the idea, even if it means going against the relationship. I don’t feel comfortable the two or three times that I did it. This is the limit: not to hurt anyone. But it’s normal that writers are influenced by everything in life you see, you talk to with others, you read, you see movies. So it’s impossible to renounce the influence of the life of others.”

And he’s passionate about making movies. As Raúl says in the film, “This is all there is to my life.” But Almodóvar has never suffered writer’s block. “I inspire myself because this is the profession that I know better than anyone, than any other,” he said. “The only thing that separates me from this alter ego is that I never lived a creative crisis. The experience I have had is more scripts that have taken me a long time to find the solution and to get them to gel together. But I’ve always succeeded ultimately.”

And he only recently discovered panic attacks, which took him by surprise. “I hadn’t previously experienced panic attacks, but now I have,” he said. “At that moment I was unconscious, and it was something awful, awful.”

Needless to say Almodóvar spends most of his days sitting at his desk at the computer. (Hence his legendary bad back.) Mostly he enjoys writing but also feels the clock ticking. “You always feel like time is lacking, right?” he said. “Especially that moment when you get that idea that’s going to become the motor of your story, you feel like there’s no time to breathe, because you want to get it all down as fast as possible. They’re quite intense days as we’re trying to get this. And then once I’ve started the story, my process is to get up in the morning and start writing. Those are some of the most pleasurable days in my life because you know where you’re going. But also, I have to pay attention to everything, because in that moment that you are possessed by the idea, you experience everything in your life filtered through the sensibility of the story that you’re writing.”

Listening to music feeds his creative beast. While he was writing “Talk to Her,” he listened to Caetano Veloso’s “Cucurrucucú Paloma,” a song that he had heard thousands of times, “but then it was like an epiphany. I discovered the song, and you feel it in a different way.” And in “Bitter Christmas,” his two actresses in the movie-within-the-movie listen to “Weeping Woman” from the filmmaker’s longtime muse, Mexican chanteuse Chavela Vargas.

Finally, the filmmaker had fun making himself the bad guy. “This was a new structure for me,” he said. “What I liked about it was that I could talk about myself as a writer-director, but mostly I also enjoyed the part of becoming the villain in a sense of that story. But the spectator does have to pay a lot of attention because if they go to the bathroom for two minutes, they’re going to miss something and be lost.”

In one scene, the filmmaker offers a close-up of the cursor on the computer screen. “Even though the cursor itself is not a very cinematic thing to see,” he said, “it’s his call to creativity, right? It’s the thing that calls him and pulls him in to have to tell his story. So it’s autofiction.”

Going forward, Almodóvar has no plans to put himself at the center of another film. “I promise not to talk about me anymore,” he said. “I was interested since the beginning of my career about the origin of creation and the relation with reality. Inspiration and life together, like the two sides of a coin. This mysterious question that so fascinates me is about not just where does creativity come from, how does it come, when does it come, how does it manifest? I have reached the end of my exploration around this.”

Up next: He’s writing, he said. “This is almost the opposite of this one. The new one will be very different.”

A Sony Pictures Classic release, “Bitter Christmas” is now playing in theaters in New York and Los Angeles. It expands nationally on November 25.

#3393. 5 Fantasy LitRPG Books Better Than 'Dungeon Crawler Carl'

LitRPG is having a moment, and it’s largely thanks to Dungeon Crawler Carl. While Matt Dinniman's book series isn't the newest entry in the video game-inspired literary genre, it's arguably one of its most recognizable titles. It has attracted 14 million readers and is even getting a live-action TV adaptation on Peacock, produced by Universal Television and Seth MacFarlane's Fuzzy Door.

Dungeon Crawler Carl won readers over with its clueless protagonist, Carl, and his ex-girlfriend's pampered tortoiseshell cat, Princess Donut, as they struggle to survive the depths of the World Dungeon, an 18-level death game reminiscent of Squid Game. While the series is undoubtedly a fan favorite, there are plenty of other books that deserve just as much attention, if not more. From an isekai-inspired adventure to a mother fighting to keep her children alive during an invasion, here are fantasy LitRPG book series that are better than Dungeon Crawler Carl.

Readers who want something with no fluff and all grind will find that The Primal Hunter gets the job done. When the universe suddenly becomes part of a multiverse governed by a mysterious System, introverted business analyst Jake Thayne finds himself trapped in a deadly 63-day survival tutorial alongside his coworkers. Armed with a bow and an unexpected knack for killing, Jake quickly discovers that he's much better at combat than he ever imagined possible.

Dungeon Crawler Carl also has plenty of RPG mechanics, including levels, skills, equipment, quests, and achievements. However, these are tied to a televised dungeon competition, where rewards, audience engagement, and entertainment shape how the game unfolds. The Primal Hunter takes a more traditional MMORPG approach. Its System provides a framework for progression through levels, classes, skills, professions, and stats. Jake develops his own build, improves his abilities, and grows stronger to survive increasingly dangerous encounters.

While there are emotional arcs, The Primal Hunter doesn't spend too much time on them, keeping the storyline entirely focused on Jake's growth and combat mastery. Readers will find him spending most of his time either in wilderness zones or alchemy labs. As the story progresses, he faces higher-tier monsters, cosmic-level challenges, and plenty of new abilities to master. It's straightforward and no-nonsense, without requiring too much emotional commitment, making it perfect for a less demanding read overall.

Carl might have his chonky Princess Donut, but Apocalypse Parenting takes things to another level: its heroes are literally a mother and her three young children. Their chances of surviving the situation seem pretty slim, but never underestimate the sheer power of motherhood. When Earth is selected for an intergalactic game show, Meghan Moretti finds herself in survival mode with her children while her husband is away. Think these monsters will spare them? Think again. Little do they know, her own kids will have to learn how to defend themselves, too.

Taking a more survival-focused, character-driven approach to LitRPG, Apocalypse Parenting follows an ordinary mother doing everything she can to keep her three children alive. Rather than focusing solely on fighting monsters or collecting rewards, its RPG mechanics revolve around practical survival skills. Meghan isn't just looking to become stronger for the next battle; she's thinking about securing drinking water by plugging bathtub drains, managing household resources, and preparing her family for the dangers ahead. These everyday decisions become essential to their survival.

Despite its alien sci-fi premise, the series uses its grounded family focus to create a surprising amount of claustrophobic, A Quiet Place-like tension. There's no grand quest to pursue or ultimate villain to defeat; Meghan's main priority is keeping her home and family intact. And when you're a parent, that kind of pressure hits a little closer to home.

The Wandering Inn is perfect for readers looking for something a little simpler and cozier than the grand adventures LitRPG is often known for. Erin Solstice is an ordinary woman from Earth who somehow finds herself transported to a fantasy world. Rather than searching for a way home, she takes refuge in an abandoned inn and eventually becomes its Innkeeper. Instead of pursuing quests or aspiring to become a hero, she focuses on turning the place into a humble home.

In typical LitRPG fashion, skill progression is often tied to killing monsters, completing quests, or finding treasures. Not in The Wandering Inn. Here, characters level up through everyday activities like cleaning, cooking, and even finding menstrual supplies, which can be surprisingly difficult when the creatures around them are unfamiliar with the concept of periods.

However, don't let its cozy, slice-of-life premise fool you. While Erin serves as the story's anchor, the series introduces hundreds of other perspectives across multiple continents, opening the door to storylines involving military strategy, medical drama, and goblin survival. This creates quite a contrast with the quieter life established at the beginning. Readers should expect plenty of whiplash, with monster attacks and wars threatening to destroy the inn just chapters after Erin has been baking bread or playing chess.

Carl might be snarky in Dungeon Crawler Carl, but Jason has even more bite thanks to his sharp tongue and sarcastic attitude in He Who Fights with Monsters. In an isekai-like twist, Jason Asano's life turns upside down when he wakes up naked in a monster-infested hedge maze, where magic and gods exist alongside video game-like mechanics. After surviving a blood cult, stopping an apocalypse-class monster, and discovering his own magical abilities, Jason eventually joins the Adventurers' Society.

Although Dungeon Crawler Carl also incorporates game-like mechanics, He Who Fights with Monsters offers a much more extensive RPG framework. Its detailed character sheets establish measurable attributes, abilities, and progression requirements, giving the fantasy world a clearly defined structure. More importantly, these mechanics are interconnected. Completing quests, defeating monsters, and collecting resources all contribute to character development, making the RPG system feel like a character in its own right. It's a great choice for readers who enjoy the more technical side of LitRPG.

Storytelling-wise, He Who Fights with Monsters takes a more philosophical approach, which makes sense given that its title comes from a Friedrich Nietzsche quote. What begins as a survival story gradually becomes a journey of self-discovery that explores Nietzsche's monster paradox. Jason must learn to fight corrupt gods and powerful elites, but the real question is whether he can do so without becoming just as monstrous as the enemies he opposes.

Alden Thorn has always wanted to be a superhero, but he's not exactly interested in punching monsters in Super Supportive. He'd rather be the guy keeping everyone else alive. That's not an easy dream in a world where an alien System decides who gets magical abilities and what powers they receive. After becoming one of Earth's Avowed, Alden gets his chance, but he'll have to figure out how to make his unusual support abilities work in a world that often values fighters more than healers.

Unlike Dungeon Crawler Carl, Super Supportive doesn't treat its RPG mechanics like a game people happen to be playing. Much of the fun comes from watching Aldren experiment with his abilities rather than simply chase higher stats. He starts with the Meister of Cudgel class but eventually trades it for Chainer, giving him access to powerful wordchains.

Sleyca also takes her time with Alden's character development, giving readers all the more reason to root for the protagonist. Between school, personal struggles, and training on Anesidora, there's plenty happening outside combat. The story also explores alien cultures, interspecies politics, and Earth's complicated relationship with the Artonans. It's a slower, more character-driven LitRPG, but readers who enjoy watching a protagonist gradually figure out his powers will find plenty to get invested in.
