#3392. 10 Hacks Every Waze User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Waze is a crowdsourced navigation app designed to help you get where you're going as quickly and with as much information about your route as possible. Where Google Maps and Apple Maps offer relatively straightforward directions, Waze tries to outsmart these alternatives by integrating real-time community feedback about hazards, speed traps, road closures, and more. If you are switching to Waze or using it alongside your other navigation tools, these are the hacks to help you maximize everything the app has to offer.

If you find yourself losing track of time or running late for events, Waze can notify you when it's time to leave—based on your current location and live traffic—so you arrive on schedule. You can set up "Time to leave" reminders in advance for individual planned drives, or you can sync your calendar to receive notifications for scheduled events. Calendar sync connects to your device's default calendar app, but you can change this to a third-party alternative if you prefer. Calendar events must include a navigable address to trigger reminders, and you must select Plan a drive in Waze for the event.

Waze has a feature called "child reminders," which are notifications to check for children before you get out of the car. This is clearly an incredibly important use case, but you can also use these alerts for custom messages, like "Don't forget the groceries!" In Waze, tap the menu button > Settings > Reminders > Child reminder and select Custom message.

Variable speed limits, especially on unfamiliar routes, can result in you speeding when you don't mean to. But Waze can alert you if you exceed a customized speed threshold so you aren't caught by surprise or at higher risk of being ticketed. From the menu, go to Settings > Speedometer and turn on Show speedometer. Tap Speeding threshold to select what limit you want to trigger alerts, and turn on Alert at threshold if you want Waze to play a sound.

Waze offers a wealth of information on routes to help drivers navigate obstacles and hazards, but this can clutter your map and distract you from the most critical information, especially in congested, high-traffic areas. Waze says it limits and prioritizes alerts automatically, but you can actually customize which alerts you see based on what's most important to you. From the menu, go to Settings > Alerts and reports > Reports and select the relevant alerts.

In the same Alerts and reports menu, you can enable Alert while driving, which will give you an audio warning and an onscreen pop-up about your selected hazards. This allows you to run navigation via a different map app (like Google Maps or Apple Maps) in the foreground while still getting Waze data in the background.

Waze integrates with toll road and HOV lane passes, so if you have an express or fast lane subscription, your route will optimize for it. If you don't, Waze can still account for HOV lane eligibility if you tell it how many passengers are in your car. From the menu, go to Settings > Toll and HOV passes and tap the plus icon to add your pass(es) from the list. If you need to add your passenger count instead, you can do so from View routes and enable the HOV option.

If you're driving through an unfamiliar, highly congested, or poorly designed area, you can ask Waze to help you avoid tricky maneuvers, such as crossing multiple lanes of traffic or turning left at intersections without lights. This prioritizes ease over speed using protected green arrows, roundabouts, and right turns. From the menu, go to Settings > Navigation, Avoid difficult intersections and select Always. You can also ask Waze to avoid toll roads, ferries, freeways, and unpaved roads.

Waze has a built-in audio player that syncs with your preferred listening platform—such as Spotify, YouTube Music, and Pandora—so you can control your music without having to navigate between apps. (As Waze is a Google product, Apple Music isn't included.) Simply tap the music icon on the map to select your audio player and hit Accept. If you don't see the icon, go to Settings > Audio player and turn on Show on the map.

If you want to make audio directions more interesting, you can select a celebrity or character voice to help you navigate. Recent appearances include Bill Hader's Cat in the Hat and Ziggy Marley. Tap the speaker icon > Current voice to search for the voice or language you want to use. You can also record directions in your own voice.

#3391. DC Announces The Justice League’s Biggest Crossover In Years After The Death Of A Beloved Anti-Hero

The Justice League unite with Darkseid and some of their greatest villains for an unexpected crossover that leaves all previous conflicts aside. The Justice League have headlined legendary crossovers pioneered by 1963's Crisis on Earth-One!, which brought together the Silver Age Justice League and the Golden Age Justice Society of America, and launched decades of annual DC multiverse team-ups. Later on, Crisis on Infinite Earths' multiverse-resetting spectacle set the bar for continuity-wide crossovers, and other events like Infinite Crisis, Multiversity, and Dark Nights: Death Metal put their own unique spin on the concept.

When the conflict becomes especially difficult or its scale grows sufficiently large, the Justice League find themselves forced to join forces with their own enemies. In Forever Evil, Batman teams up with Lex Luthor, Captain Cold, Black Adam, Sinestro, and Black Manta to overthrow Earth-3’s tyrannical Crime Syndicate after the rest of the League is trapped inside Firestorm. Similarly, Dark Nights: Metal forces Batman into a desperate alliance with the Joker to defeat the Batman Who Laughs, while Justice League: No Justice had heroes like Martian Manhunter and Wonder Woman divided into teams alongside villains like Brainiac, Starro, and Lobo to stop the cosmic Omega Titans.

Currently in primary DC Comics continuity, Justice League Unlimited's villain amnesty program has made villains as famous as Lex Luthor, King Shark, and Giganta members of the Earth's top superhero team. Yet, not even this surprising change in DC's hero-villain dynamics surpasses the latest Justice League crossover.

In Skottie Young and Jorge Corona’s Lobo #9, "Burial for a Bastich", the DC Universe's biggest icons call a truce to mourn the Main Man. Following his heroic self-sacrifice to stop the lethal Blood Garnet Lantern in "The Last Death" arc, Lobo finds himself rejected by both Heaven and Hell and stuck haunting the cosmos as a ghost. Looking down on his own memorial service, Lobo watches bitter enemies put their differences aside to pay tribute. Villains as evil and apathetic as Darkseid, the Joker, Sinestro, Cheetah, and Captain Cold are seen weeping. Notably, Darkseid's tears are actually Omega Beams that fall in their traditionally angular and asymmetric shape.

Of course, seeing Darkseid and the Justice League openly weeping at Lobo’s funeral is likely an exaggerated Czarnian hallucination. Throughout Skottie Young and Jorge Corona’s run, every battle, ally, and foe warps into an over-the-top caricature whenever filtered through Lobo’s massive ego and twisted worldview. In reality, half of the people attending Lobo's funeral would barely shred a tear, and the other half would almost certainly shrug off the Main Man's demise or throw a celebration. Even heroes like Aquaman, Mera, Nightwing, and Plastic Man would hardly be moved by Lobo's death.

Lobo's funeral is a clear parody of one of DC Comics’ oldest and most reliable crossover traditions. Justice League's most famous members gathering around a fellow hero's casket is a recurring image in DC Comics history. Landmark examples include Superman’s emotional burial in Funeral for a Friend, Barry Allen’s memorial after Crisis on Infinite Earths, Oliver Queen’s Star City service, and Sue Dibny’s tragic gathering in Identity Crisis, where heroes pack pews and stand silently in the rain. Lobo’s self-aggrandizing fantasy pokes fun at the heroes' melodramatic grief, which is almost always negated by their fallen friend's inevitable resurrection.

The superhero funeral trope is part of a long list of classic visual tropes that writers and artists love to recreate and subvert. Perhaps even more famous is the image of the Justice League lying defeated at the feet of their newest enemy, a staple cover used countless times to establish a villain or rebellious hero’s power. Similar recurring rituals include the solemn tribunal where Justice League heroes pose for a team photo, as well as the latest squad's first race towards the battlefield, with every member running or flying towards the reader. While repetitive, these tropes are so pervasive precisely because of how satisfying to see they usually are.

Which Justice League image template is your favorite?

Superman, Batman, Wonder Woman, The Flash, Green Lantern, Aquaman, and other heroes unite as the Justice League, Earth's first line of defense against threats no single champion can defeat alone. Across decades of DC stories, the team's roster repeatedly changes as its members confront alien warlords, ancient demons, powerful sorcerers, and Darkseid.

#3388. These Like-New Kindles Are up to $75 Off Ahead of Black Friday

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Amazon is offering early Black Friday discounts on like-new versions of its 2024 Kindles, with prices starting at $152.99 for the Paperwhite and savings of $27 to $75 across five models that include the color-screen Colorsoft and the pen-equipped Kindle Scribe. All five are a generation behind Amazon's current lineup: The company introduced redesigned Paperwhite and Colorsoft models (plus accessories) in October, with the new Paperwhite now starting at $199.99, and replaced the 2024 Scribe with a third-generation model in December 2025. As for its “like-new” label, it means these are pre-owned devices that Amazon has tested and certified to look and work like new.

The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite (16GB) is down to $152.99 from $179.99 and covers just about everything most people need for everyday reading, including enough storage for thousands of ebooks. Its seven-inch, 300ppi glare-free display is larger than the previous generation’s 6.8-inch screen, with faster page turns, an adjustable warm light, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life. As PCMag notes in its review, it's a great option for readers who don't need color or handwriting features.

The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition (32GB) is down to $190.99 from $224.99, making it just $38 more than the like-new Paperwhite (16GB). For that relatively small difference, you're doubling the storage to 32GB and getting wireless charging, an ad-free lock screen, and a front light that automatically adjusts to your surroundings—on top of the same sharp seven-inch display, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life as the standard Paperwhite, as noted by this PCMag review.

The Like-New Kindle Colorsoft (16GB) is down to $220.99 from $260.99 and offers something the Paperwhite models can’t: a color E-Ink display, which makes it well suited to comics, graphic novels, illustrated books, and travel guides. Its seven-inch screen shows that color content at 150ppi while keeping text at a sharp 300ppi, and you can mark passages in multiple highlight colors to keep your notes organized. That said, colors are noticeably more muted than on a conventional tablet, and battery life tops out at eight weeks, compared with 12 weeks on the Paperwhite.

The Like-New Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition (32GB) is down to $243.99 from $287.99, making it just $23 more than the standard like-new Colorsoft. For that modest increase, you're getting twice the storage at 32GB, which is particularly useful for comics, manga, and graphic novels that take up more space than regular ebooks, along with wireless charging, an automatically adjusting front light, and an ad-free lock screen. However, as PCMag notes in its review, the color display produces more subdued tones than a conventional tablet, so the Paperwhite remains the more economical choice if you primarily read novels.

The Like-New Kindle Scribe (16GB) is down to $284.99 from $359.99, the biggest dollar discount in this roundup. Unlike the other Kindles here, it's built for reading and writing, with a 10.2-inch, 300ppi glare-free display and a Premium Pen with an eraser and shortcut button—making it the most versatile option for readers who want an e-reader that doubles as a digital notebook.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

#3387. Box Office: ‘Ebenezer’ Opens to Modest $19 Million, Showing Johnny Depp Is Still a Draw for the Right Price

If Johnny Depp was hoping that “Ebenezer” would mark a glorious return to mainstream movies, he may need to hold out for another vehicle. The Christmas fable, released long before Thanksgiving, let alone the holidays, topped the box office this weekend with $19 million domestically and $42 million globally, a solid but unremarkable debut. It shows that enough moviegoers are able to look past the scandals that led Hollywood to remove Depp from their call sheets for the better part of a decade, but also exposed the limitations of his popular appeal.

The fact is that Depp was always something of a dicey commercial proposition. Put him in a “Pirates of the Caribbean” movie and you were guaranteed to earn $1 billion even if the script sucked and the plot seemed designed at the end of a wine bottle. Team him with Tim Burton, as he was quite successfully with “Sweeney Todd” ($153 million gross, $50 million budget), “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory” ($475.8 million gross, $150 million budget), and “Alice in Wonderland” ($1 billion gross, $200 million budget), and you were likely to have a big hit. Well, unless they were looking to reboot “Dark Shadows.” Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

But the rest of Depp’s track record was spotty. “Public Enemies” ($214.1 million gross, $100 million budget) and “Black Mass” ($100 million gross, $53 million budget) did well considering they were R-rated adult dramas, but struggled to break even because they cost too much to make and Depp commanded his full $20 million salary. Then there were the costly bombs, a litany of duds that includes “Mortdecai” ($47.3 million gross, $60 million budget), “The Lone Ranger” ($260.5 million gross, $250 million budget), “Transcendence” ($103 million gross, $150 million budget), and “Alice Through the Looking Glass” ($300 million gross, $170 million budget), the latter a return to Wonderland sans Burton. Many of these seemed like paycheck gigs rather than an attempt to burnish Depp’s star power. There was a private island to pay for and a pirate-themed wine cave to keep stocked on Depp’s sprawling French estate. But the promise of another Jack Sparrow adventure meant that Hollywood was able to look the other way, confident that there was more plunder to be found by allowing the actor to follow his idiosyncratic muse.

Depp could have kept going like this, but his messy personal life interceded. Depp’s reputation took a hit in 2020 when he became embroiled in a costly, two-continent legal battle against ex-wife Amber Heard, in which he was accused of domestic abuse. He denied the allegations, and later lost a U.K. libel suit against The Sun, when the court found an article calling Depp a “wife beater” was “substantially true.” Depp would go on to defamation trial against Heard in the U.S., after she wrote an op-ed in the Washington Post, calling herself a domestic abuse survivor. By that time, he’d been fired from the “Fantastic Beasts” franchise (it would be canceled after a non-Depp-led installment bombed), and was consigned to appearing in straight-to-streaming schlock or barely seen indies. But it wasn’t just the reputational damage that made major studios skittish about Depp. They had grown tired of his antics. There were reports he would show up late and unprepared, even as his salary demands and requests for perks escalated. That’s fine when your movies are making lots of money, it’s less charming when they are losing it.

So a lot is riding on “Ebenezer.” Depp looked a little uneasy on red carpets promoting the movie and Paramount, which is backing the film, wisely kept him from doing profiles with harder-hitting journalists who might ask him a probing question. He also cut his salary, reportedly receiving a $5 million paycheck to play one of his dream roles — Ebenezer Scrooge, and with it a chance to wear fright makeup and talk in a weird voice. But unlike most of Depp’s recent films, “Ebenezer” is poised to be a modest financial success. The film skewed older, with 59% of its domestic audience over the age of 30, and was slightly more female, as only 48% of ticket buyers were men. Paramount said it over-indexed in the South. One warning sign is that family crowds didn’t turn out in force for the PG-13 movie, comprising just 9% of opening weekend crowds.

However, the $38 million budget is low enough that if the film continues to draw crowds through the holidays and performs well overseas, where it has earned $23 million, it will turn a profit. But that points to a new reality — Depp is a sound bet, for the right price. Maybe that was a lesson that studios should have taken long ago. Depp’s taste is rococo, but Hollywood kept treating every one of his outings like potential blockbusters when a little more caution was warranted.

Next up for Depp is “Day Drinker,” an action thriller that seems to play into the star’s libertine image. Lionsgate will release the film in March. Will it be the vehicle that puts the 63-year-old Depp back on top, or will it, like “Ebenezer,” confirm that there’s still a smaller, but committed audience for his antics? Budget accordingly.

#3386. Ring's New $250 Indoor Camera Drone Sounds Terrifying

Ring made its name with its smart doorbells with built-in cameras, and now sells more indoor cameras than any other company, capturing more than 40% of the market. When you've already moved tens of millions of devices (enough to raise serious concerns about their use as part of the surveillance state), you always need to keep innovating, and today, the company announced a product it has been working on for a decade: an indoor camera drone powered by artificial intelligence. I got a chance to check it out during a media event yesterday, and I can report that, as harbingers of our dystopian future go, it is only mildly terrifying.

The drone camera is one of two products in the company's new Ring Robotics line, alongside a "rover cam" that looks kind of like the canister of a vacuum cleaner attached to an iPad. While the Ring Rover Cam is priced at $999.99 and targeted at businesses, the Ring Drone Cam is a much more affordable $249.99, reasonable enough that it will appeal to consumers looking for another way to keep (robot) eyes on their stuff.

The drone camera records 2K video and has a 148-degree field of view and the ability to rotate 360 degrees. It works with existing Ring cameras, doorbells, sensors, and alarms, as well as the Alexa Home Map. It has a flight time of eight minutes, and once it returns to its base station, it takes around an hour to fully recharge (eight minutes on the dock will give it one minute in the air).

As Ring founder Jamie Siminoff explained during the preview event, the company has been trying to build a workable camera drone for around a decade, but couldn't overcome certain design challenges until the advancement of AI models that allow the device to handle most of the computing—from route programming to threat detection—via the cloud, so the drones can be smaller and lighter.

According to Ring, when setting up the Ring Drone Cam, you carry it around your house, allowing it to map the interior. It will "intelligently identify rooms and suggest patrol points: spots worth extra attention." When sent out on "patrol," the drone's AI pilot will travel between hotspots, sensing and avoiding furniture and other obstacles along the way.The Ring Drone Cam works with other Ring cameras, so if an alert is triggered somewhere in your home—say, a window opening unexpectedly—the drone will take off to investigate. It has a built-in security light that will make its presence known, so it can also act as a deterrent, though the screaming sound of its spinning propellers will accomplish that just as well.

According to Ring, the drone camera can deliver peace of mind whether you're home or away, and admittedly I do like the idea of being able to check on my pets or make sure no pipes have burst while I'm at work or on vacation (though admittedly you can get the same sort of monitoring without involving an AI device that looks like a mini version of the flying robots from The Terminator).

I admit that the Ring Drone Cam seems pretty cool, provided I don't think about it too much. I don't know that I really feel the need to have every inch of my home covered in security cameras, but I do like the idea that the drone could, for example, go to check out what's going on if one of my smoke alarms' temperature sensors reports that one spot in the house is all of a sudden hotter than it should be.

If you're ready to enter this brave new world of security, you'll have to wait a bit longer: The Ring Drone Camera isn't expected to ship until January 2027, but you can sign up to be alerted when it is available for preorder now.

#3384. 7 Most Politically Subversive Movies of All Time, Ranked

There are multiple ways in which a film can be subversive, whether it's by twisting the tropes of its genres on their head, deliberately undermining traditional societal norms, or bending genres to surprise audiences. One particular thing that makes several of the most subversive movies in history so great, on the other hand, is that they disrupt and aggressively question dominant political ideologies, the mainstream media, and topics that are usually considered taboo.

It's one thing for a film to be artistically subversive, but films that actively challenge dominant power structures and cultural norms instead of reinforcing them prove that politically subversive cinema can be particularly powerful. Over the years, the big screen has been treated to several such movies, made by artists of the caliber of Stanley Kubrick and Pier Paolo Pasolini.

Infamous for being one of the most heavily censored mainstream horror films in history, Ken Russell's The Devils is about as legendary as the director himself. Based on the fall of 17th-century Catholic priest Urbain Grandier and the possessions of Loudun, it's a film which weaponizes blasphemy and sacrilege to tell a story that is, at its core, far more political than it is religious.

There is certainly plenty of religious commentary in The Devils, but what makes it one of the best horror masterpieces of the '70s is how unapologetic it is in calling out procedural injustice, the centralization of power, and government brainwashing through religious hysteria. It's a must-see NC-17 cult classic that's made all the more politically potent by the fact that it's based on true events.

Charles Chaplin had long refused to get with the times and leave behind the silent cinema that he had completely revolutionized. However, going into the late '30s, he found that the subject matter of The Great Dictator deserved to be such a direct political statement that it couldn't possibly be anything but his first true talkie. Thus, the world was treated to one of the best dark comedy movies of all time.

By the time the film came out — and certainly when Chaplin began developing it in 1938 — many in the Western world still vastly underestimated the horrors that were being committed by Hitler and the Nazis. So, Chaplin did what he did best: he took these very serious topics and ridiculed dictators like Hitler and Mussolini, loudly calling for a stop to their atrocities well before the United States entered World War II.

Sergei Eisenstein is widely regarded as one of the most important and influential filmmakers in history, largely thanks to his contributions to the art of film editing. There is no better way to learn about and understand those contributions than watching Battleship Potemkin, one of the best war thrillers of all time, which dramatizes the 1905 mutiny aboard the eponymous Russian battleship.

Battleship Potemkin is proof that even an official piece of state propaganda can be politically subversive. Indeed, though the film was commissioned by the Soviet government to celebrate the 1905 revolution, it was an explosive piece of international political subversion seeking to undermine the capitalist social order the world over. Later on, even the USSR itself came to consider Eisenstein's avant-garde techniques a bit too rebellious for their taste.

Despite how quiet it seems, Kubrick's Paths of Glory is also one of the most outwardly anti-war movies in history, based on the Souain corporals affair that took place during World War I. Due to the film's critically negative depiction of the French military, the country refused to allow Kubrick to shoot there and even refused to allow the movie to screen there until 1972.

What arguably makes Paths of Glory even more radical and subversive, as far as Kubrick's anti-war movies go, is that instead of laughing at the matter, it's an entirely solemn and serious depiction of it. One of the most hopeless war movies of all time, Paths of Glory exposes the dark underbelly of military leadership in ways that no other film had really dared to depict before. In it, patriotism and military justice are dangerous myths used to manipulate working-class young men into allowing themselves to be used like cannon fodder.

What could possibly be more politically subversive than a movie that has been documented to be used as a training manual by both insurgent and counterinsurgency groups? We are, of course, talking about Gillo Pontecorvo's Italian-Algerian masterpiece The Battle of Algiers, a docudrama shot in a newsreel style about the rebellion against the French government during the Algerian War.

It's one of the best films of the 1960s, crafted with such an unparalleled sense of visceral realism that it really does allow the audience to feel as though they're flies on the wall, watching this conflict from the outside. Without ever sugarcoating the horrific violence of anti-colonial resistance or state counter-terrorism, Pontecorvo forces the viewer to witness all of this brutality with every moral nuance and political layer laid bare for them to closely analyze.

From beginning to end and from top to bottom, Pier Paolo Pasolini's Italian-French political art horror masterpiece Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom is a movie specifically designed to be as subversive, transgressive, and provocative as possible. Loosely adapting Marquis de Sade's The 120 Days of Sodom and setting the story in WWII Italy instead of 18th-century France, the film was released a mere three weeks after Pasolini was killed, making it his final masterpiece.

Saying that you need a strong stomach to get through Salò would be the understatement of the century. Pasolini, a lifelong Marxist and critic of Italian power structures, wanted to make a movie that criticized consumerism, fascism, and systematic abuse. Boy, did he succeed. Salò is quite infamously one of the heaviest movies of the 20th century, so politically aggressive and full of unrelenting, stomach-churning horror that it was outright banned across many countries. In many territories, it still faces bans and censorship to this day.

For precisely the same reasons that arguably make it the single most politically rebellious feature film in history, Herbert J. Biberman's Salt of the Earth was one of the first fully independent movies made outside of the Hollywood studio system. That's because Biberman, as well as screenwriter Michael Wilson and producer Paul Jarrico, were all blacklisted in Hollywood at the time due to their alleged involvement in communist politics.

Salt of the Earth was a direct act of working-class political subversion starring actual striking laborers and their families, created as an explicit celebration of worker solidarity and civil rights right at the peak of McCarthyism and the Red Scare in the United States. As if that weren't enough, it's also one of the greatest American films of the '50s, making it a must-see for all those interested in how complex politically radical cinema can be at its best.

#3383. Vision's Entire Family Tree Across All Marvel Lore

Without a doubt, the Vision has one of the most complex and strange family trees in all of Marvel Comics lore. Not only does the synthezoid have one family born of magic and one of science, Marvel Comicsbut he also has an impressively unique array of "siblings" as well.

Going beyond the normal rules and limitations of typical organic biology, the Vision has a father who's an evil genocidal robot, a grandfather who accidentally created that robot, two wives with very different origins and backgrounds, and so many more siblings, children, and more "family" members (artificial, magical, and otherwise).

In honor of the MCU's recently concluded VisionQuest series, here is Vision's entire family tree in the comics explained, and how each member relates to the heroic synthezoid.

It all starts with Hank Pym, aka Ant-Man, aka Giant Man, aka Yellowjacket. In the comics, Pym was the creator of the artificial intelligence known as Ultron (not Tony Stark and Bruce Banner like in the MCU). Ultron was formed from Hank Pym's own brain patterns. However, when Ultron went rogue and became a genocidal robot hell-bent on humanity's extinction, one of his most classic schemes involved Vision's creation. As a result, Hank Pym has long been considered Vision's "grandfather" in terms of the lineage in Marvel Comics.

Janet van Dyne, The Wasp, is connected to Vision via her marriage to Hank Pym, making her Vision's grandmother of sorts. This is largely due to Ultron viewing Janet as his own mother. However, that does make Ultron's creation of his robotic wife Jocasta even stranger, seeing as how he used Janet's brain patterns to create his artificial soulmate (though it does help explain Jocasta's name).

Ultron is Vision's creator and the closest thing he has to a father. After rebelling against Hank Pym, Ultron chose to build Vision, a powerful new weapon to use against the Avengers, as seen in 1968's Avengers #57. However, just as Ultron rebelled against his father, Vision also rebelled and joined the Avengers against Ultron, eventually joining Earth's Mightiest Heroes long-term along with other superhero teams over the years.​​​​​​​

Dr. Phineas Horton is another important figure as it relates to Vision's origins and creation, despite not technically being the person who created him. Instead, Horton was the scientist responsible for building the original Synthetic Man, otherwise known as the original Human Torch or Jim Hammond. It was because of Horton's early work that Vision's construction was possible. Likewise, Ultron used spare parts and the template used to create Jim when creating Vision.

Technically, Jim Hammond's Human Torch is the closest thing Vision has to a physical twin or brother. Originally, it was believed that Ultron repurposed Jim's dormant android body to create Vision, which would have made Vision a reincarnation of sorts. However, it was later retconned that Ultron merely used the body template and spare parts from Horon to create Vision, making the synthezoid and his predecessor separate beings who eventually met one another and fought side by side on the West Coast Avengers for a time.​​​​​​​

When creating the Vision, Ultron used the brain patterns of Simon Williams, aka Wonder Man, meaning much of Vision's personality and emotions were inspired by Williams, making the two of them brothers of sorts (and have often referred to each other as such). However, their relationship has at times been complicated, seeing as how Simon also developed the same feelings for Wanda Maximoff's Scarlet Witch, who would become Vision's first wife.​​​​​​​

Victor Mancha is another artificial child of Ultron, which technically makes him Vision's younger brother. Having debuted in the beloved Runaways series, Victor is part human and part machine as a unique cyborg. Like Vision, he rejected Ultron's dark plans for him and became a hero instead, and was largely inspired by Vision himself. However, things got messy after Victor accidentally killed Vision's son, Vin, which in turn led to Vision's second wife, Virginia, murdering Victor (though Victor was eventually brought back to life).​​​​​​​

Like Vision, Jocasta was created by Ultron, which, from one perspective, would make her his sister. However, she was also designed to be Ultron's robotic bride, meaning she can also be considered Vision's stepmother. To make things even more complicated, Jocasta was based on the brain patterns of Janet van Dyne (Vision's "grandmother). However Marvel fans choose to view her familial connection to Vision, she too rejected Ultron and became a hero just like her brother/stepson/grandson.

Alkhema was Ultron's second attempt at creating a robotic companion after Jocasta. Built using the brain patterns of Bobbi Morse aka Mockingbird. While Ultron intended for her to be more obedient, she too became more obedient, though not so fully that Alkhema became a hero like many of Ultron's other created family members.

#3382. Box Office: ‘Club Kid’ Scores Best Limited Expansion of the Year as Younger Audiences Embrace Jordan Firstman’s Oscar Hopeful

Jordan Firstman’s “Club Kid” was the belle of Cannes. Critics raved about Firstman’s feature directorial debut, as well as his sensitive performance as a party promoter turned unlikely dad, and A24 swept in to buy the film for $17 million after a bidding war. But plenty of movies have been embraced at film festivals only to face rejection when they hit the wider world. Would “Club Kid” be another “Dope” or “Begin Again”?

Well, based on a very limited sample size, “Club Kid” seems to be performing just fine, thank you very much. Those raves and A24’s imprimatur of cool are paying off as the film enjoyed the best limited expansion of the year this weekend, grossing $756,060 across 27 screens. That translates into an impressive $28,002 per-screen average. Since opening in six screens on Nov. 6, “Club Kid” has earned nearly $1.5 million. But this very New York story has mostly played in major cities and liberal bastions like the Big Apple, Chicago, Austin, San Francisco, and Los Angeles. Will audiences across the country embrace the story of a drug-taking, sex-positive gay man and his adorable 10-year-old accidental son? We’ll find out on Thanksgiving when it goes wide. Related Stories Box Office: ‘Ebenezer’ Opens to Modest $19 Million, Showing Johnny Depp Is Still a Draw for the Right Price ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List

In order for “Club Kid” to be a financial success, it will need to more than double the $17 million that A24 shelled out for the rights, because theaters keep half the ticket sales. That could happen if “Club Kid” generates awards buzz and positive word-of-mouth spreads, something that seems plausible given how funny, touching, and life-affirming Firstman’s film is (seriously, audiences have been applauding as the credits roll). Plus, A24 is on a heater this year, releasing hits like “You Can See Everything” and “Backrooms” that have it rivaling the market shares of much larger studios like Warner Bros. and Paramount.

There are certainly a lot of other Oscar hopefuls out there. Searchlight’s “Wild Horse Nine,” which is seen as a near lock for a Best Picture nod, earned $4.6 million domestically in its second weekend. The film about two CIA agents up to no good in Chile has earned $28 million globally. Then there’s “La Bola Negra,” a multigenerational gay epic from Netflix. It’s earned $3.5 million domestically over five weeks in theaters. And “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” which is generating Oscar buzz for John Turturro, picked up $322,830 to bring its domestic haul to $4.7 million after four weeks in theaters.

“Wicker,” with its story of a fisherwoman who becomes romantically entangled with a wicker man, may be too weird to generate a much love from Academy voters, but it has done well for its distributor, Black Bear, earning $1.5 million in North America last weekend. Its global total stands at $36.7 million after four weeks of release.

As for “Club Kid,” A24 thinks its trajectory mirrors that of other recent arthouse hits, with ticket sales pacing alongside those of “Moonlight” ($67 million gross) and “Anora” ($59.3 million gross) at this point in its expansion. Exit scores are among the best in the studio’s history and the film is connecting with young audiences as 80% of ticket buyers were under the age of 35. Next weekend will be another test for “Club Kid” as it expands to 200 screens across the top 50 markets. If it keeps drawing crowds, Firstman and A24 will have a lot to celebrate.

#3380. 10 Shows Like 'Minimum Wage' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Spinning off of a popular web series, Netflix's Minimum Wage is currently in the middle of a 28-episode first-season run. If that sounds like a lot of episodes for a show in 2026, keep in mind that they're generally less than 15 minutes each, which is perfect for your overloaded to-watch list—especially when they go down so easily. This cringe workplace mockumentary follows the crew of teenagers running a failing pizza place and making (you guessed it) minimum wage; they're under enormous pressure from their boss (Randall Park) to save the business and their one dumb source of income.

The punchy episodes will leave you plenty of time to explore other streaming shows dealing with the utter ridiculousness of the modern workplace. Here are 10 to get you started.

Workplace comedies usually revolve around white-collar office environments (The Mary Tyler Moore Show, 30 Rock, Parks and Recreation, etc.). Like Minimum Wage, Superstore instead follows the staff of Cloud 9, a generic big-box retailer. The show’s deep bench and diverse cast are largely focused on the jokes, but much of that comedy involves the relatable situation of working a job that demands commitment and a smiley attitude in the face of both entitled customers and obnoxious bosses. It's a different venue and age bracket, but a nutty workplace is a nutty workplace. Stream Superstore on Hulu and Peacock.

We're moving away from the workplace and aging things up a bit, but no worries: the name is a little ironic given that the codependent, co-habitating twenty-somethings of the title are hardly mature. Five friends are cohabiting in the childhood home of Samir (Malik Elassal), and dealing with the uniquely Gen-Z humiliations around dating, work, and even health insurance. Only one member of the group has an actual reasonably good job, while career paths for the others include being a temp, waiter, and a part-time ballet instructor. Stream Adults on Hulu.

This offbeat workplace comedy kicks off with a fabulous premise: Jeong Bok-dong (Kim Byung-chul) was a high-level director in a major corporation until one bad meeting saw him demoted. To president! ...of the company's failing Pegasus Mart offshoot. Bok-dong makes it his mission to get revenge by bankrupting the store, hiring eccentrics to execute eccentric, entirely whackadoo plans and accidentally getting Pegasus noticed by customers, who quickly make it more popular than ever. Think The Producers, but in retail. Stream Pegasus Market on Tubi.

It might sound a little (or a lot) niche, but we’ve seen enough headlines about the working conditions at many video game production houses to understand why a workplace comedy set against such a backdrop would make for a dark and juicy comedy. Charlotte Nicdao and Rob McElhenney are the leads, playing a brilliant workaholic and an unsociable egomaniac, respectively, and the chemistry between them gives the show more than enough spark. There's also a four-episode spin-off called Side Quest. Stream Mythic Quest.

A half-hour comedy-drama with an emphasis on the comedy, Gentefied follows three Mexican-American cousins who have built lives in Los Angeles, only to be faced with a new challenge: the looming gentrification of the neighborhood they helped to build via their family's taco shop. Gentefied has a baked-in sense of place and culture and a lot of heart; the second season is even better than the first. Stream Gentefied on Netflix.

Perhaps there's a bit of counter-programming in this dramedy about a couple of scrappy New York City outsiders, but there's a fundamental goofiness to this show about a couple of nice guys who are great at getting themselves into trouble, and equally good at talking themselves out of it. Bryan Greenberg plays Ben Epstein, a quiet guy with any number of big ideas, while Victor Rasuk plays the outgoing, often shameless Cam Calderon; together they manage a startup clothing business with the benefits of neither money nor experience, amiably hustling their way to success, maybe. Stream How to Make It in America on HBO Max and Netflix.

Debuting at the beginning of the Obama administration before getting a surprise revival just a couple of years ago, Party Down is an acclaimed cult sitcom for the ages—lots of laughs, low ratings, and always worth rediscovering. A group of six (or so) struggling LA actors and writers work as cater waiters for a fancy company, with every episode into a new and wildly absurd situation, even as their aspirations far outstrip their actual lives. Stream Party Down on Prime Video and Netflix.

A legitimate sitcom that just happens to be set in Northern Ireland during the violent Troubles of the 1990s, when clashes between nationalists and unionists frequently resulted in violence. It’s a fascinating contrast, brought to life by a writer and creator (Lisa McGee) who lived it. It’s also laugh-out-loud funny—though it doesn’t make any allowances for audiences unaccustomed to Irish accents, so don’t feel bad if you need subtitles until you get the hang of it. Erin, Orla, Clare, and Michelle are joined by James, the only male student at their Catholic girls' school, dealing with normal growing-up stuff in absurd times. This world is a far cry from that of Minimum Wage, but Lisa McGee's sense of the absurd connects both shows—if the setting is a bit more dramatic, the comedy is just as wonderfully silly. Stream Derry Girls on Netflix.

Not a comedy! But about as good an indication of where we are in the modern global workplace as you're likely to find. Hyuk‑jun is a young guy saddled with debt who signs on for some part-time work at a job agency...at 50x the going rate, no less (should've been a red flag). Each new assignment places him in new and increasingly horrific situations, with increasingly arbitrary-seeming rules. But, hey, in 2026, it's a living. Stream Dead-End Job on Netflix.

It's an office (obviously) and not a pizza joint, but the point here is kinda that white-collar jobs in the 21st century can be at least as soul-killing as working customer service. The Office inherited some of the finer tropes of the workplace comedy (mostly involving tossing together a group of weirdos overly invested in their jobs) while also launching a million mockumentary-style shows, running for nine seasons, and becoming one of the most popular shows of its era. Stream The Office on Peacock.

#3378. There’s a Good Reason the NYC Marathon Winners Wore These Watches

Over 60,000 runners crossed the finish line at the New York City Marathon last week. When you think of the elites fighting for a spot on the podium, you might expect to see only the priciest, most feature-packed GPS watches money can buy—historically, this meant the most premium Garmin Forerunners. Looking at the wrists of this year's New York City Marathon podium finishers, though,  you’ll see that Garmin—the name most recreational runners reach for by default—was far from the only brand on the course.

Here are the watches I’ve been able to confirm among the top NYC Marathon finishers:

Men's winner, Andreas Almgren: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored)

Men's runner-up, Yemaneberhan Crippa: Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro (sponsored)

Women's runner-up, Jessica McClain: Garmin Forerunner 570 (sponsored)

Women's third place, Hellen Obiri: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored)

Nonbinary winner, Ryan Montgomery: Suunto Race 3S (almost certainly sponsored, since this watch was released last month)

An important disclaimer: I haven't spoken with any of these athletes. What follows is my opinion, based on what I know running watches offer the people who wear them.

"Garmin" has long been the default answer to "what running watch should I buy?" It earned that spot with reliable GPS, excellent software, and a huge ecosystem. And on this podium, it's represented by a Forerunner 570—a great watch, but at a price tag most runners would struggle to justify.

Of course, sponsorships muddy the water, since athletes wear what their sponsors put on their wrists. But that's exactly the point: Other brands are investing in elite runners because they believe their products can stand next to Garmin's, and it looks like they’re making the right bet.

It's fair to ask whether Garmin's grip is loosening. The company has increasingly pushed toward the fanciest watches with the most features at higher and higher price points. The Forerunner 570 starts north of $500. Meanwhile, COROS, Amazfit, and others are proving that a perfectly solid, competitive watch doesn't need to cost that much. Is Garmin still the best running watch overall? For ecosystem, polish, and depth of features, it's still a strong contender. But "best" no longer means "the only serious option," and the gap between Garmin and the field is narrower than it has been in years. Sponsored or not, seeing two Coros Pace 4s and an Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro among the top finishers is worth noting.

You don’t need an expensive watch to be elite—just look at the cheap running watches worn by the men who broke the sub-two-hour barrier at the London Marathon this past spring. Training load scores, recovery metrics, maps, music, and smart notifications are nice, but they're extras. If you're shopping for a watch, spend your money on the basics being done right, and don't feel pressured to pay for features you'll never use. Everything besides your time and pace is icing on the cake.

Whichever brand you choose, focus on these basics in your running watch:

The New York City Marathon podium shows a running-watch market that's a bit more competitive and intriguing than the era of "just buy a Garmin" suggests. Garmin is still excellent, but now we’re seeing proof that Coros, Amazfit, and Suunto are all making watches good enough for the fastest humans on the planet. If they can trust those watches on their biggest days, the rest of us can probably trust them with our Saturday long runs.

#3377. Stephen King’s 16-Episode Supernatural Series Rewrites The Rules Of His Greatest Sci-Fi Movie

An ongoing Stephen King series, The Institute, has cleverly re-written the rules that define the author's 44-year-old movie. Based on Stephen King's book of the same name, The Institute premiered on MGM+ in 2025. While it did not achieve the same level of success as HBO's It: Welcome to Derry, it easily ranks among some of the better Stephen King TV shows.

In season 1, The Institute was primarily criticized for being too derivative. It came off as another Stranger Things rip-off instead of etching its own identity. The Institute season 2, however, is gradually turning out to be a fascinating expansion of Stephen King's original book. With each episode, it is not only expanding its source material's lore but also dabbling with many unique high-concept ideas.

After two episodes, The Institute season 2 is primarily driven by the concept of precognition, which is the ability to see the future. Interestingly, The Institute is not the first Stephen King adaptation that centers on precognition. 1983's adaptation of The Dead Zone, too, was driven by the same concept. In The Institute, however, the rules of precognition are significantly different.

In The Dead Zone, Christopher Walken's Johnny Smith does not get random flashes of the near future. He can also not willingly look ahead in time and determine what lies ahead. He has to physically touch a person or an object connected to them to be able to see what the future holds for them. The Institute's Luke, on the other hand, either gets waking flashes of the future or he dreams about them.

The veteran precog characters in The Institute are also able to willingly look far ahead into the future. Luke, too, will eventually have more control over his powers. Johnny Smith's power in The Dead Zone is also portrayed as a random fluke, where a car accident and a five-year coma triggers his power. He is not born with it.

Found an error? Send it info@screenrant.com so it can be corrected.

The Institute's Luke Ellis, in contrast, seems to have always possessed telekinesis and telepathy.

His precognition abilities, too, started emerging after he endured extreme stress and experimentation at the titular Institute. Johnny Smith also seems to be the sole bearer of his "curse." While precognition is treated as a rare ability in The Institute, Luke is not the only one possessing it.

The Dead Zone's title, in itself, stems from the "blind spots" in Johnny Smith's visions of the future. These "blind spots" are projections of the future that do not have a deterministic outcome. Only a choice in the present can make them less shrouded. Projections of the future in The Institute are treated as random flashes that lack context. One has to draw assumptions about them before trying to change the outcome.

Despite the difference in mechanism of their central superpowers, The Institute and The Dead Zone tell a similar story. They are both driven by the "Hitler's Murder Paradox," prompting viewers to question whether one is morally obligated to murder someone who is bound to commit a crime in the future. Stephen King's The Dead Zone captures this moral dilemma from the perspective of one sole protagonist.

He must decide whether sacrificing himself and his life is worth it to serve the perceived greater good that could save the lives of millions.

In The Institute, the ones who run the titular organization attempt to reason with the same moral paradox. They torment children with special abilities and imprison them in a facility to leverage their powers to prevent future disasters. While the higher-ups in the shadow organization defend their actions, characters like Luke argue that the long-term future is not deterministic and any visions of it cannot be reliable.

The Institute's Luke faces the same dilemma as Johnny Smith specifically in season 2's episode 2. Every future threat he attempts to evade somehow leads him to more trouble. Even the act of attempting to save his friend from her imminent doom forces him to let the titular Institute capture his friends again. In both Stephen King stories, precognition is more of a curse than a blessing.

The Institute, released in 2025, follows 14-year-old genius Luke Ellis, who is kidnapped and wakes up at a mysterious facility filled with children possessing unusual abilities. Meanwhile, Tim Jamieson, a former police officer, seeks a fresh start in a nearby town, inevitably intertwining his fate with Luke's.

#3376. The 10 Best American Shows in TV History, Ranked

Feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

My favorite thing about television is that it can make somebody's stupid little habits feel important. A man adjusts his tie before lying to his wife. A child keeps waiting for a parent to say something encouraging. Or Kieran Culkin’s Roman Roy does disgusting things in the bathroom to continue living depressed.

American television has given us extraordinary spectacles, groundbreaking comedy, and dramas that changed the entire medium. But the shows I return to most aren't necessarily the ones with the biggest twists or most prestigious reputations. They're the ones that give me excellent lessons. That understands people so precisely that I feel personally implicated in their decisions. And yes, I'm still furious about things certain fictional characters did twenty years ago.

Lucy Ricardo (Lucille Ball) wants something more exciting than being a New York housewife, much to the exhaustion of her bandleader husband Ricky (Desi Arnaz). I Love Lucy turns that simple conflict into magnificent comedy, frequently involving their neighbors Fred (William Frawley) and Ethel Mertz (Vivian Vance). Lucy's ambitions aren't unreasonable. It's her methods of achieving them that tend to become spectacular disasters.

I still laugh watching Lucy and Ethel desperately stuff chocolates into their mouths when the candy factory's conveyor belt speeds up. There's no complicated joke to explain. Two brilliant performers gradually lose control of an increasingly ridiculous situation. But Ball's real achievement was making Lucy's desperate hunger for attention strangely lovable. She could be selfish, dishonest, and gloriously theatrical, yet her disappointments felt recognizable. Seventy years later, that physical comedy remains unbelievably sharp. Some sitcoms owe this show practically their entire existence.

Homer Simpson (Dan Castellaneta) works at a nuclear power plant despite demonstrating little evidence that he should be trusted near one. His long-suffering wife Marge (Julie Kavner) keeps their household functioning, while Bart (Nancy Cartwright), Lisa (Yeardley Smith), and Maggie navigate childhood in the delightfully dysfunctional town of Springfield. The Simpsons transforms an ordinary American family into a bottomless source of cultural satire, absurdity, and occasionally surprising tenderness.

Give me “Marge vs. the Monorail” and I'll happily defend the show's funniest writing for an hour. The town is talked into buying an obviously suspicious transportation system, and practically every exchange contains a joke worth remembering. Yet “Lisa's Substitute” affects me more deeply. Mr. Bergstrom recognizes Lisa's intelligence and loneliness, and his farewell note tells her something she's desperately needed to hear. That's the magic of the show's greatest years. It can make Homer an unbelievable idiot, then have him express genuine love for his daughter in a way that completely destroys me.

A man boards an airplane and becomes convinced something is destroying its wing. Another discovers that his childhood hometown might offer an escape from his unhappy adult life. Ordinary people encounter extraordinary situations in The Twilight Zone, Rod Serling's anthology series about fear, morality, loneliness, and humanity's talent for making terrible decisions.

I have an enormous soft spot for “Walking Distance.” Martin Sloan (Gig Young) returns to the town where he grew up and somehow encounters his younger self. What begins as a beautiful fantasy about recovering childhood becomes a painful lesson about the impossibility of living in the past. Serling understood that a science-fiction premise didn't need elaborate machinery to become unforgettable. Sometimes all it required was a lonely man desperately wanting one more afternoon of happiness. The show can be terrifying, funny, devastating, or cruelly ironic. Its imagination still embarrasses productions with a hundred times the resources.

There are practically no respectable people in the lawless mining settlement of Deadwood, and I wouldn't have them any other way. Saloon owner Al Swearengen (Ian McShane) controls much of the town through intimidation and cunning, while former marshal Seth Bullock (Timothy Olyphant) struggles to establish something resembling order. Deadwood watches a filthy collection of opportunists, fugitives, workers, and fortune seekers slowly become a community.

McShane is absolutely magnificent. Al can threaten somebody's life, deliver an outrageously profane monologue, and then demonstrate an unexpected concern for the town's survival. David Milch, who created the series, writes dialogue that sounds almost Shakespearean without diminishing the characters' vulgarity. I particularly love how Bullock and Al gradually recognize the necessity of cooperating despite despising each other's methods. There's something strangely beautiful about civilization emerging from such unpleasant circumstances. Nobody becomes a saint. They simply begin recognizing that other people's lives are connected to their own.

Logan Roy (Brian Cox) has built a media empire, and his four children have spent their lives competing for his approval and eventually his position. Succession introduces Kendall (Jeremy Strong), Shiv (Sarah Snook), Roman (Kieran Culkin), and Connor (Alan Ruck) as extraordinarily wealthy adults whose emotional development appears to have stopped somewhere around adolescence.

A phone call from an airplane abruptly forces the siblings into a situation that their money, influence, and practiced cruelty cannot control. They stumble over words, interrupt each other, and desperately try to communicate feelings they've spent their entire lives avoiding. It's breathtaking acting. I love how Jesse Armstrong's writing makes these people simultaneously hilarious and pathetic. Their boardroom victories are often elaborate attempts to win a father's affection. They possess practically everything imaginable, except the emotional security that might allow them to enjoy any of it. The ending was heartbreaking. This is probably one of the greatest shows of all time.

Don Draper (Jon Hamm) is an extraordinarily successful advertising executive whose polished appearance conceals a carefully constructed identity. At Sterling Cooper, he sells beautiful versions of American life while struggling to maintain anything resembling genuine happiness in his own. Mad Men also follows Peggy Olson (Elisabeth Moss), Joan Holloway (Christina Hendricks), and the colleagues navigating an industry transformed by social change during the 1960s.

I will never stop thinking about the Kodak Carousel pitch. Don uses photographs of his family to sell nostalgia, describing the emotional power of returning to a place where we felt loved. It's a wonderful presentation, made devastating by how badly he's damaging those very relationships. Matthew Weiner, who created the show, understood that Don's professional brilliance came partly from recognizing desires he could never satisfy himself. And Peggy's growth is equally extraordinary. She enters the agency as a secretary and slowly discovers how much of herself she's unwilling to surrender for approval. This show understands ambition, loneliness, and the exhausting business of pretending to be somebody else.

Before becoming Saul Goodman, Jimmy McGill (Bob Odenkirk) is a struggling lawyer desperate to establish himself while living under the judgment of his successful older brother Chuck (Michael McKean). His relationship with fellow attorney Kim Wexler (Rhea Seehorn) offers something dangerously close to stability. Better Call Saul follows Jimmy's transformation while demonstrating how much damage two intelligent, affectionate people can cause when they start enjoying their own dishonesty.

I genuinely think “Chicanery” contains some of the finest acting ever produced for television. Chuck's courtroom testimony deteriorates into an eruption of resentment, exposing how deeply his feelings toward Jimmy have shaped both their lives. Yet the tragedy belongs to both brothers. Jimmy wants Chuck's respect, but his methods keep justifying Chuck's worst assumptions. And Kim! Seehorn makes her gradual moral compromises almost physically painful to witness. Vince Gilligan and Peter Gould created a prequel that somehow made the destination more heartbreaking because we understood exactly what Jimmy was throwing away. I could watch these people negotiate a legal technicality for an entire hour.

Walter White (Bryan Cranston) is a high-school chemistry teacher diagnosed with lung cancer who begins manufacturing methamphetamine to provide financial security for his family. He partners with former student Jesse Pinkman (Aaron Paul), gradually building a criminal enterprise that places everybody around him in danger. Breaking Bad turns a desperate financial decision into one of television's most horrifying studies of pride.

What absolutely destroys me is watching Jesse continue searching for affection from a man who repeatedly manipulates him. Walt recognizes Jesse's need for approval and exploits it whenever convenient. Meanwhile, his wife Skyler (Anna Gunn) becomes trapped in circumstances that Walt keeps insisting are for the family's benefit. Cranston makes Walt's transformation frightening because each terrible decision arrives with an explanation that sounds reasonable to him. By the time he finally acknowledges how much he enjoyed the power, the damage is almost impossible to comprehend. I love this show for refusing to let intelligence excuse cruelty. Walt's greatest talent becomes the weapon he uses to ruin everything.

Four criminal masterminds. One of them was always going to be yours. Here is who comes for you, why they picked you out of everyone available, and what they want from the encounter.

Your nemesis does not want to beat you. He wants to know you completely, and he is patient enough to wait for it. The frightening part is how good the conversation is.

Your nemesis is not after money, territory or revenge. He is after a demonstration, and you are the person he has chosen to prove his point on.

Your nemesis respects you, which sounds flattering until you work out what it means. He chose you because nobody else was worth his time.

Your nemesis has no personal interest in you whatsoever, and that is precisely what makes him unsurvivable. You are not a rival. You are a stop on the way.

Tony Soprano (James Gandolfini) runs a New Jersey criminal organization while attending therapy for panic attacks. His psychiatrist Dr. Jennifer Melfi (Lorraine Bracco) attempts to understand a patient whose anxieties involve his mother, his marriage, his children, and the people he's ordered killed. The Sopranos places a deeply troubled family man inside a profession that rewards practically every one of his worst instincts.

The argument between Tony and Carmela (Edie Falco) in “Whitecaps” is devastating. Years of resentment come pouring out, and neither can escape the uncomfortable truths the other knows. They're married people who understand exactly where to hurt one another. Gandolfini and Falco make the confrontation feel almost indecent to witness. That's David Chase's extraordinary achievement. He never lets us forget Tony's brutality, even while making his personal struggles painfully recognizable. I can laugh at Tony complaining about his family, then feel revolted when he inflicts suffering upon somebody else. Few television characters have demanded so much sympathy while doing so little to deserve it.

Baltimore's drug trade, police department, shipping industry, political establishment, schools, and newspapers become the interconnected subjects of The Wire. Detective Jimmy McNulty (Dominic West) initially investigates a drug organization led by Avon Barksdale (Wood Harris), but the series gradually expands far beyond any single investigation. The institutions remain, even as the people attempting to change them come and go.

Season 4 is the reason I will defend this show forever. Four boys enter a school system where their futures are already being shaped by poverty, street violence, and decisions made by adults who rarely understand their lives. Watching Randy (Maestro Harrell) desperately seek help as his circumstances deteriorate is heartbreaking. And Bubbles (Andre Royo), a man struggling with addiction, eventually reaching a point where he can join his sister's family upstairs for dinner feels like an extraordinary victory. The police may celebrate an arrest, politicians may announce progress, but somebody's child still has to walk home through the same dangerous neighborhood. That's why The Wire belongs at number one.

#3374. iPadOS 27.3 adds new iPad setting I instantly turned on

iPadOS 27.3 is currently available in beta, and it introduces a new iPad setting for app windowing that I instantly turned on. Here are the details.

I use the iPad Pro as my primary computer, and for the most part have found Apple’s software changes in iPadOS 26 and 27 to be great upgrades.

But with the powerful new windowing capabilities, there have definitely been some quirks that need refining. One of them involves resizing windows with the traffic light controls in the top-left corner.

For example, in iPadOS 27 the controls move locations and even disappear depending on the size of the window. It can be pretty frustrating.

I need to just get better about learning keyboard shortcuts for window controls. But in the meantime, iPadOS 27.3 adds a new optional setting that I instantly turned on and have been loving.

Inside Settings ⇾ Multitasking & Gestures, if you have ‘Windowed Apps’ enabled you’ll see a new option below it: ‘Double-tap Top of Window to Zoom’

If you use your iPad mostly with touch input, or simply haven’t used keyboard shortcuts enough to remember them, this new setting is a great way to quickly resize windows.

When the setting is enabled, two taps (or a double-click with the trackpad) will zoom the window to take up the full screen. Then you can double-tap again to revert it to its previous size.

I generally keep my app windows in specific size setups, but regularly find myself wanting to go fullscreen temporarily. The new setting provides a convenient way to do that quickly without needing the traffic light controls or my keyboard, and is a welcome refinement to iPadOS windowing.

Will you enable this new iPadOS 27.3 setting? Why or why not? Let us know in the comments.

#3373. This Actively Exploited Chrome Vulnerability Is Putting Your Browser at Risk

If you've seen an uptick in security updates as of late, you're not alone. AI models have become very good at finding new security vulnerabilities throughout 2026. Researchers and hackers alike are increasingly relying on these models in their individual pursuits: Hackers want to find these flaws to exploit them, while researchers want to block hackers from doing so. Microsoft's latest Patch Tuesday update included more than 1,400 patches; meanwhile, Apple's latest security update fixed two iMessage flaws that let both bad actors and innocent parties alike access texts they shouldn't.

Whether you use a Mac or a PC, you probably browse the web with Chrome, or a Chromium-based browser. As it happens, Google's web browsing platform is the latest to receive an important security update—but it's far from the first important Chrome update of the year.

As reported by The Hacker News, Google released a new update for Chrome on Monday that patches nine security flaws. While all vulnerabilities are important to patch, one in particular is more serious than the rest: CVE-2026-125350, a use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component.

Use-after-free vulnerabilities happen when the system frees up a memory location, but a program tries to access it anyway. It's a glitch in programming, but it offers bad actors an opportunity to break into your system. At worst, it allows arbitrary code execution, or, in other words, gives hackers the ability to run their own code in the app or system.

That's bad enough on the surface, but, unfortunately, Google confirmed that CVE-2026-125350 has an active exploit in the wild. The company is keeping other details close to the vest, but it's dangerous nonetheless. At least someone, somewhere, has used this flaw against a target, which puts all Chrome users (as well as users of Chromium-based browsers) at risk.

What's more, this isn't Chrome's first active exploit of the year—this is its eighth. The company is playing catch-up with hackers looking to target users of its browser, which makes sense, seeing as Chrome is by far the world's most popular browser.

If you're using Chrome on your computer, you'll want to update it as soon as possible. Make sure you're running at least versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 on Mac or PC, or 157.0.8103.50 on Linux. To check, click the three dots in the top-right corner of your Chrome window, then go to More > Help > About Google Chrome.

Other Chromium-based browsers may not have the update yet, but they are affected by this flaw. If you use browsers like Microsoft Edge, Opera, or Brave, keep an eye on your updates to install any of the latest patches.

#3370. High-Protein Packaged Foods May Not Be As Healthy As They Look

Of the three major macronutrients—protein, carbs, and fat—protein has the best reputation, and it’s fairly well deserved. We need significant amounts of protein in our diet, and nothing particularly bad happens if we get too much. Dietary protein helps you build muscle, and if you’re trying to lose weight it helps stop you from losing too much muscle along with the fat. It also helps to make meals feel filling. Great! But.

Once the general public gets the idea that something is good for you, the companies that make packaged food start putting it in everything. Or, they make products where the good-for-you thing features prominently on the label, whether or not there is very much inside. So a lot of packaged food now boasts protein on the label. Here’s what you should ask yourself about those foods:

Take a close look here—sometimes a food will boast of a certain amount of protein per package but the package contains two or three servings. Other times, the protein per serving is correct, and we're supposed to be excited to have, say, 7 grams per serving. That's just not very much—and certainly not worth paying extra or choosing a less-delicious food just for those few added grams.

It’s good to know how much protein you need in your diet. If you’re not gaining or losing weight, and not doing very much exercise, a 150-pound person only needs about 54 grams of protein a day. (I've done the math for various body weights here.) If you’re working out a lot, or if you’re trying to gain or lose weight (yep, either way), that same 150-pound person will need more like 81 to 95 grams of protein per day. More is OK, but not necessary.

So if you’re trying to get 90 grams per day, 30 grams per meal is a reasonable amount to shoot for. Coincidentally, 30 grams is the amount of protein that tends to make a meal feel satisfying. You can do the math to figure out whether a protein-added product is going to be helpful in your day’s diet.

I think this is the most important question about protein-added foods. It’s not hard to get protein in a meal; meats, dairy, tofu, beans, and grains all tend to supply plenty. So what is this protein-added thing you’re considering, and are you eating it instead of a traditional meal?

Here’s an example. If I’m heading straight from the gym to run some errands, and I need something to substitute for a meal—yeah, this isn’t great planning, but sometimes it happens—a protein bar with 20 grams of protein is a step in the right direction. Much better than a candy bar, anyway.

But then there are things like this "protein mix" trail mix: 7 grams of protein with 200 calories. A double serving would be 400 calories and only 14 grams of protein. Hardly a great choice if your goal is just to add to your protein intake for the day.

And then there are the chips that my kid, for a time, couldn't stop eating. He loves Doritos and such; on a whim, we bought him some protein chips (yes, these are a real thing). Are they better for him than the equivalent amount of Doritos? Arguably, sort of yes. But then he started arguing that since they have protein, he should be able to eat them in place of dinner. We nixed that, but admit it: Are you having that same argument with yourself, feeling better about a snack food because it contains extra protein? If so, the marketing is working—you’re feeling good about your supposedly healthy choices, even though you’re just eating a bag of chips.

#3368. VisionQuest's Lauren Morais Addresses The MCU's Potential Debut Of Villain Team After Finale

Lauren Morais, who brought Marvel's Lisa Molinari to life in VisionQuest, breaks down her future with the MCU after the finale of the Disney+ series.

WARNING: This interview contains MAJOR spoilers from VisionQuest season 1, episode 8, "Forever."The Marvel Cinematic Universe continues a key theme through one of its most beloved trilogies.

While WandaVision may have begun as one of the many new shows to debut in the MCU timeline after the launch of Disney+, the Elizabeth Olsen and Paul Bettany-starring adventure became the start of a popular era in the franchise. Not only did it lead to the Agatha All Along spinoff, but also one final project that brought everything full circle.

As viewers got to see VisionQuest, which picked up on the events of the 2021 series, bring the long-time hero back, it also served as a massive payoff for the Maximoff twins, with Tommy's story being properly explored. While his brother was off with Agatha Harkness, the Phase 6 drama showed how his life became a bit different, once his soul was placed in Thomas Shepherd.

I was honored to speak with Lauren Morais, who became one of the latest additions to the MCU franchise, as she plays Marvel's Lisa Molinari, a player from the comics who has gone from villain to hero throughout her time in the lore. Throughout the interview, the Welsh star opened up about bringing Lisa's history to life in live-action, and what may be in store for the character after the finale.

As she landed the role of Lisa, Morais broke down her audition process, which, similar to a lot of other Marvel projects, was kept heavily under wraps. The actress also opened up about the kind of research she did once boarding the show.

Lauren Morais: Well, when I first auditioned, I had no idea who she was. It was just a fake name, fake everything, so I had no idea it was Lisa until my last audition, which [was] my third or fourth audition, so that was fun! Then I read the comics, and I dove into her, and I thought she was such a complicated but such a strong woman, which [is the type of] characters that I love to play. But I really loved the aspect of her being an artist and questioning superheroes, and becoming a villain with the Young Masters, itself. I thought it was a real treat to be able to play this character.
